A specialty coffee guide, from first principles

The Physics of Coffee

A cup of coffee looks simple: hot water, ground beans, time. Underneath, it is a coupled problem in diffusion, fluid mechanics and thermodynamics — whether the water falls by gravity through a paper filter or is driven at 9 bar (131 psi) through a puck. Once you see the equations, you can taste them.

Coffee brewing is
applied physics.

One small system, four physical processes: flow, diffusion, heat and chemistry. This guide takes them in order: filter brewing first, then espresso, then pour over, then the science behind it all.

About this guide: how it is organised, measurements, and a note on honesty

Part 1 covers filter brewing, water moving by gravity through a bed of grounds. Part 2 covers espresso (the same processes, driven under pressure) and the steamed-milk science behind latte art. Part 3 covers pour over, how the dripper's own shape sets the geometry those processes run inside. Part 4 covers the science behind it all, the disciplines, the people, the published research, and how to test the claims yourself.

In a dripper, a fluid moves through a complex, porous medium, carrying dissolved material with it, while temperature quietly rewrites every rate in the problem. The system fits on a kitchen scale, the experiment takes three minutes, and you can drink the result.

This guide treats brewing as a sequence of well-defined physical processes, each with its own governing equation. Water must first flow through a porous bed of grounds. Dissolved compounds must diffuse out of each particle into that water. Heat sets the speed of every step, and the water's own chemistry decides what it can carry. Master those four ideas (flow, diffusion, heat, chemistry) and every recipe variable you have ever argued about, from grind size to the bloom, becomes a knob on a machine you finally understand. Espresso, in Part 2, is the same system with a pump attached. And the brewer itself, in Part 3, is the boundary condition: its shape decides the bed the water must cross, where it may drain, and how much of the flow you control versus how much the hardware does. Part 4 then steps back and asks where all of this knowledge comes from, and how much of it you should believe.

Every chapter below is a dropdown, and every dropdown starts closed. Nothing opens on its own, click or tap a chapter title to open it, and click it again to close it. Charts, diagrams, tables and worked details are folded inside each one, so you open only what you need and leave the rest shut. Each equation comes with a legend defining every symbol (its units and its typical value) and a worked example you can follow step by step with your own numbers.

Measurements, in both systems. Every measurement in this guide is given twice, metric first, imperial in parentheses: temperatures in °C (°F), masses in grams (ounces), water in grams (ounces and fluid ounces), lengths in µm, mm and cm (inches and feet), and pressures in bar and pascals (psi). Percentages, ratios, seconds and kelvin need no conversion, they are the same in both systems. Chart axes are plotted in metric, with the imperial equivalents given in the labels and notes beside them.

A note on honesty: where this guide shows a curve, it is either a measurement framework the coffee community actually uses, or a physical model with its assumptions stated next to it. Physics you can check beats folklore you cannot.

Part 1 · Introduction

Filter

Gravity does the work. Water pooled above a bed of grounds percolates down through it (through a paper, cloth or metal filter) driven only by its own weight. Chapters 1–8 cover the processes that decide the cup: the bean, diffusion, measurement, grind, flow, heat, water and gas. Chapter 1 covers processing in one section of its own, the five ways a cherry becomes a green bean (washed, natural, honey, aerobic and anaerobic) compared side by side.

How these eight chapters join into one pipeline, feedbacks included, is drawn in How everything fits together (Figures 2–5).

This drawer is Part 1's introduction, Chapters 1–8 follow below as their own dropdowns.

If you brew immersion (French press, cupping, a steeped AeroPress): start with Diffusion (Chapter 2), Heat (Chapter 6) and the cupping protocol (Chapter 21). The flow chapters assume water moving through a bed, which immersion never does; diffusion, temperature and tasting carry over unchanged.

Gravitydriving force, a pressure drop of only a few centimetres of water above the bed
~600 µm (0.024 in)typical main particle size for filter grinds, diffusion time matched to a brew of minutes
1.15–1.45%filter strength (TDS) in the preferred window, at the same 18–22% extraction as espresso

Chapter 1 · The bean

Before water, there was fire.

What you will learn
  • Explain what roasting changes inside the bean: porosity, solubility, density and trapped CO2.
  • Follow the Maillard reactions and caramelisation from green bean to first crack, and say what each stage adds to the cup.
  • Compare the five processing methods (washed, natural, honey, aerobic and anaerobic) by what stays on the seed and whether air can reach it.
  • Read a processing claim critically: which numbers are measured, and which are marketing.

Every extraction problem starts as a materials problem. A green coffee bean is a dense, hard seed, mostly cellulose cell walls packed with proteins, sugars, lipids, chlorogenic acids and caffeine, at about 10–12% moisture. Brewed as-is it would give up almost nothing: the structure is too tight, the chemistry too raw. Roasting is the violent edit that makes brewing possible, and it is physics and chemistry at once.

As the bean's internal temperature climbs past 100 °C (212 °F), its water turns to steam and pressure builds inside the cellular structure; at that stage it is drying and pressure, not yet browning. The browning starts higher up: the Maillard reactions between sugars and amino acids begin around 140–150 °C (284–302 °F), building the brown melanoidin pigments and hundreds of aromatic compounds, and sucrose caramelisation begins around 160–170 °C (320–338 °F). Chlorogenic acids break down as the roast deepens: some hydrolysing to quinic and caffeic acids, a small share forming bitter chlorogenic lactones (the main lactone, 3-CQL, peaks at about 230 mg per 100 g at light-medium roast and declines at darker roasts, roughly 2–4% of the green bean's total chlorogenic acid mass of 6–10%; Farah et al. 2005), and more, at darker roasts, forming bitter phenylindanes, which shape acidity and, increasingly, bitterness. Around 196–205 °C (385–401 °F) the steam and CO2 pressure wins outright: the bean audibly fractures, first crack, expands, and its interior becomes a porous, brittle sponge shot through with gas.

12–20%of the bean's mass is lost in roasting, water vapour and CO2 driven off by heat
196–205 °C (385–401 °F)first crack: internal steam and gas pressure fracture the bean open
800+volatile aromatic compounds identified in roasted coffee, the payload extraction must deliver

Three consequences of roasting run through everything that follows. First, porosity: the fractured cell structure is what lets water in and solubles out, roast degree literally sets the diffusion geometry of Chapter 2. Second, brittleness: a roasted bean shatters instead of crushing, which is why grinding produces the jagged size distribution of Chapter 4 rather than uniform grains. Third, gas: a fresh bean is loaded with CO2 that will spend the whole brew trying to escape, the subject of Chapter 8, and of espresso's crema in Chapter 11.

What roasting changes, physically
  • Density falls. Mass leaves as gas while volume grows by roughly half to double (50–100%), a roasted bean is a foam of its former self, which is why it floats and grinds light.
  • Porosity rises. Fractured cell walls open pathways tens of micrometres wide. Water can finally reach the interior; diffusion distances shrink.
  • Solubility is created. Maillard products and caramelised sugars are far more water-soluble than their raw precursors. Roasting manufactures much of the ~30% of the bean that can dissolve at all.
  • Gas is loaded. CO2 generated by the reactions stays trapped in the pore network, pressurising the bean, a reservoir that degasses over days to weeks (Chapter 8).
  • The clock starts. The same aromatics that make coffee smell extraordinary are volatile and oxidise readily. Roasting starts a countdown that grinding accelerates enormously, surface area again.

Visual · The roast spectrum: what changes from light to dark

One bean, taken further. Every step darker trades the raw materials of acidity for the products of deeper browning — and makes the bean physically easier to extract.

Schematic, roast is a continuum and “light / medium / dark” are loose labels, but the directions are consistent: darker means more porous, less dense, more soluble, less acidic, more bitter. Practical consequence: a dark roast usually wants a slightly coarser grind or cooler water than a light roast of the same coffee, because its extraction runs ahead of the clock, and a light roast's stubbornness is why it so often tastes sour when under-extracted.

Before the roast: origin, variety and processing
  • Origin is chemistry before it is geography. Altitude, soil and climate set the green bean's density and its stock of sugars, acids and lipids. High-grown beans are typically denser, harder, slower to take heat in the roaster, and often slower to give up their solubles in the brewer.
  • Variety changes the raw recipe. Arabica averages more lipids (~15% vs ~10%) and sugars and about half the caffeine of robusta (the ranges overlap: 0.9–1.5% vs 1.2–2.4%), and robusta usually, though not invariably, carries more chlorogenic acids, more bitterness, and, under pressure, more of the compounds that stabilise crema (Chapter 11). Varieties within arabica differ in bean size and density, which is part of why one coffee grinds differently from another at the same setting.
  • Processing rewrites the surface. Washed coffees have their fruit removed before drying, a cleaner, brighter starting chemistry. Natural (dry) processing ferments sugars in contact with the seed, adding fruity, winey compounds the water will later extract. Honey processes sit between, aerobic fermentation is the open-tank baseline inside the washed method, and anaerobic processing seals the tank. The full comparison is the next section of this chapter, “Processing: how the cherry becomes a green bean”. None of this changes the physics of Chapters 2–8; it changes what the physics has to work with.
  • Density is the thread. Origin, variety and roast all express themselves partly through one physical variable (how dense and porous the particle is) which feeds straight into diffusion distance, fracture behaviour and degassing rate. When a new coffee behaves strangely, density is a good first suspect.

Processing: how the cherry becomes a green bean

Before any roasting, the seed has to come out of the cherry, and how that is done sets the chemistry the roast and the brew will work with. There are five ways worth comparing, and this section gives each of them the same space and the same structure: what happens step by step, the physics and chemistry underneath, the flavour it tends to produce, and where it can go wrong. Three of them (washed, natural and honey) are defined by what stays on the seed while it dries. The other two (aerobic and anaerobic) are defined by the air around a fermentation: open to the air, or sealed away from it. The two families overlap in practice: an anaerobic coffee still has to be dried afterwards, usually as a natural or a washed coffee, and the fermentation inside a classic washed coffee is an aerobic one. The numbers come from the sources in References [21] to [33]; where two sources give different figures, the text says so and names both.

Five ways from cherry to green bean (Diagram)

The five methods side by side: what stays on the seed, whether air can reach it, and how long the defining step takes. Every method ends the same way, dried to about 10 to 12 percent moisture and hulled.

Schematic summary of the five subsections below; the times are the ranges those subsections cite, and the full comparison, with water use and cup profile, is in the table at the end of this section.

Washed

Washed: what happens, step by step
  1. Pick and depulp, fast. Ripe cherries are picked, and within 24 hours of harvest a machine (a depulper) squeezes the seeds out of the skin and pulp. Speed matters: left in the fruit, the cherry starts fermenting on its own terms.
  2. Ferment the mucilage loose. The seeds come out coated in mucilage, a sticky, sugary layer that water alone will not shift. They go into a tank, dry or under water, and microbes digest that layer until the parchment (the papery shell around the seed) feels gritty rather than slimy. The Codex code of practice gives 12 to 36 hours; a 2016 review gives 12 to 48 hours; a 2023 review gives 6 to 72 hours depending on climate (References [28] to [30]).
  3. Wash. The loosened mucilage is rinsed away in clean water, in channels or tanks, until the parchment is clean.
  4. Optional soak. Some producers hold the washed coffee in clean water before drying: about 12 hours in Kenya, overnight and rarely up to 48 hours elsewhere. Kenya's double fermentation is a version of this: a second, shorter tank after the first wash, typically 12 to 24 hours.
  5. Dry. The wet parchment dries on patios or raised beds for 7 to 15 days, or mechanically for 18 to 36 hours, down to 10 to 12 percent moisture. Then it rests, and the parchment is hulled off before export.

The step order in this subsection follows Cafe Imports' Processing 101 [31] and Coffearium's washed-process entry [26].

Washed: the physics and chemistry

Water does three jobs here: it carries the fruit away, it is the medium the microbes live in, and it is what finally leaves during drying. The fermentation itself is a digestion, not a soak: microbes secrete enzymes that break the mucilage's pectin chains into soluble pieces the wash water can carry off. The microbes arrive in a set order. Yeasts work first, then lactic acid bacteria, and acetic acid bacteria come late, once alcohol and air are both available. As they work, the tank's pH falls from about 6.0 to 6.5 at the start to about 4.0, and that falling pH is the producer's clock: it tracks the acids being made, and it tells them the mucilage is nearly gone (Particular Coffee's fermentation-science guide [32] is the source for this sequence and pH fall).

Because the fruit is removed before drying, very little sugar stays in contact with the seed, and the contact lasts hours rather than weeks. Some acids and alcohols still diffuse a short way into the seed, by the same diffusion Chapter 2 describes, but the dose is small. Drying is then a simple moisture problem: water leaves the parchment until the seed sits at 10 to 12 percent moisture, stable for storage. The method's real physical cost is water. A conventional washed mill uses about 40 litres of water per kilogram of dry parchment (about 10.6 US gallons per 2.2 lb), a figure from Cenicafé, the Colombian coffee research centre. A DESLIM mechanical demucilager, which scrapes the mucilage off by friction instead of fermenting and rinsing it away, brings that under 1 litre per kilogram (under 0.26 US gallons per 2.2 lb).

Washed: flavour, risks and limits

In the cup: clean and bright, with clear acidity and the coffee's own origin character standing in front, because so little fermentation flavour is added on top. Washed is the reference process the others are usually described against.

  • Over-fermentation is the named failure. Leave the tank too long and the late acetic bacteria take over: the coffee picks up sour, vinegary notes that no washing removes.
  • Under-fermentation leaves a mess. Mucilage that survives the wash dries patchily on the parchment and can ferment again, unevenly, on the drying bed.
  • Water is the limit. The conventional process needs a lot of clean water and produces a lot of sugary wastewater, which is why mechanical demucilagers and water recycling matter where water is scarce.
  • Weather still matters at the end. Sun drying takes 7 to 15 days, and rain on wet parchment slows it and invites mould, the same drying risk every method shares.

Natural (dry)

Natural: what happens, step by step
  1. Pick ripe cherries, and change nothing. The whole cherry, skin, pulp, mucilage and seed together, goes straight to drying. There is no depulper and no tank.
  2. Spread thin. The cherries are spread on raised beds or patios in a layer 3 to 5 cm thick (1.2 to 2 in), thin enough for air to reach every fruit.
  3. Turn, often. In the first week the layer is turned 6 to 12 times a day, so every cherry spends time on the surface and none sits in its own moisture long enough to rot.
  4. Dry for weeks. The fruit dries intact for 15 to 30 days (up to 30 days on average, weather permitting), until the seed inside reaches about 11 percent moisture and the cherry has become a hard, dark pod.
  5. Rest, then hull. A clean natural typically dries in 18 to 24 days and goes into rest with the pulp at about pH 4.0 to 4.3. After resting, a huller strips the whole dried fruit off the seed in one go.

Natural: the physics and chemistry

A natural is a fermentation that happens inside a drying fruit. As long as the pulp holds sugars and moisture, the microbes living on and in the cherry keep working, and their acids and alcohols sit pressed against the seed for the whole drying period. Diffusion does the rest, slowly: compounds formed in the pulp migrate inward, down their concentration gradients, for days to weeks instead of the washed tank's hours. That long, wet contact is the whole chemical story of the method.

Drying is what ends it. The fermentation stops when the seed reaches about 11 percent moisture, because below that there is too little available water for microbes to live on. So the two processes, drying and fermenting, race each other inside the same fruit: dry fast and the fermentation is cut short; dry slowly, in thick layers or humid air, and it runs long. This is why the method needs dry weather. Rain does double damage: it re-wets fruit that was part-dried, restarting the microbes, and it washes sugars out of the pulp, taking potential flavour with it. Turning the layer is the producer's control on all of this: it evens out moisture and temperature through the bed of cherries and keeps any one fruit from sitting wet and airless at the bottom. The moisture gradient inside each cherry points outward the whole time, skin driest, seed last to dry, which is why the seed's moisture, not the fruit's appearance, is the number producers check.

Natural: flavour, risks and limits

In the cup: bold and fruity, often winey or boozy, with a heavy, syrupy body and a softer, rounder acidity than a washed coffee. The pulp's sugars and the long fermentation leave more of their products in the seed, and the cup shows it. Naturals also divide tasters more than washed coffees do: the same intensity that reads as ripe fruit at its best reads as ferment at its worst, sometimes within one lot.

  • Mould is the standing risk. Weeks of slow drying in a sugary fruit is an open invitation; the turning schedule and the thin layer exist to refuse it.
  • Uneven drying, uneven coffee. Cherries picked at mixed ripeness, or a layer turned too rarely, dry at different rates and ferment by different amounts, so one lot can taste ripe and over-fermented at once.
  • The weather sets the limits. The method belongs to dry harvest seasons. In a wet climate the fruit cannot dry fast enough, and the same process that builds fruit flavour builds rot instead.
  • It is slow and land-hungry. Fifteen to thirty days on beds, turned by hand, ties up drying space far longer than a washed lot does.

Honey (pulped natural)

Honey: what happens, step by step
  1. Pulp the cherry. As in the washed method, a depulper removes the skin and pulp soon after picking. The name has nothing to do with bees: the sticky mucilage left on the seed looks and feels like honey.
  2. Keep some or all of the mucilage. Instead of fermenting and washing it off, the producer leaves the mucilage wholly or partly on the parchment. How much stays is the method's main dial.
  3. Skip the tank and the wash. There is no fermentation tank and no washing step. The sticky, sugar-coated parchment goes straight to the drying beds.
  4. Dry with the coating on. The mucilage dries onto the parchment over 8 to 30 days overall (the 2023 review gives 12 to 30 days, Reference [29]; the 2016 review's yellow grade below dries in about 8 days, which widens the full range), the sugar layer darkening as it dries, which is where the colour names below come from.
  5. Rest and hull as usual. Once the seed reaches storage moisture, the parchment, with its dried mucilage, is hulled off.

The method began in Brazil in the 1990s under the name pulped natural: a way to get some of the natural process's sweetness while using far less water than a washed coffee and drying faster than a whole cherry can.

Honey: the physics and chemistry

The mucilage is a sugar-rich gel, and leaving it on changes the drying physics. The sticky layer holds moisture against the parchment, so the seed dries more slowly than a washed coffee's, and while it stays moist its sugars ferment gently, in the open air, on the seed's surface. More mucilage means more sugar in contact with the seed, a slower dry, and more fermentation products available to diffuse inward. Less mucilage behaves more like a washed coffee. It is a dial, not a switch, and producers name settings of the dial by colour: white, yellow, red and black, in order of how much mucilage is left and how dark it dries.

Those colour grades are producer conventions with no standard behind them (Coffearium's honey-process entry [27]), and the two reviews used here disagree, so treat any single figure with care. A 2016 review gives yellow honey about 25 percent of the mucilage kept, red about 50 percent, and black usually fully covered, drying in about 8 days (yellow), about 12 days (red) and about 30 days (black) (Reference [30]). A 2023 review instead gives a range of 20 percent to 80 percent of the pulp material left on the seed across the grades (Reference [29]). The honest summary is the direction, not the decimals: more mucilage kept means a darker grade name, a slower dry, and a sweeter, heavier cup, and one farm's red is not necessarily another farm's red.

Honey: flavour, risks and limits

In the cup: between washed and natural, as the method sits between them in construction: sweet and rounded, with more body than a washed coffee and less of the natural's winey intensity. Turning the mucilage dial up moves the cup toward the natural end: sweeter, heavier, and slower to dry. Because the coating ferments gently in the open air rather than in a tank, the fruit notes stay soft rather than winey, closer to dried fruit and brown sugar than to the natural's punch.

  • The fault risk rises with the dial. More mucilage means a stickier, wetter layer that dries slowly and unevenly, and a greater chance of mould or uncontrolled fermentation on the bed.
  • Sticky coffee is hard to handle. Mucilage-coated parchment clumps together, so the beds need frequent turning to keep air moving and stop the layer matting into a solid sheet.
  • The names do not travel. Because the colour grades have no standard, a bag labelled red honey tells you the producer's intention, not a measured amount of mucilage; the reviews above cannot even agree on the percentages.
  • Water saved, time spent. Skipping the wash saves the washed method's water, but drying takes 8 to 30 days, closer to a natural's calendar than a washed coffee's.

Aerobic fermentation (the baseline)

Aerobic: what happens, step by step
  1. Pulp the cherries. Aerobic fermentation is the fermentation step inside the classic washed process: depulped, mucilage-coated seeds go into a tank, exactly as in the washed subsection above.
  2. Leave the tank open. Aerobic means air is free to circulate over and through the fermenting coffee. There is no lid, no seal and no airlock; the surface of the mass breathes for the whole run.
  3. Ferment for 12 to 36 hours, typically. The microbes digest the mucilage, as in any washed fermentation, and the run ends when the parchment feels gritty and the coffee is washed.
  4. Wash and dry as washed. From the tank the coffee follows the washed path: rinse, optional soak, then dry to 10 to 12 percent moisture.

It earns its own subsection because it is the baseline every sealed-tank claim is measured against. When a study compares anaerobic with ordinary fermentation, this open tank is the ordinary fermentation, and the anaerobic subsection below only makes sense next to it.

Aerobic: the physics and chemistry, and the anaerobic contrast

Temperature sets the clock, because it sets the microbes' working speed. The same fermentation takes roughly 24 to 36 hours at 20 °C (68 °F), about 12 hours at 30 °C (86 °F), and 48 to 72 hours at 10 to 15 °C (50 to 59 °F): cool highland nights can stretch a one-day ferment into three. With air freely available, yeasts and acetic acid bacteria dominate the community (acetic acid bacteria alone were 20 to 57 percent of the bacterial community in the open tanks of one trial, Reference [21]). The oxygen is the reason for the second group: acetic acid bacteria use it to turn the yeasts' ethanol into acetic acid, so an open tank steadily makes vinegar's acid alongside the fruit's own citric and malic acids. Those three, acetic, citric and malic, are the main acids of a clean aerobic ferment. Producers watch the pH: 3.8 to 4.5 is the target window for a clean ferment, and below 3.5 the tank has gone too far, with vinegary off-flavours to show for it.

Aerobic against anaerobic, in one place:

  • Dominant organisms: yeasts plus acetic acid bacteria (aerobic) against yeasts plus lactic acid bacteria (anaerobic).
  • Main acids: acetic, citric and malic (aerobic) against lactic above all (anaerobic).
  • Esters: the fruity-smelling compounds build up far more in the sealed tank, where their alcohol ingredients are not being burned off into acetic acid.
  • Typical duration: 12 to 36 hours (aerobic) against 24 to 192 hours (anaerobic).
  • Defect risk: acetic over-fermentation, the vinegar direction (aerobic), against butyric and propionic over-fermentation, the rancid direction (anaerobic).

Aerobic: flavour, risks and limits

In the cup: bright, clean and defined acidity, the classic washed profile. The open tank's job is mostly subtractive: it removes the mucilage and adds only a light fermentation signature of its own. That lightness is the point of the baseline: whatever a sealed tank adds beyond it can be credited to the seal, because everything else, the fruit, the water and the drying, can be held the same.

  • Over-fermentation tastes of vinegar. Given time and air, the acetic bacteria keep converting ethanol to acetic acid; past pH 3.5 the cup turns sharp and vinegary, the defect this method is known by.
  • The open tank takes the weather in. A cold night can double the run; a hot afternoon can halve it. The producer is managing a clock they do not fully control, which is the practical limit of the method.
  • The surface and the depths differ. The top of the mass breathes while the bottom runs short of air, so an open tank is really aerobic at the top and partway anaerobic below; a 2025 Colombian study calls the set-up semi-anaerobic for exactly this reason (Reference [21]).
  • It is short, and that caps its effect. Twelve to thirty-six hours of contact can only move so much chemistry into the seed; producers wanting a stronger fermentation signature have to change the conditions, which is the sealed tank's whole pitch.

Anaerobic (sealed tank, SIAF and carbonic maceration)

Anaerobic: what happens, step by step
  1. Fill a sealable vessel. Whole cherries or pulped coffee go into a tank or bag, dry or with water. Trial vessels run from 20-litre buckets (5.3 US gallons) to 200-litre tanks (53 US gallons): small lots, not silos.
  2. Seal the air out. In SIAF (self-induced anaerobic fermentation) the lid closes: the microbes use up the oxygen inside, CO2 builds up in its place, and an airlock lets CO2 out while stopping air coming in. Two machine-set variants: vacuum bags with the air drawn out, and vacuum plus pure CO2 pumped in, called carbonic maceration, a name borrowed from winemaking.
  3. Ferment long. Trial runs lasted 24 to 192 hours, far longer than the open tank's 12 to 36. Whole cherries bring more fuel: their juice started one trial at 23.65 °Brix against 7.33 °Brix for pulped coffee.
  4. Open, then dry as usual. The coffee is dried like any other, to about 11 to 12 percent moisture, which is why bags are named for both steps: anaerobic natural, anaerobic washed.

Sealed-tank fermentation was first applied to coffee by da Mota et al. and Martins et al., both in 2020 (References [22] and [38]). In practice the tank is low in oxygen, not perfectly free of it: no fresh air arrives to replace what the microbes use.

Anaerobic: the physics and chemistry inside the seal

Two pieces of gas physics run the tank. The CO2 the microbes release has nowhere to go: by the ideal gas law (PV = nRT; worked in the appendix note after the comparison table), it would add about 0.61 bar (8.8 psi) in a sealed headspace, which is why the airlock bubbles and sealed bags swell. Some CO2 also dissolves and forms carbonic acid, a small extra push on pH. What the microbes make reaches the seed by diffusion (Chapter 2), one reason these runs last days.

  • pH falls, steadily. From 5.8 to 4.4 in 72 hours in one Brazilian tank of pulped coffee (da Silva Vale et al. 2023 [39]); from about 5.1 to as low as 3.70 in 72 hours in another trial (Rocha et al. 2024 [24]).
  • Lactic acid is the main acid formed. After 180 hours of SIAF, dried natural coffee held 13.20 g/kg (about 0.21 oz per lb), from none at the start (Jimenez et al. 2023 [41]). Ethanol builds alongside: at 72 hours, about six times more than at 24 hours.
  • The sealed mass stays cooler. In a room at 20 °C (68 °F), sealed tanks warmed only 0.5 to 3.7 °C (0.9 to 6.7 °F), against 5.1 to 17.6 °C (9.2 to 31.7 °F) for open tanks (Reference [21]): little oxygen means little heat-making aerobic activity. (The rises are ΔT above ambient: the room was at 20 ± 1 °C (Peñuela-Martínez et al., Foods 2025, §3.1/Fig. 1).)
  • The tank is not uniform. Lactic acid at 72 hours reached 5.06, 4.70 and 2.18 g/L in the bottom, middle and top layers of one tall tank, so producers stir to even it out.
  • The microbes change shifts. Yeasts (Saccharomyces, Pichia, Issatchenkia, Torulaspora) work first; then lactic acid bacteria take over, Weissella dominant, then Leuconostoc and Lactiplantibacillus. Acetic acid bacteria, which need oxygen, were far more common in open tanks (Reference [21]).

Anaerobic: flavour, risks and limits

In the cup: tropical fruit and winey, fermented notes. A Zurich study (ZHAW, a 2023 conference presentation, not peer-reviewed) found ethyl 3-methylbutanoate, a fruity ester, 125 times more abundant in natural carbonic macerated coffee than in washed. Scores can be high: all the SIAF coffees in one trial scored 84 or more (da Silva Vale et al. 2023 [39]), and the best, 87.50 (whole cherries, no water, 96 hours), beat 83.30 natural and 83.60 pulped controls (Silva et al. 2024 [40]); in Peru, one Catimor scored 87.38 anaerobic against 85.75 natural, 84.00 washed, 82.88 honey (per Coffearium's synthesis [25], reported rather than verified). A 2025 meta-analysis of 22 studies (Soares et al. 2025 [42]) found fermentation raised SCA scores by 0.6 to 1.4 points on average; a 2026 metabolome study reports processing methods regulating flavour precursors in Arabica beans (Fu et al. 2026 [43]).

The counter-evidence: a 2025 Colombian trial found sealed versus open tanks did not significantly change sensory quality (Reference [21]), and the same meta-analysis [42] found fully anaerobic conditions scored 1.22 points lower than aerobic ones. Fermentation changes a coffee; it does not guarantee a higher score.

  • The seed is alive, and can die in the tank. The worst measured loss was in open tanks: embryo viability fell to 25% by 192 hours, while sealed tanks stayed above 80% to 120 hours (Peñuela-Martínez et al. 2025 [21]). In SIAF trials viability fell from 85–87.5% to 52.5–70% by 180 hours (Jimenez et al. 2023 [41]).
  • Unwelcome fungi gain ground with time. Mycotoxin-producing fungi became more common as fermentation went on, a cost of the same long runs that build the flavour.
  • Butyric acid is the named failure. An undesirable product of prolonged fermentation (propionic acid is its over-fermentation partner), though it was not detected in two Brazilian SIAF trials.

Five processes, side by side (Table)

Read the table as tendencies, not promises: the ranges overlap, coffees cross categories (an anaerobic coffee is usually also a natural or a washed coffee underneath, and a washed coffee's tank fermentation is the aerobic row), and method alone does not fix flavour. Variety, fruit, temperature and time move the result as much as the process name does.

Appendix note: the sealed-tank equations in brief

The three equations behind the anaerobic subsection, in brief, kept at section level so no single method carries more apparatus than the others. Symbols: P pressure (Pa), V volume (m3), n amount of gas (mol), R the gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K), T absolute temperature (K).

  • Ideal gas law, PV = nRT. Worked example: 0.5 mol of CO2 released into a rigid 20-litre (5.3 US gallon) headspace at 293 K adds ΔP = nRT / V ≈ 60,900 Pa ≈ 0.61 bar (8.8 psi). Real set-ups refuse to hold that pressure: the airlock bubbles the CO2 away as fast as it forms, and a sealed bag swells. The airlock is the pressure relief that lets the seal survive its own fermentation.
  • Carbonic acid equilibrium, CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−. Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, a small extra push on pH in the same direction as the fermentation acids. pH is logarithmic: the fall from 5.8 to 4.4 in one Brazilian tank means [H+] rose from 1.6 × 10−6 to 4.0 × 10−5 mol/L, about 25 times as many hydrogen ions, most of them from the microbes' own acids, lactic acid above all.
  • Microbial growth, N(t) = N0 · 2t/g. Early on, the population doubles every doubling time g: at an illustrative g of 1 hour, ten hours gives 210 = 1,024 times the starting population, before sugar runs down and acid levels growth off. A general rule of thumb for microbes, not a coffee-specific rate.

Key takeaways
  • Roasting manufactures the material brewing works on: a porous, brittle, gas-loaded sponge in place of a dense seed.
  • Processing is decided before roasting: what dries on the seed, and the air around a fermentation, set the starting chemistry.
  • The five methods overlap in time and flavour; a method name alone never guarantees a cup character.
  • First crack (196–205 °C / 385–401 °F) is a pressure event: steam and CO2 fracture the bean open.

Chapter 2 · The particle

Extraction is diffusion.

What you will learn
  • State the d² law and use it to compare extraction times for two particle sizes.
  • Place diffusion in the whole system using the pipeline and interaction diagrams in How everything fits together (Figures 3–4).
  • Explain the boundary layer, and why agitation speeds extraction without changing the particle.
  • Describe the order in which compound families leave the particle, and what that order tastes like.
  • Use the Péclet number to say whether flow or diffusion is doing the work in a given brew.

Grind a coffee bean and you shatter it into fragments of plant cell wall, each one a tiny sponge loaded with soluble material, acids, sugars, caffeine, melanoidins, aromatics. Hot water surrounding a fragment does not simply rinse this material off. Most of it is locked inside the particle, and it can only escape by random-walking its way out, molecule by molecule. That random walk is diffusion, and it obeys one of the most consequential scaling laws in all of brewing:

τ ≈ d² ∕ D τ (time for a particle to give up its solubles · d) particle diameter · D, diffusion coefficient

Legend: every symbol

  • τ (tau), characteristic extraction time: how long a particle needs to give up most of its solubles.Units: seconds (s) · Typical: ~1–2 s for 60 µm (0.0024 in) fines · ~144 s for a 600 µm (0.024 in) filter particle · ~8 min for a 1,100 µm (0.043 in) coarse chunk
  • d: particle diameter, the distance a molecule must random-walk to escape.Units: metres (m), usually quoted in micrometres (µm; 1 µm = 10−6 m) · Typical: 60 µm (0.0024 in) fines · ~200 µm (0.0079 in) espresso · ~600 µm (0.024 in) filter main population
  • D: the model's diffusion coefficient. Read it honestly: 2.5 × 10−9 m²/s is a lumped, fitted effective D, calibrated so the model's brew timescales land in the right range. It is not a measured diffusion coefficient inside the wet particle (the measured intraparticle value is far smaller, see the note under this panel).Units: m²/s · Typical: ~2.5 × 10−9 m²/s, fitted · large, heavy compounds diffuse more slowly than small ones

Worked example: a 600 µm (0.024 in) filter particle

  1. Convert the diameter to metres: d = 600 µm (0.024 in) = 6.0 × 10−4 m.
  2. Square it: d² = (6.0 × 10−4)² = 3.6 × 10−7 m².
  3. Divide by D = 2.5 × 10−9 m²/s: τ = 3.6 × 10−7 ∕ 2.5 × 10−9 = 144 s ≈ 2.4 minutes, neatly matched to a pour-over's contact time.
  4. Now the fines, d = 60 µm (0.0024 in): τ = (6.0 × 10−5)² ∕ 2.5 × 10−9 = 1.4 s. One tenth the size, one hundredth the time.

Try yours: pick your grind size for d, keep D = 2.5 × 10−9, and compare τ with your brew time. If τ is much longer than the brew, that particle size cannot finish extracting, no recipe tweak changes the square.

What the d² law leaves out, stated plainly. τ ≈ d²/D is order-of-magnitude scaling, not the exact solution. For diffusion out of a sphere, the long-time constant is τ1 = R² ∕ (π²D) = d² ∕ (4π²D) ≈ d² ∕ 39D, so the prefactor matters if you quote a number rather than a scaling. And the fitted D above is doing quiet work: the intraparticle diffusivity in Moroney et al. (2015) [5] is Ds = 0.1 × Dl ≈ 2.2 × 10−10 m²/s, which on the d² scaling would give a 600 µm particle τ ≈ 1,640 s (about 27 minutes), far longer than any brew. Real extraction is fast because it runs in two stages (Wang & Lim 2021 [34]): a quick surface wash-off from cells the grinder broke open, then slow diffusion out of intact cells. The single-τ model folds both stages into one fitted constant; it gets the timescales and the d² hierarchy right, and the mechanism only half right.

The time a particle needs to extract grows with the square of its size. Double the diameter and the particle needs four times as long. This single exponent explains an astonishing amount of coffee behaviour. It is why a fine powder surrenders everything in seconds while a coarse chunk is still holding most of its sugars when the brew ends. It is also why a mixed pile of particle sizes tends to extract unevenly at any single brew time: the small ones race ahead, the large ones lag, and the cup averages the two.

One law, three particles (Chart)

Modelled extraction of a single particle over time, for three particle diameters. Each curve uses τ ∝ d², normalised to a 250 µm (0.0098 in) particle with τ = 25 s, approaching the ~30% of bean mass that is soluble. Note the ceiling: 30% is the single-particle soluble share. The bed-level tools elsewhere in this guide (Home Lab Test 2, Chapter 10) use a lower, 24% practical ceiling, because a real bed never reaches every particle's full soluble share.

Model: extracted fraction = 30% × (1 − e−t/τ), the standard first-order approach to equilibrium for diffusion out of a particle. Real particles are irregular and their surfaces wash off faster than this, but the d² hierarchy between sizes is robust — it is the reason grind distribution, Chapter 4, matters as much as grind size.

There is a second transport process competing with diffusion: advection, the bulk flow of water carrying dissolved material away. Physicists compare the two with the Péclet number, high where flow dominates, low where diffusion rules. Inside a coffee particle, flow is essentially zero: diffusion is the only way out, and it is slow. Between particles, in the channels of the bed, flow dominates and sweeps the escaped solubles down into the cup. Brewing well means keeping these two regimes in balance, giving diffusion enough time, while advection keeps the water around each particle fresh enough that the concentration gradient, diffusion's engine, never flattens.

Pe = vL ∕ D The Péclet number, advection versus diffusion. Pe ≫ 1: flow carries the cargo. Pe ≪ 1: diffusion walks it. A brew contains both regimes at once, in different places.

Legend: every symbol

  • Pe: Péclet number, dimensionless.Typical: ≈ 6–70 in the pores between particles · ≈ 0 inside a particle, where there is no through-flow
  • v: local flow velocity of the water.Units: m/s · Typical: ~3 × 10−4 m/s percolating through the bed (Chapter 20) · effectively 0 inside a particle
  • L: the length scale of the region you are asking about.Units: m · Typical: ~50 µm (0.0020 in) for a pore between particles · ~300 µm (0.012 in) for a particle's radius
  • D: diffusion coefficient, the same D as the d² law above.Units: m²/s · Typical: ~2.5 × 10−9 m²/s

Worked example: one brew, two regimes

  1. In a pore: v = 3 × 10−4 m/s, L = 5 × 10−5 m, D = 2.5 × 10−9 m²/s. Pe = (3 × 10−4 × 5 × 10−5) ∕ 2.5 × 10−9 = 1.5 × 10−8 ∕ 2.5 × 10−9 = ≈ 6, advection wins: escaped solubles are swept away, which keeps the gradient at each particle's surface steep.
  2. Inside a particle: the pore network is dead-ended, so v ≈ 0 and Pe ≈ 0, pure diffusion, at the d² pace, no matter how hard you pour.
  3. The boundary between the two regimes is the particle's surface, which is exactly where agitation acts (below).

Reading it: pouring harder raises Pe in the bed but does nothing inside the particle. That asymmetry is the whole reason grind size (which shortens the diffusion leg) beats pouring tricks (which only speed the flow leg) when a brew under-extracts.

Why agitation works: the boundary layer, drawn (Diagram)

A particle sitting in still, already-concentrated water stops extracting: the gradient at its surface collapses. Swirling, stirring or pouring in pulses replaces that saturated boundary layer with fresher water and restarts the gradient. You are not "helping the water in", you are restoring the slope that diffusion climbs down.

The compounds leave in shifts (Chart)

Not everything diffuses at the same speed. Small, highly soluble molecules (salts and the bright organic acids) exit first; sugars follow; the large, heavy, bitter-leaning compounds arrive last. Modelled share of each class extracted, over a filter brew.

Model: first-order curves 100 × (1 − e−t/τ) with illustrative time constants, τ ≈ 20 s for salts & acids, τ ≈ 90 s for sugars, τ ≈ 220 s for heavy bitter compounds; the τ values are illustrative and are labelled as such wherever this chart is used. Read the picture as a cumulative-share model: each curve is that class's share of its own total, arriving on its own clock. One caveat the simple story misses: bitterness as a sensation is not last. In fraction measurements, in-cup bitterness is highest in the earliest, strongest fractions and falls as TDS falls (Batali et al. 2020 [37]). “Bitter last” applies to the slow bitter compounds (chlorogenic lactones, phenylindanes), not to bitterness itself; caffeine is bitter, and it is early. The ordering of the compound classes is the established part; it is why an under-extracted cup is dominated by the fast shift (sour, salty) and an over-extracted one by the slow shift, and why balance lives in the middle window of Chapter 3.

Key takeaways
  • Extraction time grows with the square of particle size: halve the particle, quarter the time.
  • Fines finish in seconds, coarse particles in minutes; every cup is a blend of clocks.
  • Salts and acids leave first, sugars next, heavy bitter compounds last: under-extraction is sour by construction.
  • Agitation works by thinning the saturated layer around each particle, not by pushing water inside it.

Chapter 3 · Measurement

Two numbers run the whole brew.

What you will learn
  • Define TDS and extraction yield, and compute one from the other with the beverage mass and dose.
  • Plot a brew on the brewing control chart and read off which axis is off.
  • Use the calculator and trend plotter to turn single brews into a pattern.
  • State what a refractometer cannot measure, and why TDS is not flavour.

Coffee becomes a measurable, repeatable process the moment you can quantify it, and it needs only two measurements. The first is strength: the total dissolved solids, or TDS, what fraction of the liquid in your cup is coffee rather than water, read off a refractometer from the way the liquid bends light. The second is extraction yield: what fraction of the dry bean's mass ended up dissolved in the cup. They are linked by simple bookkeeping:

Extraction yield = TDS × beverage mass ∕ dose All masses in grams, with ounces alongside. The beverage weighs a little less than the water you poured, the bed keeps roughly 2 g (0.07 oz) of water per gram (0.035 oz) of coffee: beverage mass ≈ brew water − 2 × dose.

Legend: every symbol

  • Extraction yield (EY): the share of the dry coffee's mass that dissolved into the cup.Units: % · Typical: target window 18–22% for both filter and espresso · below 18% trends sour, above 22% bitter
  • TDS: total dissolved solids: the strength of the beverage, read from a refractometer.Units: % (grams of coffee solids per 100 g / 3.5 oz of beverage — % is the same in both systems) · Typical: 1.15–1.45% filter · espresso 8–12% most commonly cited (7–12% wider range)
  • Beverage mass: the liquid that actually lands in the cup or server.Units: grams (g) / ounces (oz) · Typical: ~280 g (9.9 oz) from a 20 g (0.71 oz) / 320 g (11.3 oz) filter brew, after the bed retains ~2 g (0.07 oz) of water per gram of coffee
  • Dose: the dry coffee you started with.Units: grams (g) / ounces (oz) · Typical: 15–22 g (0.53–0.78 oz) for filter · 18–20 g (0.63–0.71 oz) for a double espresso

Worked example: the calculator's default brew

  1. Dose = 20 g (0.71 oz), ratio 1:16, so brew water = 20 × 16 = 320 g (11.3 oz · 10.8 fl oz).
  2. Beverage mass = 320 − (2.0 × 20) = 320 − 40 = 280 g (9.9 oz).
  3. Measured TDS = 1.32%, so dissolved coffee = 0.0132 × 280 = 3.70 g (0.13 oz).
  4. EY = 3.70 ∕ 20 = 0.185 = 18.5%.

Reading it: 18.5% sits inside the 18–22% window and 1.32% inside 1.15–1.45%, a balanced brew, the same result the calculator below gives for these inputs. Plug in your own TDS, beverage mass and dose in steps 3–4.

Plot every brew as one point (strength on one axis, extraction on the other) and you get the brewing control chart, the map this entire field navigates by. The rectangle in the middle descends from Lockhart's 1957 taste-panel work [44] at the Coffee Brewing Institute (centre ≈ 20% extraction, ≈ 1.25% TDS), and the chart built on it has been used since the 1950s; the 55 g/L ± 10% ratio is the Golden Cup brewing ratio: most people, most of the time, prefer 18–22% extraction at 1.15–1.45% TDS on the Version 3 chart (revised March 2019). The classic Golden Cup Standard (2018) used the same extraction range with a narrower 1.15–1.35% TDS. Below 18% the cup trends sour and thin, the fast-extracting acids arrived but the sugars never caught up. Above 22% it turns bitter and hollow, as slow, harsh compounds accumulate. The diagonal lines are brew ratios: pick a ratio and a strength, and the chart tells you the extraction you must have achieved.

The brewing control chart

Each diagonal is a brew ratio (water : coffee). The shaded rectangle is the commonly preferred window. The marker is your brew, set it with the calculator below.

Framework: the classic brewing control chart, with the Version 3 chart window (revised March 2019, “SCA Ideal”) of 18–22% extraction and 1.15–1.45% TDS; the classic Golden Cup Standard (2018) used the same extraction range with a narrower 1.15–1.35% TDS. Ratio lines assume beverage mass ≈ brew water − 2 × dose (liquid retained in the bed). The two fixed example dots: blue ≈ 1.04% TDS / 16.8% extraction, a typical under-extracted brew, sour and thin; tan ≈ 1.55% TDS / 23.5% extraction, a typical over-extracted brew, bitter and drying. The orange marker is your brew, set by the calculator below. (The chart's axes are the filter framework; espresso lives at 7–12% TDS (the wider range; 8–12% is the most commonly cited), far off the right-hand edge, and is judged here against the same 18–22% extraction window, which is the filter chart's window: for espresso it is a borrowed rule of thumb, not an SCA standard. In Espresso mode the marker therefore pins to the chart's right edge: its height still reads your extraction truthfully, while its strength sits off-chart.) A newer edition of the chart exists: in 2023, Guinard and colleagues at the UC Davis Coffee Center published a revision built on sensory and consumer testing [45]. This guide keeps the 2019 Version-3 chart as its framework, the version most refractometer software prints.

Find your brew: the calculator

Filter mode, ratio is brew water per gram of coffee; the bed keeps some of it, so the cup weighs less than you poured. Strength window: 1.15–1.45% TDS.

320 g (11.3 oz · 10.8 fl oz)brew water
280 g (9.9 oz)beverage in the cup
18.5%extraction yield

Plot your brews: see the trend

One brew is weather; a run of brews is climate. Type in the TDS and extraction yield of your recent brews (the calculator above turns a refractometer reading into the yield) and the plot joins them in brew order, oldest first, so drift becomes visible instead of anecdotal. The first three rows carry example values so you can see it working: replace them with your own. Nothing is saved, the plot lives only while this page is open, so copy the numbers you care about into the brew log in Next Steps.

Brew 1
Brew 2
Brew 3
Brew 4
Brew 5
Brew 6
Rows left empty are ignored: a brew plots only when both its TDS and its extraction yield are filled in.

The axes are the filter control chart's (0.9–1.7% TDS, 14–28% extraction), so espresso strengths (7–12% TDS) live far off the right-hand edge and are not plotted; for shots, the trend that matters is extraction against time, which the brew log captures. Read the line, not just the latest dot: a steady climb usually means one variable creeping (a grinder drifting finer as it warms, beans ageing, water cooling), and creep is fixed by finding the creep, not by chasing the last brew.

Notice what the chart does to recipe arguments. "This coffee tastes weak" is two different complaints wearing one coat: too little extraction, or too much water. The chart separates them, extraction is fixed by grind, time and temperature; strength is fixed mostly by ratio. Diagnose which axis you are off on before touching a single variable, and change one thing at a time. That is not a coffee rule. That is the scientific method.

Reading a refractometer honestly
  • Cool the sample. Refractive index drifts with temperature; a hot sample reads wrong. A spoonful cooled to room temperature takes seconds.
  • Filter the sample. Suspended fines scatter light and inflate the reading, the same fines from Chapter 4, now corrupting your measurement instead of your drawdown.
  • Zero on your brew water. The minerals in the water bend light too. Calibrate against the water you brewed with, not distilled water, or your TDS carries an offset into every calculation.
  • Trust the pair, not the point. One brew is weather; a week of points on the chart is climate. Log dose, ratio and TDS together — extraction yield computed from a forgotten dose is fiction.

Beyond the refractometer: measuring the flavour itself

TDS is a bulk number: it counts dissolved mass, not which compounds make it up. Two brews can share a TDS and an extraction yield and still taste different, different roast colour, different acid balance, same total. A 2026 result points at the instrument that may eventually sit next to the refractometer:

  • Peer-reviewedCyclic voltammetry reads the cup electrochemically. Bumbaugh and colleagues, with Christopher H. Hendon among the authors (Nature Communications, 2026, References [13]) showed that sweeping a voltage through a coffee sample and recording the current (a technique borrowed from analytical chemistry) separates strength from roast colour as two independent signals, with no sample preparation. The refractometer folds both into one refractive index; the voltammogram keeps them apart (doi:10.1038/s41467-026-71526-5).
  • What it means at the counter, today. Nothing to buy yet, this is a laboratory method, published in 2026. Its lesson for now is interpretive: when two brews plot on the same point of the control chart but taste different, that is not your palate failing. The chart's two numbers were never the whole description of the cup, they are the two cheapest coordinates of it, which is exactly why this guide navigates by them and tastes everything else.

Key takeaways
  • Two numbers run the brew: strength (TDS) and extraction yield; ratio moves one, grind and time move the other.
  • The 18–22% / 1.15–1.45% window is the 2019 Version-3 framework, a map for diagnosis, not a law of taste.
  • Extraction yield = TDS × beverage mass ÷ dose; the beverage weighs less than the water you poured.
  • One brew is weather; a run of logged brews is climate.

Home Lab · Interactive tools

Plug in your own numbers.

Every chapter so far has run on example numbers. These four tools run on yours, the tests a home brewer can actually perform with a scale, a thermometer, a refractometer, a water test kit and a milk thermometer. Type or slide, and the outputs update as you go, in metric and imperial, with a plain-language reading of what the numbers mean and the one thing to change next. Nothing is saved: the tools live only while this page is open. The fifth home test (plotting a run of brews to see the trend) lives with the Chapter 3 calculator (“Plot your brews”), and the Cheat Sheet gathers the target windows these tools judge against.

Test 1 · Measure your brew: dose, water, beverage, TDS

Weigh what you actually did, not what the recipe said. Dose and brew water before, the beverage in the cup after, and the TDS from a cooled, filtered refractometer sample (Chapter 3). The tool works out the ratio you really brewed at, the extraction yield, and how much water the bed kept, then reads the result the way the control chart would.

1 : 16.0actual brew ratio (water : coffee)
18.5%extraction yield
2.0 g per gwater the bed kept

The arithmetic is Chapter 3's: extraction yield = TDS × beverage mass ÷ dose. Strength is judged against 1.15–1.45% TDS for filter; if your TDS reads 3% or higher the tool assumes a shot and judges against the espresso window, 7–12%, flagging 3–7% as “check the reading”, since that range is neither typical filter nor typical espresso. The tool applies the 18–22% extraction window to both; that window is the filter chart's, borrowed for espresso as a rule of thumb, not an SCA espresso standard.

Test 2 · Predict a brew: grind, temperature, time

Before you brew, forecast it. Set the grind size, water temperature and contact time you are planning, and the guide's own models estimate the extraction and the flow, so you can feel, before wasting a dose, how much a finer grind or a hotter kettle actually buys.

~22%predicted extraction yield
× 1.0flow vs. the reference brew
~3:00drain-time index (not the contact time)

Model, the guide's own, stated in Chapters 2, 6 and 10: extraction approaches a 24% practical ceiling (the bed-level ceiling; Chapter 2's single-particle chart uses the 30% soluble share) as EY = 24% × (1 − e−t/τ), with the bed-level time constant τ = 75 s at 600 µm (0.024 in), scaling with the square of particle size, and temperature speeding the clock by Chapter 6's Arrhenius factor (×1.00 at 93 °C · 199 °F). Do not interchange the two τ values: this tool's 75 s is a bed-level effective τ; Chapter 2's 144 s at the same grind is a single-particle τ. They describe different things. The “estimated total brew time” readout is a drain-time index derived from flow, not the contact time; the forecast caps effective contact at the shorter of your set time and that index, and warns when the two disagree widely. Flow follows Darcy: permeability scales with particle size squared and water thins as it heats, both measured against a reference brew, 600 µm (0.024 in), 93 °C (199 °F), ≈ 3:00 total. These are planning estimates from a deliberately simple model, not measurements: channeling, agitation and your grinder's fines share will move a real brew off them, which is what Test 1 is for.

Test 3 · Read your water: the GH/KH drop kit & TDS meter

The home water test is three numbers. A drop kit (the aquarium GH/KH kits of Chapter 7) counts drops until the colour flips, each drop is one German degree, 17.8 mg/L as CaCO3. A TDS meter reads total dissolved solids directly. Enter all three and see each one against the SCA targets, with the fix for whichever is out.

71 mg/Lgeneral hardness (GH), as CaCO₃
36 mg/Lalkalinity (KH), as CaCO₃
150 mg/Ltotal dissolved solids

Targets (2009 SCAA standard, Chapter 7): total dissolved solids 150 mg/L (≈150 ppm), range 75–250; calcium hardness in the 17–85 mg/L range with 68 mg/L the named target, note that standard names calcium hardness, while a drop kit reads total hardness (calcium + magnesium), so a kit reading is an upper bound on the calcium part; alkalinity at or near 40 mg/L. A different, newer document, SCA Standard 310-2021, instead specifies calcium hardness 50–175 ppm, alkalinity 40–70 ppm and pH 6–8, with no TDS target; the SCAE Water Chart (2016) is a separate document specifying total hardness 50–175 ppm, alkalinity 40–75 ppm and pH 6.5–8. Do not mix the documents, and tie each band to its own: the KH band 40–70 belongs to SCA 310-2021 only, and a 55 mg/L reading is 37% above the 2009 standard's “at or near 40” target. US hardness is often quoted in grains per gallon (gpg): 1 gpg ≈ 17.1 mg/L, and the readouts show it alongside.

Test 4 · Steam by the numbers: milk temperature & bubble size

Chapter 12's two dials, live. Set the temperature your thermometer (or palm) says the milk reached, and the bubble size you can see (microfoam bubbles are individually invisible, froth bubbles are not) and read the Laplace pressure inside them and what the pair means for the foam.

5,600 Pa (0.81 psi)pressure inside a bubble, ΔP = 2γ/r
Microfoamfoam class at this bubble size
In the windowtemperature zone, 60–65 °C (140–149 °F)

Model, Chapter 12's: ΔP = 2γ/r with γ ≈ 0.042 N/m for warm milk (60–65 °C · 140–149 °F) and r = half the diameter you set. A single bubble's pressure is not what breaks foam, the difference between neighbouring bubbles is, driving Ostwald ripening from small bubbles into large ones. Read the pressure here as a stability gauge: the higher and more uniform it is, the longer the foam holds.

Run the loop the way Chapter 16 runs an experiment: predict with Test 2, brew, measure with Test 1, and (once a week) check the water and the milk with Tests 3 and 4, because those two drift quietly (a new filter cartridge, a different milk) and re-tune everything else when they do. Log each round in the brew log in Next Steps; five logged rounds teach more than fifty remembered ones.

Chapter 4 · The grind

No grinder makes one particle size.

What you will learn
  • Describe a grind as a bimodal distribution: a main population plus a fines population.
  • Explain how burr geometry and the exit gap write the distribution before the motor turns.
  • Use the 1/d surface-area law to show why fines carry about half the surface on a tenth of the mass.
  • Explain fines migration and static, and what each does to flow and flavour.

Ask for "600 microns (0.024 in)" and a burr grinder hands you a distribution: a main population near the setting you chose, plus a second, shadow population of fines, fragments tens of microns across, torn off as beans shatter. This bimodality is not a defect of cheap grinders; it is what brittle fracture does. And because diffusion time scales with d², the two populations live in different physical worlds. The fines extract almost instantly. The main population sets the pace of the brew. The boulders, if any, barely contribute at all.

A bimodal particle size distribution

Mass per size interval for a typical burr-grinder distribution at a medium filter setting, plotted as a density and normalised so the main peak = 1. It is peak-normalised, not a raw mass share, read the shape and the peak positions, and use the annotations for the mass split. Note the main peak (the mode, ≈ 520 µm · 0.020 in) sits below the distribution's ≈ 600 µm (0.024 in) median: a log-normal population is lopsided, with a long coarse tail pulling its middle above its most common size.

Model: two log-normal populations, fines centred near 60 µm (0.0024 in) carrying about a tenth of the mass, and a main population centred near 600 µm (0.024 in). Exact shares vary with grinder, burr geometry and coffee; the two-humped shape is the reproducible part. What sets those shares (the burr set's geometry) and what the distribution means in surface area get their own panels below.

Fines punch far above their mass. A gram (0.035 oz) of 60 µm (0.0024 in) fines has roughly ten times the surface area of a gram of 600 µm (0.024 in) particles, and area is where extraction happens. Worse, fines are mobile: flowing water carries them down through the bed until they lodge against the filter paper, forming a dense, low-permeability layer, the fines migration that slows drawdown and can stall a brew entirely. This is why two brews at the same nominal grind setting can behave completely differently, and why sifting, paper quality and gentle pouring are physics interventions, not rituals.

~10×more surface area per gram (0.035 oz) in 60 µm (0.0024 in) fines than in 600 µm (0.024 in) particles, area scales as 1/d
100×faster diffusion equilibration for a particle one tenth the diameter, time scales as d²

Burrs, blades and the shape of fracture
  • Cutting happens in two stages. A burr set is not one edge but a landscape of teeth. Coarse breaker teeth near the entry crack whole beans into chunks; finer finishing teeth toward the exit shear those chunks down. A fragment can only leave when it is smaller than the gap between the burr faces, so the tooth pattern decides how many times a particle is cut, and the gap decides when it is allowed to escape. Distribution width is written into that geometry before the motor ever turns.
  • Conical vs. flat burrs. Both fracture beans between steel surfaces; they differ in the path particles take through the burr set, and so in the width of the distribution and the share of fines. In a conical set, a cone sits inside a ring and gravity feeds beans down the cone's flank, a short, steep path, usually at lower speed. In a flat set, two rings face each other and centrifugal force walks particles outward across the full radius, a longer path with more cutting edges per particle, which typically buys a narrower distribution. Neither escapes bimodality.
  • Diameter and speed are geometry too. Common flat burrs run 50–98 mm (1.97–3.86 in) across; conical burrs about 38–83 mm (1.50–3.27 in). The ends of those ranges are real products: 50 mm flat burrs in the Eureka Mignon line, 98 mm flat in the Mahlkönig EK43, 71 mm conical in the Mazzer Robur S, and 83 mm conical in the Weber HG-2 / KEY. A larger burr carries more teeth and more cutting edge, so each particle meets more edges per revolution, and the set can run slower for the same throughput, with less frictional heat. Small, fast burrs grind hotter and, as Uman 2016 (Chapter 19) showed for bean temperature, heat itself shifts the distribution.
  • Espresso burrs and brew burrs want different things. Tooth patterns are tuned to a job. Espresso burrs are cut to produce a deliberate share of fines, the puck needs them for resistance and body. Brew burrs are cut the other way, minimising fines for clarity, pushing the distribution toward a single hump (unimodal). Same steel, same motor, opposite intentions, which is why a grinder can be excellent at one job and ordinary at the other.
  • Blade grinders chop, they don't grind. Particles recirculate through a spinning blade at random, the distribution is enormously wide, from dust to chunks, and brew-to-brew repeatability is poor. The d² law turns that width directly into uneven extraction.
  • Alignment matters. Burrs mounted slightly off-parallel produce a wider, drifting distribution. In plain terms: the gap is no longer the same all the way around the ring, so the grinder is effectively set fine on one side and coarse on the other at the same time. The tolerance is not abstract: a tilt of a few tens of micrometres (a few ten-thousandths of an inch) across the burr face is the same size as the fines themselves, so one side of the ring cuts espresso-fine while the other passes boulders. The symptom is a grinder that seems to change personality between brews at the same setting.
  • Retention is geometry too. Every chamber corner and exit chute is dead space where grounds lodge, often 0.5–3 g (0.02–0.11 oz) in hopper-fed designs, exchanging with the next dose and smearing yesterday's setting into today's. Near-vertical chutes and single-dose designs shrink that dead space; purging a few grams after a setting change clears it.
  • The numbers, side by side. Flat sets: 50–98 mm (1.97–3.86 in) diameter, two rings face to face, particles walk the full radius outward — more teeth met per particle. Conical sets: ≈ 38–83 mm (1.50–3.27 in), a cone inside a ring, gravity feeds a short, steep path, fewer cuts per particle, usually at lower rotational speed. Cutting angle and tooth depth are ground into the steel by the maker and are not user-adjustable; the two numbers a user can ruin are the gap (the grind setting) and the alignment (a tilt of a few tens of micrometres · a few ten-thousandths of an inch across the face, the size of the fines themselves).
  • What that does to the distribution, schematic. Same coffee, same nominal setting, drawn as the two typical shapes (schematic curves, not measurements of a specific grinder):
  • A worked comparison (illustrative, run yours by Chapter 16's method). Take two grinders at the same 600 µm (0.024 in) median. Suppose, illustratively, the flat set puts 8% of mass in fines and the conical set 14%. By Chapter 4's surface arithmetic, fines carry ≈ 47% of the working surface in the first grind and ≈ 62% in the second, so at the same setting the conical grind presents roughly a third more extraction interface, and its bed permeability is lower (fines throttle flow, Chapter 5): expect it to draw down slower and extract ahead of the flat grind until you open the setting up. The percentages are a worked example, not a measurement, sieve or image your own grinders' output to get your numbers.
  • Heat and static are side effects. Friction warms the grounds slightly and static scatters fines onto every surface, annoying, measurable, and mostly a workflow problem rather than a flavour one at home scale.

Diagram · Burr geometry: two paths through the teeth

Cross-sections, schematic and not to scale. Follow one bean: where it enters, which teeth it meets, and the single gap it must fit through to leave. The path is the difference between the two designs, everything else follows from it. On a narrow phone screen this diagram keeps its full size inside its panel, so scroll it sideways to read both cross-sections at readable type.

Read the two paths against the distribution chart above: the flat burr's longer gauntlet of teeth is why flat sets typically produce the narrower main population, and the conical set's short gravity path is part of why conical sets typically carry the fatter fines shoulder. Typically, not always, tooth design, diameter, speed and alignment can each outweigh the family difference, which is why two grinders of the same type still brew differently.

Visual · Particle surface area: what a gram is really made of

Chapter 20 derives SA/V = 6/d for one particle. Per gram of coffee, the same geometry reads: surface = 6/(ρ·d), with particle density ρ ≈ 1,400 kg/m³ (87 lb/ft³). Halve the size and a gram doubles its working surface, the curve below is that 1/d law, with the three sizes this guide keeps meeting marked on it.

Model: smooth spheres at a single density, a floor, not a measurement. Real fragments are jagged shards with more surface than spheres of the same size, and this counts only the external surface: the internal pore network left by roasting (Chapter 1) carries far more area still, which is precisely why diffusion through the particle's interior, not washing of its surface, sets the pace in Chapter 2.

  • Counting a gram. At 600 µm (0.024 in), a gram (0.035 oz) holds roughly 6,300 particles presenting ≈ 71 cm² (11 in²) of external surface. At 60 µm (0.0024 in), the same gram is roughly 6.3 million particles and ≈ 714 cm² (111 in²), ten times the surface, a thousand times the pieces.
  • A whole dose, laid flat. A 20 g (0.71 oz) filter dose ground entirely at 600 µm would spread its external surface over ≈ 0.14 m² (1.5 ft²), about an A3 sheet of paper. Ground as a real bimodal distribution it is closer to 0.27 m² (2.9 ft²), and an 18 g (0.63 oz) espresso dose at ~200 µm (0.0079 in) reaches ≈ 0.39 m² (4.2 ft²). That is the interface your water has minutes — or seconds, to work across.
  • Fines carry half the surface on a tenth of the mass. Mix 90% of mass at 600 µm with 10% at 60 µm and the surface splits almost evenly: the fines' share is 0.10/60 against the main population's 0.90/600, ≈ 53% of the working surface from ≈ 10% of the coffee. This is the arithmetic underneath Chapter 5's fines layer and Chapter 10's puck resistance: remove or add a few percent of fines and you have rebuilt half the extraction interface.
  • Surface is also where coffee dies. The same area that admits water admits oxygen. Ground coffee stales in hours-to-days where whole beans last weeks (Chapter 8) because grinding multiplies the exposed surface by orders of magnitude, one more reason to grind seconds before brewing, not the night before.

Static, fines and blind burrs: the newest measurements

Three measurement campaigns from 2024 sharpened what this chapter can claim, and one creator-led question is still open. Each is labelled by the kind of evidence it is.

  • Peer-reviewedStatic is set by the bean's moisture, not its colour. Méndez Harper and colleagues (Matter, 2024, References [16]) measured the charge on grounds across roasts and moisture contents: beans with less than ~2% residual internal moisture charge negatively, and the fracture itself (fractoelectrification) contributes more charge than rubbing does. That is why darker, drier roasts fly around the grinder and light, moister ones behave (doi:10.1016/j.matt.2023.11.005).
  • Peer-reviewedA drop of water is a distribution tool. The follow-up study (iScience, 2024, References [11]) tested the Ross Droplet Technique, a home-barista forum trick long before it was a paper: under 0.05 mL of water per gram of beans (under ~0.9 mL · 0.03 fl oz on an 18 g · 0.63 oz dose). Wetting the beans cut grinder retention from ~12% to ~2.5% of the dose and, by stopping fines clumping to larger particles, shifted the particle size distribution enough to raise espresso concentration by at least 15% for darker roasts. Ionisers cleaned up the visible mess but did not change the extraction, only the water, added before fracture, did (doi:10.1016/j.isci.2024.110639).
  • Peer-reviewedFines are a flow variable first. Smrke, Eiermann & Yeretzian (Scientific Reports, 2024, References [15]) added sieved fines (under 100 µm · 0.0039 in) to espresso doses in controlled steps. The fines share mainly cut the bed's permeability and stretched shot time; extraction yield followed the same curve against time with or without the added fines, and, as reported in secondary coverage of the study, even fast 10–15 s shots already reached 17–18% extraction (that figure comes from reporting on the paper, not from its abstract). So this chapter's surface-area arithmetic stands (fines do carry half the interface) but "more fines = over-extraction and bitterness" does not: in the measurement, fines bought time, and time did the extracting (doi:10.1038/s41598-024-55831-x).
  • Creator experimentBlind burrs, promising, not settled. Burr sets with no screw holes through the grinding face ("blind" burrs) promise an uninterrupted cutting surface. Robert McKeon Aloe's blind-vs-regular tests on a Zerno Z1 (Instagram reel, November 2025) and Sprometheus's Z1 blind-burr tests (summarised by Perfect Daily Grind, December 2025) report measurable differences between the two sets. These are careful single-creator experiments, not controlled studies: treat any burr-geometry claim from them as a hypothesis to test with Chapter 16's method, not as a result.

The grind models, in full: the distribution and the surface area

Two models do the heavy lifting in this chapter: the log-normal distribution behind the chart above, and the surface-area arithmetic behind “fines punch above their mass”. Each comes with a full legend and a worked example, as everywhere in this guide.

f(d) = exp(−(ln d − μ)² ∕ (2σ²)) ∕ (d · σ · √(2π)) The log-normal distribution: particle sizes are spread evenly in logarithm, not in micrometres, which is what gives the curve its long coarse tail.

Legend: every symbol

  • d: particle diameter, the variable the distribution is over.Units: micrometres (µm) · Typical: 20–1,500 µm across a filter grind
  • f(d): the density of the distribution at size d; the area under the curve between two sizes is the mass share between them.Units: per µm (1/µm) · The chart above plots it peak-normalised, main peak = 1
  • μ: the mean of ln d; eμ is the median particle size.Unit-free (a logarithm) · Typical: eμ = 600 µm for the chart's main population, 60 µm for its fines
  • σ: the spread of ln d; bigger σ, wider distribution.Unit-free · Typical: 0.42 for the chart's main population, 0.55 for its fines

Worked example: how much of the grind is over a millimetre?

  1. Take the chart's main population: median eμ = 600 µm (0.024 in), σ = 0.42.
  2. For d = 1,000 µm (0.039 in): z = ln(1,000 ∕ 600) ∕ 0.42 = 0.511 ∕ 0.42 ≈ 1.22.
  3. A standard normal table puts about 89% of a population below z = 1.22, so about 11% of the main population's mass sits above 1,000 µm.

Reading it: the long coarse tail is not a drawing error. A log-normal with these parameters keeps about a ninth of its mass in particles over a millimetre, which is why the distribution's middle (median 600 µm) sits above its most common size (the peak of the curve): the tail pulls the middle up.

SA ∕ V = 6 ∕ d Surface-area-to-volume ratio of a spherical particle: the geometry inside “finer extracts faster”. Chapter 20 derives it; here is the arithmetic this chapter uses.

Legend: every symbol

  • SA: the particle's external surface area, the area water can touch.Units: square metres (m²)
  • V: the particle's volume.Units: cubic metres (m³)
  • d: particle diameter; use the same length unit throughout and the ratio follows.Units: metres (m), or micrometres (µm) consistently · Typical: 60 µm fines, 600 µm main population
  • Per gram: at one density, surface per gram is proportional to mass ∕ d, which is the form the worked example uses.Real fragments are jagged, with more surface than spheres: the sphere is a floor, not a measurement

Worked example: why 10% of the mass holds about half the surface

  1. A 600 µm particle: SA ∕ V = 6 ∕ 600 = 0.010 per µm. A 60 µm fine: 6 ∕ 60 = 0.10 per µm. Per gram, the fines carry 10× the surface.
  2. Now weight by mass, at this chapter's split: 0.10 g of fines at 60 µm and 0.90 g of main particles at 600 µm in a 1 g (0.035 oz) sample. Surface is proportional to mass ∕ d: fines contribute 0.10 ∕ 60 = 0.00167; the main population contributes 0.90 ∕ 600 = 0.00150 (in shared, arbitrary units).
  3. The fines' share of the total surface is 0.00167 ∕ (0.00167 + 0.00150) = 0.00167 ∕ 0.00317 ≈ 0.53.

Reading it: about 53% of the external surface sits on 10% of the mass. That is the whole fines story in one line of arithmetic: they dominate the surface the water meets first, while contributing little of the mass that must be extracted through.

Key takeaways
  • No grinder makes one size: a setting names a distribution, not a diameter.
  • Fines are roughly a tenth of the mass but about half the surface area, so they extract first and clog last.
  • Flat and conical burrs differ in the path through the teeth, and so in distribution width and fines share.
  • The log-normal model and the surface-area arithmetic at the end of this chapter are the tools behind every grind claim in the guide.

Chapter 5 · The bed

Water obeys Darcy.

What you will learn
  • State Darcy's law and name every variable in it.
  • Trace how flow feeds back into contact time and diffusion in the pipeline diagram, Figure 3.
  • Predict what grinding finer, or a deeper bed, does to flow and drawdown time.
  • Explain channeling as a permeability shortcut, in filter beds as in pucks.
  • Describe what a pour does besides add water: mixing, avalanches and bed disturbance.

Between the particles, water moves through a porous medium, the same mathematics that describes groundwater creeping through sandstone and oil through reservoir rock. In 1856 Henri Darcy condensed it into one relation for the flow rate through such a bed:

Q = kA ΔP ∕ (μL) Q (flow rate · k) permeability of the bed · A (cross-section · ΔP) pressure drop · μ (viscosity · L) bed depth

Legend: every symbol

  • Q: volumetric flow rate through the bed.Units: mL/s (fl oz/s in imperial; m³/s in SI) · Typical: ~2–4 mL/s (0.07–0.14 fl oz/s) early in a pour-over drawdown, falling below 1 mL/s (0.03 fl oz/s) as the pool drains
  • k: permeability of the coffee bed: how open its pore network is. At fixed porosity it falls roughly with the square of particle size (Kozeny–Carman, Chapter 20).Units: m² · Typical: ~5 × 10−12 m² as an illustrative filter-bed value · bed porosity φ ≈ 0.35–0.45 for a settled filter bed · a migrated fines layer is far lower, which is why it can dominate the flow
  • A: cross-sectional area of the bed, perpendicular to the flow.Units: m² (in² in imperial) · Typical: ~0.009 m² (90 cm² · 14 in²) for a cone dripper bed
  • ΔP: pressure drop across the bed. In a dripper the drive is gravity, and it acts on the whole wet column, not just the pool: the liquid inside the bed has weight too.
