Written as a flux, Darcy's law in a gravity field is q = (k/μ)(Δp/L + ρg); with no pump pressure (Δp = 0) and a pool of depth h over a bed of depth L, that gives Q = kAρg(h + L) ∕ (μL), i.e. an effective ΔP = ρg(h + L).Units: pascals (Pa) / pounds per square inch (psi) · Typical: ρg(h + L) ≈ 785 Pa (0.11 psi) for a 5 cm (2 in) pool over a 3 cm (1.2 in) bed (ρ = 1,000 kg/m³ · 62.4 lb/ft³, g = 9.81 m/s² · 32.2 ft/s²); the pool alone contributes ~490 Pa (0.07 psi) of that
  • μ: dynamic viscosity of the water.Units: Pa·s · Typical: 0.30 × 10−3 Pa·s at 95 °C (203 °F) · 1.0 × 10−3 Pa·s at 20 °C (68 °F)
  • L — bed depth, the distance water must travel through the grounds.Units: m (inches in imperial) · Typical: 0.02–0.04 m (2–4 cm · 0.8–1.6 in) in a filter dripper

Worked example: a healthy pour-over

  1. Driving head from gravity: the pool (5 cm · 2 in) plus the liquid inside the 3 cm (1.2 in) bed itself: ΔP = ρg(h + L) = 1,000 × 9.81 × (0.05 + 0.03) = 785 Pa (0.11 psi). Counting only the pool (490 Pa) understates the drive, because the bed's own liquid weighs something too.
  2. Numerator: kAΔP = (5 × 10−12) × 0.009 × 785 = 3.5 × 10−11.
  3. Denominator: μL = (0.30 × 10−3) × 0.03 = 9.0 × 10−6.
  4. Q = 3.5 × 10−11 ∕ 9.0 × 10−6 = 3.9 × 10−6 m³/s = ≈ 3.9 mL/s (0.13 fl oz/s), a healthy drawdown rate.
  5. Grind finer so the pores halve: at fixed porosity k falls to about a quarter, so Q falls to ≈ 1.0 mL/s (0.03 fl oz/s) at the same pool depth. In a real bed fines also cut the porosity φ, and near the percolation threshold k falls much faster than the square law (Wadsworth et al. 2026 [36]), which is why a real stall is worse than this step suggests.

Try yours: the ratio form needs no k at all, but mind the head: doubling the pool from 5 cm to 10 cm (2 in to 4 in) raises Q only ×1.63 (3.9 → 6.4 mL/s), because the head is h + L, not h alone. And with no pool at all (h = 0) the bed still drains on its own weight, at Q = kAρg ∕ μ ≈ 1.5 mL/s (0.05 fl oz/s), not zero. Halve k and Q halves. Every pour-over adjustment you make moves exactly one symbol in this equation.

In a dripper, the drive is gravity: the weight of the water pooled above the bed plus the weight of the liquid already inside it, ρg(h + L) in the worked example's terms. Everything else is a lever. Grind finer and the pores shrink, permeability k collapses, roughly with the square of pore size, and flow slows dramatically. Let fines migrate to the paper and they add a second, nearly impermeable layer in series. Pour deeper and the taller water column raises ΔP, pushing back. The drawdown curve of every pour-over (fast at first, slowing as the pool drains and the fines settle) is this equation playing out in real time.

Darcy's law assumes the water uses the whole bed evenly. Real beds cheat. Water is lazy: if one path offers less resistance, a crack, a thin spot, the gap where the bed pulls away from the filter wall, flow concentrates there, that channel washes out wider, and still more flow follows. This runaway is channeling, and it is the percolation version of a short circuit: the channelled water over-extracts a fraction of the bed while the rest sits nearly dry, and the cup gets sour and bitter at the same time, the signature of uneven flow, not of any single wrong variable.

Diagram · Anatomy of a coffee bed

A dripper in cross-section. Gravity drives flow; the bed and the paper resist it; any weak path steals it.

Schematic, not to scale. The physics to carry away: total resistance is the bed's resistance plus the fines layer's, in series, the thinnest, finest layer can dominate the whole flow.

Drawdown: watching Darcy in real time (Chart)

Modelled flow rate out of a dripper after the final pour. A healthy bed decays smoothly as the pool drains; a bed choked by migrated fines collapses early and stalls.

Model: healthy bed Q(t) = 1.5 + 2.4·e−t/184 mL/s, starting from the worked example's 3.9 mL/s (0.13 fl oz/s) and decaying toward 1.5 mL/s, not to zero. That floor is this chapter's own h = 0 result: with no pool left, the bed still drains on the weight of its own liquid, Q = kAρg ∕ μ ≈ 1.5 mL/s. The form assumes the pool's area equals the bed's area (Apool = Abed), so the pool depth falls in step with the flow. At t = 184 s, Q ≈ 2.38 mL/s. The time constant is the one this chapter's own Darcy parameters imply: as the pool drains, τpool = μL ∕ (kρg) ≈ 184 s. Fines-choked bed: the same start, multiplied by a collapse factor as the fines layer seals the paper around t ≈ 95 s. The stall you see at the end of a real drawdown is that second curve, the bed's permeability falling mid-brew.

Practical corollaries fall straight out of the equation. A level, evenly distributed bed keeps L and k uniform so no channel wins. A gentle pour keeps the pool shallow and limits the jet's agitation, so fines stay suspended evenly instead of being blasted into the paper (flow inside the bed itself is laminar at any pour rate; what a hard pour changes is the disturbance, not the flow regime). And when a brew stalls, the culprit is almost never "the coffee", it is k, collapsing somewhere near the filter.

Geometry: cone, flat bed, and bed depth
  • Cone drippers concentrate flow. The bed deepens toward a single exit, so L is longest (and flow fastest to organise) at the centre. Drawdown is quick and a little unforgiving of uneven pouring.
  • Flat-bed brewers spread flow. A shallow, wide bed shortens L and evens the pressure field; multiple drain holes resist single-channel dominance. Forgiving, at the price of a larger minimum dose to keep the bed deep enough.
  • Bed depth is a hidden variable. Doubling the dose in the same dripper deepens L and slows flow even at the same grind, which is why scaling a recipe up is never just multiplying the numbers.
  • The paper is part of the circuit. Thick, slow papers add series resistance and trap fines differently than thin, fast ones. Swapping paper brands is swapping a component, not an accessory.

The pour is a mixer: new fluid mechanics, and the argument about it

This chapter treats pouring as plumbing: a pool, a head of pressure, a bed. A 2025 study watched the pour itself, and found it doing mechanical work on the bed. The result is genuinely contested, so both sides are given here, labelled.

  • Peer-reviewedThe jet digs, and the bed avalanches. Park, Young & Mathijssen (Physics of Fluids, 2025, References [17]) imaged a transparent model bed with a laser sheet and high-speed camera. A thick, laminar jet from a gooseneck kettle, poured from greater height, penetrates the bed and triggers miniature avalanches that stir the particles, agitation delivered by the pour, renewing particle surfaces the way Chapter 2's stirring does. Measured on real coffee, extraction rose with the better mixing. Press coverage described that as reaching the same strength with fewer beans; no percentage figure appears in the paper itself, so none is quoted here. The paper's full recommendation is a jet that is high, slow and laminar, not thickness alone. There is a ceiling: pour too high and the jet breaks up into droplets before it lands, entraining air and losing the digging effect (doi:10.1063/5.0257924).
  • ContestedThe counter-argument. Sprudge's critique (“That Scientific Study on Pouring Misses the Point”, April 2025) argues the model bed is silica gel, not coffee: it cannot swell, release gas or fines, and the study measures extraction efficiency rather than flavour, while a higher pour also sheds heat on the way down, a cost Chapter 6 would price in. Read the paper for the fluid mechanics, which are real; read the critique for everything fluid mechanics leaves out. This guide's position: the avalanche mechanism is plausible and the imaging is direct, but "pour higher" is not yet a protocol, it is an experiment (Chapter 16) with a predicted direction.
  • Social summaryHow it travelled. Science Sphere's Instagram summary (September 2026) carried the result to a wide audience as "pouring higher makes stronger coffee" — and the comments were sceptical, largely on the critique's grounds. A fair snapshot of where the community landed: intrigued by the mechanism, unconvinced by the headline.

Key takeaways
  • Flow = permeability × area × pressure drop, divided by viscosity × bed depth: Q = kAΔP/(μL).
  • Permeability is the bed's master variable, and fines migration rewrites it mid-brew.
  • A stall is a permeability collapse, not a mystery: the fines layer on the paper is the usual suspect.
  • In a dripper the pressure drop is only a few centimetres of water head, so the theft by a channel is gentle, unlike espresso.

Chapter 6 · Temperature

Heat is the throttle.

What you will learn
  • Use the Arrhenius law to compare extraction rates at two temperatures.
  • Say what temperature changes besides diffusion, using the feedback lines in Figure 3 and the meeting point in Figure 4.
  • Follow the slurry's temperature through a brew with Newton's law of cooling.
  • Explain heat's second lever: viscosity falls as water heats, so flow speeds up too.
  • Say why kettle temperature is not slurry temperature, and what preheating buys.

Every chemical step in extraction (diffusion itself, and the reactions that liberate flavour compounds) runs faster when hot, and not by a little. Reaction rates follow the Arrhenius law: they grow exponentially with temperature. Diffusion coefficients climb too, both because molecules move faster and because hot water is less viscous, near boiling, water flows about three times more easily than at room temperature, which feeds straight back into Darcy's law.

rate(T) ∝ exp(−Ea ∕ RT) The Arrhenius law. To compare two temperatures: rate₂ ∕ rate₁ = exp[ −Ea/R × (1/T₂ − 1/T₁) ], with every T in kelvin.

Legend: every symbol

  • rate(T): the extraction rate constant at temperature T.Units: 1/s, used here as a relative rate · Typical: defined as 1.00 at 93 °C (199 °F) in this chapter's chart · ~0.89 at 85 °C (185 °F) · ~1.07 at 98 °C (208 °F), with Ea ≈ 16 kJ/mol
  • Ea: activation energy: the energy barrier a compound must clear to dissolve and react.Units: joules per mole (J/mol) · Value used in this guide's model: ≈ 16,000 J/mol (16 kJ/mol), the coffee-specific value reported by Wang & Lim (2021) [34]. Individual compounds vary around it, which is the reason temperature changes a cup's balance, not just its strength
  • R: the universal gas constant.Units: J/(mol·K) · Value: 8.314, the same constant everywhere, not a coffee number
  • T: absolute temperature of the slurry (not the kettle display).Units: kelvin (K) = °C + 273.15 (°F = °C × 9/5 + 32) · Typical: 88–96 °C (190–205 °F) in the slurry = 361–369 K · 93 °C (199 °F) = 366.15 K

Worked example: dropping from 93 °C (199 °F) to 88 °C (190 °F)

  1. Convert: T93 = 366.15 K, T88 = 361.15 K.
  2. Ea/R = 16,000 ∕ 8.314 = 1,925.
  3. 1/T88 − 1/T93 = 0.002769 − 0.002731 = 3.8 × 10−5 per kelvin.
  4. rate88 ∕ rate93 = exp(−1,925 × 3.8 × 10−5) = exp(−0.073) = 0.93.

Reading it: five degrees cooler costs about 7% of the extraction rate, matching the chart's rule of thumb that every +5 °C (+9 °F) adds ≈ 7% (1 ∕ 0.93 ≈ 1.07). Temperature is a real throttle, but a gentler one than folklore says: at 85 °C (185 °F) the rate is still ≈ 0.89 of the 93 °C rate, and even at 50 °C (122 °F) it is ≈ 0.50, at room temperature (23 °C · 73 °F) ≈ 0.29. To compensate at 88 °C (190 °F), you buy the missing rate back with a finer grind or a longer brew.

Extraction rate vs. temperature (Chart)

Relative extraction rate from the Arrhenius law, normalised to 1.0 at 93 °C (199 °F). Axis in °C, for reference: 75 °C = 167 °F · 80 °C = 176 °F · 85 °C = 185 °F · 90 °C = 194 °F · 95 °C = 203 °F · 100 °C = 212 °F. Move the slider to feel how steep the throttle is.

75 °C (167 °F) 100 °C (212 °F) rate × 1.00

Model: k ∝ exp(−Ea/RT) with Ea ≈ 16 kJ/mol, the coffee-specific value reported by Wang & Lim (2021) [34]. Individual compounds have their own Ea, which is precisely why temperature changes the balance of a cup, not just its strength: cooler water doesn't extract "less of everything equally," it extracts a different mixture.

Here is the subtlety most recipes miss: the kettle temperature is not the brew temperature. The moment water meets room-temperature grounds, a ceramic dripper and open air, the slurry sheds heat and settles several degrees below the kettle, then keeps cooling along an exponential decay for the rest of the brew, Newton's law of cooling doing its quiet work. Two brewers using "94 °C (201 °F) water" can run slurries six to seven degrees (about 11–13 °F) apart because one preheated everything and one didn't. When you change temperature, change the system: preheat the vessel, mind the kettle's own drop between pours, and expect the last, coolest water to extract the least, one more reason the final pours contribute body more than brightness.

T(t) = Troom + (T0 − Troom) · e−t∕τc Newton's law of cooling: the slurry's temperature falls exponentially toward room temperature. Note τc here is the cooling time constant, a different τ from Chapter 2's diffusion time.

Legend: every symbol

  • T(t): slurry temperature at time t into the brew.Units: °C (°F) · Typical: starts at ~93 °C (199 °F) in a preheated system and falls several degrees (roughly 9–14 °F) across a 3-minute brew
  • Troom: room (ambient) temperature the slurry is cooling toward.Units: °C (°F) · Typical: 22 °C (72 °F) in this guide's model
  • T0: slurry temperature at the moment the brew starts, after the first pour has met the grounds and brewer.Units: °C (°F) · Typical: 93 °C (199 °F) with everything preheated · ~87 °C (189 °F) into cold ceramic, the kettle said the same number both times
  • t — time since the brew started.Units: seconds (s) · Typical: 0–210 s for a pour-over
  • τc: cooling time constant: the time for the gap to room temperature to shrink to ~37% (1/e) of its start. Bigger means better insulated.Units: seconds (s) · Typical: 1,500 s preheated system · 1,100 s cold ceramic, in this guide's model

Worked example: preheated brewer at 2 minutes

  1. Set the values: Troom = 22 °C (72 °F), T0 = 93 °C (199 °F), t = 120 s, τc = 1,500 s.
  2. Starting gap: 93 − 22 = 71 °C (128 °F of difference).
  3. Exponent: −t/τc = −120 ∕ 1,500 = −0.08, and e−0.08 = 0.923.
  4. T(120) = 22 + 71 × 0.923 = 22 + 65.5 = ≈ 87.5 °C (190 °F).

Reading it: two minutes in, the slurry is already ~5 °C (~9 °F) below where it started, so the last water extracts at a noticeably slower Arrhenius rate than the first. Repeat steps 1–4 with τc = 1,100 s and T0 = 87 °C (189 °F) for the cold-ceramic curve (≈ 80 °C · 176 °F): the two curves sit 6 °C (11 °F) apart at t = 0 and about 7.3 °C (13 °F) apart at 120 s. Read that gap as what these illustrative constants imply, not as a measurement: T0 = 87 °C and both τc values are invented inputs with no energy balance behind them. Measure your own T0 and τc once with a thermometer and use yours.

The slurry cools: Newton's law in the dripper

Modelled slurry temperature across a pour-over, for a preheated brewer versus a cold one. The kettle said the same number both times; the slurry disagrees. Axis in °C, 70 °C = 158 °F · 80 °C = 176 °F · 90 °C = 194 °F.

Model: Newton's law of cooling, T(t) = Troom + (T0 − Troom)·e−t/τ, room at 22 °C (72 °F). Preheated system: T0 = 93 °C (199 °F), τ = 1500 s. Cold ceramic: the first pour's heat is spent warming the brewer, so the slurry starts at 87 °C (189 °F) and cools faster, τ = 1100 s. Illustrative constants, measure your own setup once with a thermometer and the shape will be familiar. For scale, the material numbers any preheating claim has to answer to: water's specific heat is ≈ 4.18 kJ/(kg·K) at 90 °C (194 °F) and its thermal conductivity ≈ 0.67 W/(m·K) at 93 °C (199 °F).

Viscosity: heat's second lever

Darcy's law has viscosity μ in the denominator, and water's viscosity is strongly temperature-dependent: about 1.0 mPa·s at 20 °C (68 °F), roughly 0.55 at 50 °C (122 °F), and near 0.30 at 95 °C (203 °F). The same bed that resists room-temperature water lets near-boiling water through about three times faster. This is a second, purely mechanical reason hot brews draw down quickly, and why a brew that stalls as it cools is not imagining things: its driving fluid is literally thickening as the temperature falls.

20 °C (68 °F)
50 °C (122 °F)
95 °C (203 °F)

Water viscosity μ, in mPa·s, the μ in Darcy's law. Flow through the same bed scales as 1/μ, so the 95 °C (203 °F) row flows about 3.3× more easily than the 20 °C (68 °F) row.

It also explains a small espresso mystery in advance: a shot's flow visibly loosens as the puck warms through the first seconds. Part of that is puck erosion, but part is simply μ falling as cold steel and coffee come up to temperature.

Key takeaways
  • Temperature throttles reaction and diffusion rates exponentially, not linearly.
  • This guide's model uses an activation energy of about 16 kJ/mol, the coffee-specific value from Wang & Lim (2021).
  • The brew spends most of its life below kettle temperature; the slurry cools from the first pour.
  • Hotter water is also thinner water: near-boiling water flows through the same bed about three times faster than cool water.

Chapter 7 · The solvent

Water is not water.

What you will learn
  • Distinguish general hardness (GH) from alkalinity (KH), and say what each does in the cup.
  • Place water chemistry among the five interacting processes in Five processes, one meeting point (Figure 4).
  • Read the SCA water targets and place a given water inside or outside them.
  • Convert between drops on a test kit, mg/L as CaCO3 and mmol/L without a calculator error.
  • Build a remineralised water to a target, and measure what you actually made.

Your brew is roughly 98.7% water, so the solvent deserves the same scrutiny as the solute. Two properties matter physically. The first is mineral content: calcium and magnesium ions interact with coffee compounds and measurably change what dissolves and how it tastes; distilled water still extracts, but with no hardness and no buffer the cup tastes flat and sharp, because minerals shape extraction and acid balance rather than switching extraction on, while very hard water dulls acidity and can choke the cup with chalky weight. The second is alkalinity: the bicarbonate buffer dissolved in the water. Coffee is acidic; bicarbonate neutralises acid on contact. Too much buffer and the bright organic acids that make a coffee taste alive are chemically erased before they reach your tongue. Too little and the cup turns sharp and sour.

150 mg/L (≈150 ppm)target total dissolved solids for brewing water in the 2009 SCAA standard (acceptable range roughly 75–250 mg/L · ≈75–250 ppm)
~40 mg/L (≈40 ppm)target alkalinity, enough buffer to round the cup, not enough to mute it
6.5–7.5pH window in the 2009 SCAA standard (target 7.0); Standard 310-2021 allows pH 6–8

Diagram · The SCA water targets as ranges

Brewing water is a specification, not a purity contest. Each bar is the accepted range; the tick is the target.

Ranges and targets follow the 2009 SCAA water standard [2] (alkalinity is specified as "at or near 40 mg/L (≈40 ppm)," shown here as a narrow band around the target). Note the asymmetry: the targets sit well below the top of each range, the standard is steering you away from hard water, not toward it. A different, newer document, SCA Standard 310-2021, specifies calcium hardness 50–175 ppm as CaCO3, alkalinity 40–70 ppm and pH 6–8, with no TDS target. The SCAE Water Chart is a separate, older document (2016) specifying total hardness 50–175 ppm, alkalinity 40–75 ppm and pH 6.5–8. The three documents are not interchangeable.

The lesson generalises: you are not looking for the purest water, but for water whose chemistry sits in the narrow band where extraction and acid balance coexist. If your tap water smells of chlorine or leaves scale in a kettle within weeks, it is telling you its chemistry is outside that band, filter it, or build brewing water from distilled water plus a mineral concentrate and measure what you made.

Hardness vs. alkalinity: two different numbers
  • General hardness (GH) counts calcium and magnesium, the ions that interact with extraction and flavour. This is the "mineral content" lever.
  • Alkalinity (KH) counts the bicarbonate buffer, the acid-neutralising capacity. This is the "brightness" lever, and it is the one most often out of range in tap water.
  • TDS conflates them. A conductivity meter reads everything at once. Two waters at identical TDS can brew completely differently if one carries its minerals as buffer and the other as hardness, which is why the standard specifies the components, not just the total.
  • Scale is the same chemistry, precipitated. Heat drives bicarbonate to drop its calcium as limescale, in your kettle, and far more expensively inside an espresso boiler (Part 2). Water in spec protects the machine as well as the cup.

Diagram · Mineralization in practice: four waters, side by side

Hardness (GH) and alkalinity (KH) for four waters you might actually brew with, in mg/L as CaCO3 (≈ ppm). Only the third row is a standard, the 2009 SCAA targets. The tap rows are worked examples: yours will differ, which is the entire argument for measuring (recipe panel below).

Mineralization is a recipe with two independent ingredients, not a single “amount of minerals”. Note how the rows fail differently: distilled water fails on both axes (nothing to extract with, nothing to buffer with), while hard tap water fails mostly on alkalinity, its 190 mg/L (≈190 ppm) of buffer erases acidity long before its hardness becomes the problem. That is why diluting hard water (Route A, below) works: it cuts the buffer back toward 40 while the hardness is still usable.

Mineralization, ion by ion
  • Magnesium (Mg²⁺), the strongest hand. A small ion with double charge: the highest charge density of the common water cations, and in Hendon, Colonna-Dashwood & Colonna-Dashwood's 2014 calculations [3] (Chapter 19) it binds many coffee flavour compounds more strongly than any rival, the proposed mechanism behind mineral water “pulling” more flavour out. Magnesium salts also stay dissolved when heated, so magnesium hardness builds far less scale than calcium. Many built-water recipes lean on it for exactly these two reasons. A measured caution (2024): Bratthäll, Figueira & Nording's GC-MS/NMR study (References [12]) found that at normal drinking-water concentrations, added magnesium and calcium barely moved the measured organic acids, and pre-brew versus post-brew addition gave similar acid contents, suggesting acid extraction itself proceeds largely independently of the cations, and any flavour effect may act mainly after extraction, in the cup. The binding calculations say the interaction is real; how much of it survives into taste at recipe-level doses remains an open measurement.
  • Calcium (Ca²⁺), the familiar one, with a catch. Also divalent, also binds flavour compounds (some, like certain acids, preferentially), and the ion the SCA standard names explicitly: target 68 mg/L (≈68 ppm) as CaCO3. The catch is thermal: heated with bicarbonate present, calcium drops out as limescale (Ca²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻ → CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O) on kettle elements and, expensively, in espresso boilers. Calcium is welcome in the cup and unwelcome on the heating element; the standard's modest target is that compromise.
  • Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), the buffer, i.e. the alkalinity. Not a hardness ion at all, but the partner that decides how much of coffee's acidity survives: each bicarbonate ion can neutralise one hydrogen ion from the coffee's organic acids, becoming CO2 and water. ~40 mg/L (≈40 ppm) rounds the sharpest edges; two or three times that flattens a bright coffee into dullness. Bratthäll et al. 2024 (Chapter 19) add the subtler finding: the divalent cations also change which organic acids extract, so minerals edit the acid profile, not just its volume.
  • Sodium and potassium (Na⁺, K⁺), the quiet monovalents. Single charge, weak binding, sodium contributes little to extraction, and past low levels tastes flat to salty (the SCA target for sodium itself is ~10 mg/L · ≈10 ppm). Potassium is mostly coffee's own contribution: the bean is potassium-rich, so a meaningful share of your cup's final mineral content arrived in the grounds, not the water.
  • Sulfate and chloride, the anions in the background. They arrive with the hardness salts (Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate) and in tap water. At high concentrations sulfate can read dry and bitter-leaning, and chloride is the boiler engineer's worry, hot chloride solutions pit stainless steel. At recipe levels both are passengers; they are reasons to measure a very mineral tap water, not to fear a built one.
  • Temporary vs. permanent hardness. Hardness paired with bicarbonate is temporary, boiling precipitates it as scale, which is why a kettle furs up. Hardness paired with sulfate or chloride is permanent, it survives boiling and stays in the brew. One water can carry both, and a GH test reads their sum.

Remineralizing: putting minerals back into pure water

Reverse-osmosis and distilled water are blank pages, everything the cup needs must be written back in. That deliberate act is remineralization, and it is the mirror image of filtering: filtration removes what you don't want, remineralization adds, in measured amounts, what you do. Three working methods, beyond the packets and salts of the recipe panel below:

  • A mineral concentrate. Dissolve the recipe's salts in a small bottle of distilled water at, say, ten times strength, then dose the concentrate by the millilitre (a fraction of a fluid ounce) into each litre (33.8 fl oz) of brewing water. Concentrates turn gram-scale weighing (where a home scale's error is the recipe's error) into millilitre-scale measuring, and one bottle mineralises weeks of brews identically.
  • A remineralization cartridge. plumbed RO systems can run their output through a calcite or blended-mineral cartridge that dissolves a little calcium and buffer back into the stream. Convenient and always on, but the dose is whatever the cartridge gives, it drifts as the cartridge ages, so the GH/KH test kit still applies.
  • Blending. Commercial machines often mix a stream of RO water with a stream of filtered tap water (a bypass blend) landing between the two. At home, Route A's dilution in the recipe panel is the same idea run in a jug.
  • Espresso machines need some minerals. Two practical reasons, beyond taste: boiler water-level probes work by electrical conductivity, and near-pure water conducts too poorly to read reliably; and very low-mineral water is mildly corrosive to boiler metals over years. “Pure” is a brewing-water failure mode for espresso even before the first sip, one more entry for the four-waters diagram above.

A practical water recipe: and how to measure yours

Step 1, measure what you have. A TDS meter alone cannot tell hardness from alkalinity (see the panel above), so use a drop test kit — the aquarium GH/KH kits sold for a few dollars read both, one drop at a time, in mg/L as CaCO3 (≈ ppm). Test the tap water once, and any water you build, the same way. Checked against the SCA standard, the diagram above is right: calcium hardness target 68 mg/L (≈68 ppm), acceptable range 17–85 mg/L, note that SCA Standard 310-2021 instead specifies calcium hardness at 50–175 ppm, and the SCAE Water Chart (2016), a separate document, specifies total hardness (calcium + magnesium) at 50–175 ppm, alkalinity 40–75 ppm and pH 6.5–8.

  • Route A, dilute. If your tap water is simply too hard or too alkaline, cut it with distilled or reverse-osmosis water. The maths is linear: half tap, half distilled halves every concentration. Aim the alkalinity at ~40 mg/L (≈40 ppm) first, it is the number that most changes the cup.
  • Route B, a mineral packet. Products such as Third Wave Water are pre-measured mineral blends (magnesium, calcium and buffer salts) dosed for a gallon (3.8 L · 128 fl oz) of distilled water. Zero measuring, consistent results, the packet is doing Route C's weighing for you.
  • Route C, build it yourself. To 3.8 L (1 US gallon · 128 fl oz) of distilled water add ≈ 0.9 g (about ¼ tsp) Epsom salt, specified as the heptahydrate, MgSO4·7H2O (the common drugstore form; the hardness below only holds for it, the same mass of anhydrous MgSO4 carries roughly twice the magnesium and would roughly double the hardness) and ≈ 0.3 g (a small pinch, ~1/16 tsp) baking soda (sodium bicarbonate, the buffer). That lands near ~96 mg/L (≈96 ppm) of magnesium hardness as CaCO3 (96.2 mg/L computed) and ~47 mg/L (≈47 ppm) alkalinity as CaCO3 (57 mg/L as HCO3−). The built water's total TDS is ≈ 194 mg/L (≈194 ppm) (Mg²⁺ ≈ 23.4 + sulfate ≈ 92.3 + Na⁺ ≈ 21.6 + bicarbonate ≈ 57.3 mg/L; total ≈ 194.6 mg/L) above the SCA's 150 mg/L target, because a TDS meter sums all ions, including the sulfate that arrived with the magnesium; the hardness and alkalinity, the numbers that act on the cup, are the ones in range. Why magnesium, when the SCA target quoted above is calcium hardness (68 mg/L)? Magnesium sulfate is soluble, cheap and scale-safe, magnesium does not precipitate as boiler scale the way calcium carbonate does. Calcium would add two things: a real limescale risk in kettles and boilers, and a different extraction selectivity, Bratthäll et al. 2024 (Chapter 19, References [12]) found Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ do not pull coffee's organic acids identically, so a calcium-built water is a different recipe, not a neutral substitute. Weigh the salts if you can; spoons vary. Route C against the standards, honestly: Route C contains no calcium, so it does not meet either standard's calcium-hardness figure as written; it is a magnesium substitute, not a standard water. Its sodium (~22 mg/L) is about twice the 2009 target of ~10 mg/L, and its TDS (~194 mg/L) is above the 150 target but inside the 75–250 acceptable range.
  • Step 2, verify, then taste. Whatever route you take, run the GH/KH kit on the finished water and write the numbers on the container. Then brew the same coffee with your old water and your new water, side by side: water changes are one of the few upgrades you can blind-test in five minutes (Chapter 20's method).

One caution: built water with no buffer at all (pure distilled plus hardness salts only) can taste sharp and can be mildly corrosive to boiler metals over years. The small bicarbonate addition in Route C is there for the machine as much as for the cup.

The water arithmetic, in full: hardness, alkalinity and ppm

This chapter quotes water three ways: drops on a test kit, mg/L (about the same as ppm), and the mmol/L underneath both. Here are the two conversions, each with a legend and a worked example, landing on the same numbers the Home Lab water test uses.

GH: H (mg/L as CaCO3) = c (mmol/L of Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺) × 100.09
KH: H (mg/L as CaCO3) = c (mmol/L of HCO3−) × 50.045 Hardness and alkalinity are reported as if all the charge were calcium carbonate, but the factor depends on the charge per ion. A divalent ion (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺) carries 2 equivalents per mmol, so GH uses the full CaCO₃ molar mass, 100.09. Bicarbonate carries only 1 equivalent per mmol, so KH uses half of it, 50.045. Using 100.09 for bicarbonate doubles the alkalinity.

Legend: every symbol

  • H: hardness (GH) or alkalinity (KH), expressed as CaCO3 equivalents.Units: mg/L as CaCO₃ (≈ ppm) · Typical: GH 40–100, KH 30–70 in the SCA window
  • c: the amount of the ion per litre: Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺ for GH, bicarbonate (HCO3−) for KH. The two c values are different ions, counted the same way.Units: millimoles per litre (mmol/L)
  • 100.09 / 50.045: 100.09 is the molar mass of CaCO3 (calcium 40.08 + carbon 12.01 + three oxygens 3 × 16.00), in g/mol, which is mg/mmol. One mmol of a divalent ion is 2 milliequivalents, and one milliequivalent as CaCO3 is 50.045 mg, so GH is 2 × 50.045 = 100.09 mg per mmol. One mmol of bicarbonate is 1 milliequivalent, so KH is 50.045 mg per mmol.Equivalently: convert mmol/L to meq/L first (×2 for Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺, ×1 for HCO3−), then multiply by 50.045 either way
  • GH / KH: GH (general hardness) counts the extraction-active cations; KH (carbonate hardness) counts the alkalinity, the buffer. Different conversion, different chemistry: the factor follows the ion's charge, not the reporting scale.Both are conventions of reporting, not claims that CaCO₃ is present

Worked example: the SCA targets in mmol/L, GH and KH

  1. GH first. The 2009 SCAA target for calcium hardness is 68 mg/L as CaCO3. Calcium is divalent, so divide by 100.09: c = 68 ∕ 100.09 ≈ 0.68 mmol/L. Round trip: 0.68 × 100.09 ≈ 68 mg/L.
  2. KH next. The alkalinity target is about 40 mg/L as CaCO3. Bicarbonate is monovalent, so divide by 50.045, not 100.09: c = 40 ∕ 50.045 ≈ 0.80 mmol/L of HCO3−. Round trip: 0.80 × 50.045 ≈ 40 mg/L.
  3. Check against Route C above: its baking soda gives ≈ 0.94 mmol/L of bicarbonate, and 0.94 × 50.045 ≈ 47 mg/L, the alkalinity the recipe panel quotes. (The single-factor version would have said 94 mg/L, double the water's real buffer.)

Reading it: “as CaCO3” is a reporting convention, a common currency that lets calcium, magnesium and bicarbonate be quoted on one scale. Nothing in your water needs to be CaCO3 for the number to be correct.

mg/L as CaCO3 = drops × 17.85 The drop-kit conversion: each drop of reagent counts one German degree of hardness, °dH.

Legend: every symbol

  • drops: the count of reagent drops until the kit's colour changes, read separately for GH and KH.Unit-free count · Typical: GH 4 drops, KH 2 drops in the Home Lab example
  • 17.85: the size of one °dH on the CaCO3 scale.Value: 1 °dH = 17.85 mg/L as CaCO₃ (often rounded to 17.8)
  • ppm: parts per million by mass; for water this dilute, 1 mg/L ≈ 1 ppm, because a litre of water weighs about 1,000,000 mg.So the SCA TDS target of 150 mg/L is the same number as 150 ppm

Worked example: reading a drop kit

  1. Your kit reads GH = 4 drops and KH = 2 drops.
  2. GH = 4 × 17.85 = 71.4 ≈ 71 mg/L as CaCO3. KH = 2 × 17.85 = 35.7 ≈ 36 mg/L.
  3. These are the Home Lab water test's default readings: a water inside the SCA hardness range, with alkalinity just under its 40 mg/L target.

Reading it: a drop kit is coarse (one drop is a 17.85 mg/L step) but honest: it measures the two numbers this chapter actually uses, GH and KH, which a TDS meter alone cannot separate.

Key takeaways
  • Hardness is the extraction-active cations (calcium and magnesium); alkalinity is the buffer that resists acidity. They are different numbers.
  • Water numbers are quoted as CaCO3 equivalents: GH is mmol/L × 100.09 (divalent ions), KH/alkalinity is mmol/L × 50.045 (bicarbonate), and one drop on a °dH kit is 17.85 mg/L.
  • Distilled water brews flat and sharp; very hard water brews muted and chalky; the SCA window sits between.
  • ppm and mg/L are the same number for water this dilute, because a litre of it weighs about a kilogram.

Chapter 8 · The gas

The bloom is a degassing event.

What you will learn
  • Explain where the bloom's CO2 comes from and why it peaks in the first days after roasting.
  • Describe the two degassing clocks, in whole beans and in grounds.
  • Use the Washburn equation to show why wetting is fast, and why the pause is really for the gas.
  • Run the bloom step (2–2.5× the dose in water, 30–45 s) and say what each part does.

Roasting builds pressure inside the bean: the chemistry of browning generates carbon dioxide, and a freshly roasted coffee holds a remarkable amount of it, trapped in the bean's cellular structure. Grinding shatters the cells and opens the escape routes. Add hot water and two things happen at once, the water wets the particles, and the CO2 comes boiling out, inflating the bed into the dome brewers call the bloom.

Left alone, that gas is an enemy of extraction. A bubble clinging to a particle is a patch of surface the water cannot touch, and a bed full of gas is a bed full of dry pockets, Darcy's law applied unevenly, again. The bloom pour, 2–2.5× the coffee's mass in water (40–50 g · 1.4–1.8 oz of water for a 20 g · 0.71 oz dose, the range used consistently across this guide's chapters, protocols and cheat sheet; the exact grams matter less than wetting every ground), then a pause of 30–45 seconds, is simply giving the gas time to leave before the real extraction begins, and letting the water finish wetting every particle. Swirling or excavating the bloom with a spoon speeds both processes: it pops bubbles, collapses dry pockets, and evens out the wetting.

Degassing: the gas leaves on two clocks

Modelled CO2 remaining in whole beans after roasting. Gas near fractured surfaces escapes in days; gas deep in the pore network takes weeks, the d² law again, at cellular scale.

Model: two-pool decay, remaining = 100 × (0.72·e−t/6d + 0.28·e−t/40d), a fast pool and a slow pool, illustrative time constants. Grinding collapses both clocks to hours or less, faster where cells are fractured open, which is why ground coffee stales so much faster than whole beans, and why the bloom is biggest in the first days after roasting.

Freshness, measured in bubbles

The size of a bloom is a crude gas gauge. Coffee roasted days ago blooms vigorously; month-old coffee barely sighs, because its CO2 has already diffused away through the bag — the same d² diffusion law, working on a timescale of weeks instead of seconds. Stale coffee extracts easily but tastes flat, because the gas left in company: many of the volatile aromatics you brew coffee for escaped with it.

The bloom, step by step

Forty grams of water and forty seconds, doing three physical jobs before the brew proper begins.

1 · Pour 2×

~40 g (1.4 oz) on 20 g (0.71 oz)

wetting begins

↓

2 · The bed domes

CO₂ boils out, inflating the bed

degassing · 30–45 s

↓

3 · Swirl

bubbles pop, dry pockets collapse

wetting completes

↓

4 · Main pours

extraction starts on an even bed

Darcy, applied evenly

Skip the pause and the gas leaves during extraction instead, as bubbles clinging to particles, holding water off their surfaces, and as dry pockets the flow routes around. The bloom is not a ritual; it is scheduling the degassing before it can interfere.

The bloom equation, in full: Washburn imbibition

One equation describes the wetting half of the bloom: the Washburn equation, for a liquid soaking into a narrow tube by capillary action (imbibition: soaking in). It earns its place by what it rules out.

L² = (γ · r · cos θ ∕ (2μ)) · t The Washburn equation: the wetting front advances with the square root of time, fast at first, then slowing.

Legend: every symbol

  • L: how far the wetting front has travelled into the pore.Units: metres (m) · Typical: a filter bed is 0.02–0.04 m (0.8–1.6 in) deep
  • γ: surface tension of the water, the pull that drags it into the pore.Units: newtons per metre (N/m) · Typical: ≈ 0.060 at 90 °C (194 °F)
  • r: the pore's radius; narrower pores pull harder but admit less flow.Units: metres (m) · Typical: micrometre-scale gaps between and inside particles
  • θ: the contact angle where water meets the solid; cos θ ≈ 1 when water wets the surface well.Unit-free · Fresh, oily grounds wet less readily than stale ones
  • μ: the water's viscosity, resisting the motion (Chapter 6's second lever).Units: pascal-seconds (Pa·s) · Typical: ≈ 0.00032 at 90 °C (194 °F)
  • t: time since the water arrived.Units: seconds (s)

Worked example: how fast is wetting, really?

  1. Take a pore of radius r = 2 µm (0.000002 m), hot water at γ = 0.060 N/m and μ = 0.00032 Pa·s, wetting well (cos θ ≈ 1).
  2. The bracket is (0.060 × 0.000002 × 1) ∕ (2 × 0.00032) = 0.00000012 ∕ 0.00064 ≈ 0.00019 m²/s.
  3. After 1 s: L = √(0.00019 × 1) ≈ 0.014 m = 1.4 cm (0.55 in). After 40 s: L = √(0.00019 × 40) = √0.0076 ≈ 0.087 m = 8.7 cm (3.4 in), deeper than any filter bed.

Reading it: even through 2 µm pores, capillarity alone would soak a whole bed in about a second. The model is a straight, empty tube: it ignores tortuous paths, swelling and, above all, the CO2 pushing back out. That is the point. Wetting was never the slow part of the bloom; the 30–45 s pause is priced by the gas leaving, which is why the degassing chart above, not this equation, sets the bloom's length.

Key takeaways
  • The bloom is a degassing event scheduled before extraction, so bubbles cannot hold water off particle surfaces.
  • Capillarity alone would wet the bed in seconds; the 30–45 s pause is the gas leaving, not the water arriving.
  • Bloom size is a crude freshness gauge: the gas and the aromatics leave together.
  • Grinding collapses the degassing clocks from weeks to hours, which is why grounds stale faster than beans.

Part 2 · Introduction

Espresso

The same physics, under pressure. Everything in Part 1 ran on gravity, a pressure drop of a few centimetres of water. Espresso replaces gravity with a pump at 9 bar (131 psi), roughly ninety metres (about 300 ft) of water column, and compresses three minutes of percolation into thirty seconds. The equations don't change. Their consequences do. And in Chapter 12 the shot meets its second foam (steamed milk) where bubble pressure, protein chemistry and pour momentum decide whether latte art is possible at all.

Espresso as the same pipeline with a pump for a driver is drawn in One pipeline, three drivers (Figure 5).

This drawer is Part 2's introduction, Chapters 9–12 follow below as their own dropdowns.

9 bar (131 psi)typical brew pressure, about 1,150× the driving pressure of a pour-over (785 Pa (0.11 psi), pool plus the liquid in the bed)
~200 µm (0.0079 in)typical espresso particle size, far finer than filter, because contact time is far shorter
7–12%espresso TDS, roughly 5–10× the strength of filter coffee (7–12% against filter's 1.15–1.45% is a 4.8–10.4× range), at the same 18–22% extraction

Chapter 9 · The puck

Darcy's law at 9 bar (131 psi).

What you will learn
  • Apply Darcy's law at 9 bar (131 psi) and compute what a permeability change does to shot flow.
  • Explain pressure profiling: pre-infusion, ramp and taper, and what each phase is for.
  • Describe poroelasticity: how the puck pushes back and flow settles over the shot.
  • State the 9-bar convention's origin and the argument about it, with its evidence grade.

An espresso puck is Darcy's porous bed rebuilt to survive a pump: some 18–20 g (0.63–0.71 oz) of very finely ground coffee, compressed, tamped (into a dense, shallow disc) about 58 mm (2.28 in) across and about 12 mm (0.47 in) deep, locked in a steel basket. Water arrives at the top at 9 bar (131 psi) and must force its way through pores a fraction of the size of filter coffee's. Darcy's law still governs the flow, with the pump supplying ΔP:

Q = kA ΔP ∕ (μL) Now with ΔP ≈ 9 bar (131 psi). At fixed pressure, flow is set by k, at fixed ΔP, μ, A and L; the grind, the dose and the tamp decide k.

Legend: every symbol, espresso values

  • Q: flow rate through the puck.Units: mL/s (fl oz/s) · Typical: ~2.0 mL/s (0.07 fl oz/s) of water through a saturated, dialled-in puck at 9 bar (131 psi), that is the through-puck flow. The beverage in the cup averages slower, ≈ 1.2–1.4 mL/s (0.04–0.05 fl oz/s): of the ≈ 54 g (1.9 oz) pushed through, ≈ 18 g (0.63 oz) stays in the puck, leaving 36 g (1.27 oz) in the cup over 25–30 s (36 ∕ 27 ≈ 1.33 mL/s)
  • k: puck permeability, manufactured by grind, dose, distribution and tamp.Units: m² · Inverting this chapter's own numbers (Q ≈ 2.0 mL/s at 9 bar, A = 0.00264 m², L = 0.012 m, μ = 0.30 × 10−3 Pa·s) gives k ≈ 3.0 × 10−15 m², an implied value, not a measured one. Published steady-state measurements for espresso-style packed beds run 2.6 × 10−14 to 3.4 × 10−13 m² (Corrochano et al. 2015 [35]), so the implied k sits about 9× below the low end of the measured range; different packing, grind and pressure, transient versus steady-state flow, and puck compaction all push the numbers apart. Read the 2.0 mL/s as the observed flow the model is fitted around, not as a prediction from a measured k · grind finer and k falls; a crack makes k locally enormous
  • A: basket cross-section.Units: m² (in²) · Typical: 0.00264 m² (26.4 cm² · 4.1 in²) for a 58 mm (2.28 in) basket
  • ΔP: pressure drop across the puck, supplied by the pump instead of gravity.Units: bar, pascals (Pa) or psi · Typical: 9 bar = 900,000 Pa = 131 psi, compare with a pour-over's ~785 Pa (0.11 psi) (pool plus the liquid in the bed; the pool alone contributes ~490 Pa (0.07 psi))
  • μ — viscosity of the brew water.Units: Pa·s · Typical: ~0.30 × 10−3 Pa·s at ~93–95 °C (199–203 °F), falling as the puck warms through the first seconds of the shot
  • L: puck thickness.Units: m (in) · Typical: ~0.012 m (12 mm · 0.47 in) for an 18 g (0.63 oz) dose in a 58 mm (2.28 in) basket, a deeper dose at the same grind is a slower puck

Worked example: what 9 bar (131 psi) really is

  1. Convert the pressure: 9 bar × 100,000 Pa/bar = 900,000 Pa (131 psi).
  2. As a water column: h = ΔP ∕ (ρg) = 900,000 ∕ (1,000 × 9.81) = ≈ 92 metres (302 ft), the pump stacks a 92 m (302 ft) waterfall on top of the puck, versus a filter pool's 5 cm (2 in).
  3. Ratio to filter: 900,000 ∕ 785 ≈ 1,150× the driving pressure, the puck survives it only because its k is so much smaller and its bed so compacted.
  4. Keep the shot's frame: an 18 g (0.63 oz) dose and a 36 g (1.27 oz) target in the cup (1:2). Now grind finer so k halves, everything else fixed: through-puck Q halves, ~2.0 → ~1.0 mL/s, and the beverage rate halves with it, ≈ 1.33 → ≈ 0.67 mL/s on average, so the time to 36 g (1.27 oz) in the cup stretches from 36 ∕ 1.33 ≈ 27 s toward 36 ∕ 0.67 ≈ 54 s, the choking shot. Label that number honestly: it is a rigid-bed approximation, reasonable at pressures up to about 5 bar (73 psi); at 9 bar the puck is poroelastic and flow plateaus instead (the closing panel below, Waszkiewicz et al. 2026 [20]), which invalidates the 27 → 54 s prediction at full pressure. (Keep the two flows separate: 2.0 mL/s is water through the puck; 1.33 mL/s is beverage into the cup, after the puck keeps its ≈ 18 g · 0.63 oz.)

Try yours: the machine fixes ΔP, so dialling in is pure ratio work on k: a shot 20% too fast needs k about 20% lower, a small step finer, not a leap.

This reframes the espresso dial-in completely. The machine holds pressure constant, so the barista's real job is manufacturing a permeability. Grind finer and k falls; the same 9 bar (131 psi) now pushes water through more slowly, contact time stretches, extraction climbs. Grind coarser and the shot gushes, water races through in 12 seconds, barely pausing to dissolve anything. The famous 25–30 second shot is not a magic number; it is the contact time at which a well-made puck at 9 bar happens to land in the 18–22% extraction window.

Flow vs. pressure, for three pucks (Chart)

Darcy's law is linear only up to about 5 bar (73 psi): in that range, flow is proportional to puck permeability. Above about 5 bar, poroelastic compaction flattens the flow, then reduces it (Waszkiewicz et al. 2026). The dashed line marks the classic 9 bar (131 psi) operating point, inside that plateau region, so read the curves there as the Darcy approximation bending over, not a straight-line prediction.

Model: Darcy curves Q = (kA/μL)·ΔP, linear to about 5 bar (73 psi) and flattening beyond it as the puck compacts, with three permeabilities chosen so the dialled-in puck passes ≈ 2.0 mL/s (0.07 fl oz/s) of water at 9 bar (131 psi) once saturated. Read the chart's Q as through-puck water flow, not cup flow: a 25–30 s shot pushes ≈ 54 g (1.9 oz) through (≈ 2.0 mL/s × 27 s), the puck retains ≈ 18 g (0.63 oz), and 36 g (1.27 oz) reaches the cup, an average beverage rate of ≈ 1.2–1.4 mL/s (0.04–0.05 fl oz/s), slower still in the first seconds while the puck saturates and swells. Real machines add pump curves and puck erosion on top of this skeleton; the ordering of the three pucks is the physics, and the curves are Darcy-linear only to about 5 bar (73 psi): above that, poroelastic compaction flattens them into a plateau and then a fall (Waszkiewicz et al., Physics of Fluids 38, 063113 (2026), doi:10.1063/5.0319611).

Diagram · Anatomy of a puck

A portafilter in cross-section during extraction. Pressure is nearly uniform above the puck and near zero below it, almost the entire 9 bar (131 psi) drops across about 12 mm (0.47 in) of coffee.

Schematic, not to scale. Because the pressure drop is concentrated in the puck, any local weakness (a crack from a knock, a low-density streak from uneven distribution) becomes the path of least resistance for the entire flow.

Pressure profiling: the shape of a shot

Pressure at the puck over time. A classic machine slams to 9 bar (131 psi) almost instantly; a profiled shot pre-infuses gently first, then ramps, the puck is consolidated before it is challenged.

Illustrative profiles. The pre-infusion curve holds ≈ 3 bar (44 psi) for the first several seconds (wetting, swelling, degassing), ramps to 9 bar (131 psi), and can taper late in the shot as the puck erodes and flow would otherwise accelerate. Profiling changes no physics, it schedules ΔP so the puck's permeability stays uniform while it is still fragile.

Does the puck push back? Poroelasticity and the 9-bar question

Everything above treats the puck as a rigid resistor: set k, apply 9 bar (131 psi), read Q off Darcy's line. (The modelling tradition behind this chapter runs through Sano et al. 2019 [7], Ellero & Navarini 2019 [8], Cameron et al. 2020 [9] and Mo et al. 2021 [10].) Three results from 2025–2026 (and one industry's worth of machine logs) say the puck is not rigid, and that "9 bar" is a convention with a history, not an optimum anyone measured. Each claim is labelled by its evidence.

  • Peer-reviewedThe puck is poroelastic, it compacts under its own pressure drop. Waszkiewicz, Myck, Bialas, Puciata-Mroczynska, Dzikowski, Szymczak & Lisicki (Physics of Fluids, 2026, References [20]) modelled the puck as a deformable porous solid whose porosity and permeability respond to the flow itself. In that model, flow does not rise linearly with pressure forever: flow plateaus above ~5 bar (73 psi), then falls, as further pressure compacts the bed. Scope note: the study used one light-to-medium roast Brazilian coffee on one machine setup. Darcy's law remains the right skeleton, but for espresso, k is a function of ΔP, not a constant, and "more pressure = faster flow" fails exactly in the range machines operate in (doi:10.1063/5.0319611).
  • Peer-reviewedThe wetting front, photographed. Foster, Lee, Moroney and colleagues (Physics of Fluids, 2025, References [18]) used time-resolved X-ray micro-CT to watch water infiltrate an espresso bed directly, the saturation stage this chapter previously had to infer from the stream below the basket. Infiltration is a moving front with its own dynamics, not an instant soaking (doi:10.1063/5.0245167).
  • Peer-reviewedThe shot, resolved into regions. Grudeva and colleagues (European Journal of Applied Mathematics, online 2025, issue 2026, References [19]) built a multiscale asymptotic model that separates a shot into distinct regions (infiltration, then saturation, then rapid extraction) each with its own governing balance. It is the current state of the art behind Chapter 20's modelling, and the formal version of the story this chapter tells in words (doi:10.1017/S095679252500018X).
  • Industry dataMachine logs point the same way. Decent Espresso's “Nine-Bar Question” (Instagram reel, August 2026) presented logged DE1 shots in which flow peaked near 4.5–5 bar (65–73 psi) rather than at full pressure — the poroelastic model's signature, visible in a manufacturer's own telemetry. Industry data is not peer review, but it is a second, independent instrument agreeing with the model.
  • Technical educationThe argument, at the machine. Lance Hedrick's “The 9 Bar Fallacy” (YouTube) works through the same question with real shots, why the industry's standard pressure is a historical inheritance from lever machines and pump ratings, and what changes when you profile below it.
  • What survives. None of this retires 9 bar (131 psi) as a working standard: baskets, recipes and palates are calibrated to it, and a dialled-in 9-bar shot is a known, repeatable thing. What it retires is the idea that 9 bar is a law of nature, or that pressure is a simple throttle. Treat pressure as a profile to schedule (as the chart above does), and treat the puck as a material that answers back.

Key takeaways
  • At fixed pressure, flow is set by permeability: the puck, not the pump, meters the shot.
  • 9 bar is about 1,150× the pressure drop across a filter bed; that multiplier is why espresso failures are violent.
  • The puck is not a rigid resistor: it swells, compacts and erodes, so its resistance changes during the shot.
  • Profiling changes no physics; it schedules pressure so wetting, extraction and erosion happen in a kinder order.

Chapter 10 · Evenness under pressure

Channeling, amplified.

What you will learn
  • Explain channeling as parallel flow paths competing for the same pressure.
  • Work the two-path example: how a 2× permeability streak takes two thirds of the flow.
  • Describe puck preparation as permeability engineering: distribution, tamping, pre-infusion.
  • Diagnose a shot by sight: first drops, stream shape, colour and dead spots.

Filter channeling wastes a brew; espresso channeling detonates one. The reason is pressure. In a dripper, a weak path sees the same few centimetres of gravity head as everywhere else, so the theft is gentle. In a puck, the weak path sees the full 9 bar (131 psi), and because flow through a widening crack grows faster than linearly as the crack erodes, the channel hogs an ever-larger share of the pump's output. Within seconds most of the water is sprinting through a fraction of the coffee: that fraction over-extracts into bitterness while the untouched majority contributes almost nothing, and the shot tastes sour and bitter simultaneously, thin despite its strength. When an espresso tastes like two mistakes at once, it is one mistake (uneven resistance) wearing both masks.

Puck preparation is permeability engineering

Every puck-prep tool is an attack on variance in k. Distribution, stirring the grounds with fine needles (WDT) or settling them evenly, removes density streaks before they become channels. Tamping compresses the bed to a uniform density and, critically, a level surface: a tilted puck is a thin puck on one side, and water finds the thin side. Note what tamping pressure does not do: beyond the point where the bed is fully compacted, pressing harder barely changes k, the pump's 9 bar (131 psi) dwarfs anything your arm adds. Consistency of the tamp matters; heroics do not.

Pre-infusion: wetting before the hammer

Dry grounds hit with instant 9 bar (131 psi) water are at their most fragile, the bed can fracture, and CO2 (the same gas as the filter bloom) erupts through the puck, prising channels open. Pre-infusion wets the puck gently first, at line pressure of a few bar (roughly 30–45 psi) or a restricted flow, for several seconds. The physics is threefold: particles swell as they absorb water and seal small gaps; trapped gas escapes without violence; and the bed consolidates into a more uniform resistor before full pressure arrives. It is the bloom, re-invented for a system where the degassing problem arrives with a pump behind it.

Same destination, different clocks

Modelled extraction yield over time for filter percolation and espresso. Espresso's fine grind (d² law) and pressure-driven (laminar Darcy) flow compress the whole curve into half a minute.

Model: first-order approach curves, EY = 24% × (1 − e−t/τ), with τ = 12 s for espresso and τ = 75 s for filter, both landing in the 18–22% window. The shaded band is that window. Reconciling the constants with Chapter 2: the 24% ceiling is a practical one for these conditions, below the ~30% of bean mass that is soluble at all, because the last fraction stays locked in coarse cores and in liquor already near equilibrium. And these τ values are effective, bed-level constants, not single-particle ones. Chapter 2's d² law, scaled from its 250 µm (0.010 in) / 25 s baseline, gives ≈ 16 s for a 200 µm (0.0079 in) espresso particle, the same order as the 12 s used here, with pressure-driven surface washing making up the difference, and ≈ 144 s for a lone 600 µm (0.024 in) filter particle. The filter bed averages over the whole size distribution of Chapter 4, most of whose mass sits in smaller, faster particles, so the bed-level curve runs ahead of its coarsest member: 75 s, not 144 s. Same law, two levels of description.

Puck prep, as a process

Four steps, one goal: a bed whose permeability k is the same at every point, before pressure arrives to audit it.

1 · Distribute (WDT)

needles erase density streaks

variance in k → down

↓

2 · Tamp level

uniform density, level surface

L the same everywhere

↓

3 · Pre-infuse

swell, seal, degas, gently

the puck consolidates

↓

4 · Extract at 9 bar

one resistor, one stream

25–30 s to target mass

Read backwards when a shot channels: the failure appears at step 4, but it was manufactured at step 1 or 2. Pressure only reveals the variance; prep is where it is created or removed.

Diagnosing a shot by sight
  • First drops after ~5–10 s, evenly across the basket, saturation is uniform; the puck wetted as one resistor.
  • Streams converge to one steady "mouse tail", flow is distributed; resistance is even. This is the shot in the Part 2 photograph.
  • An early, pale jet off to one side, a channel. The jet is blond because it is mostly fast, under-extracted water sprinting through a crack, while its colour also tells you the rest of the puck is being starved.
  • Dead spots that never drip, the opposite failure: zones so dense, or so dry from trapped gas, that flow never arrives. Distribution and pre-infusion are the fixes.
  • Flow accelerates and turns pale late, the puck is eroding and thinning; k is rising mid-shot. A declining pressure profile (Chapter 9) is the machine-side compensation.

Puck prep, on camera and on the forums

This chapter's techniques were mostly developed in public (on video channels and forum threads) before any journal touched them. The best of that record, labelled for what it is:

  • Technical educationWDT, shown slowly. Lance Hedrick's WDT technique video (YouTube) demonstrates needle distribution at the basket (depth, pattern and pace) the clearest visual companion to this chapter's account of manufacturing an even k.
  • Technical educationReading extraction as it happens. Hedrick's “Understanding Espresso Extraction” (YouTube) connects flow, colour and timing to the diagnosis table above, what a channel looks like from below the basket, and what to change first.
  • Community hypothesis“Soup”: the deliberate rule-break. Forum threads (the Home-Barista discussion) developed a low-pressure, coarse-ground, fast-running style for ultra-light roasts that would choke or sour at standard parameters — thin, tea-like shots on purpose. It contradicts the 25–30 s convention this guide teaches, which is precisely its value: it marks where the convention's assumptions (a roast that extracts readily) stop holding. File it as an experiment to run by Chapter 16's method, not as a protocol.

Worked example: one puck, two paths

The channeling story of this chapter, reduced to arithmetic. Darcy's law (Chapter 9) does all the work.

  1. Split the puck mentally into two halves of equal mass. The left half is evenly packed, permeability k. The right half has a density streak, permeability 2k.
  2. Both halves see the same pressure drop (the pump does not choose), the same viscosity and the same thickness. By Darcy, flow through each half is proportional to its k: the total flow splits k : 2k, that is one third through the tight half, two thirds through the loose half.
  3. So the loose half receives twice the water per gram of coffee. Its local brew ratio doubles; it races ahead in extraction while the tight half lags: one half over-extracts as the other under-extracts, in the same shot.
  4. Now let the fast path erode, as channels do: its permeability climbs to 4k. The split becomes k : 4k, and the loose half takes 4 ∕ 5 = 80% of all the water, through half the coffee.

Reading it: that is the arithmetic inside “sour and bitter at once”: no new ingredient appears, just a redistribution. It is also why puck prep is aimed at the variance in k, not its average: the average can be perfect while the split ruins the shot.

Key takeaways
  • Flow splits between parallel paths in proportion to their permeability; a small streak steals a large share.
  • A channel that erodes wider takes an ever-larger share: 80% of the flow can end up through half the coffee.
  • Tamping pressure beyond full compaction barely changes permeability; a level, even bed is what matters.
  • Pre-infusion is the bloom under pressure: wet, swell and degas gently before the full 9 bar arrives.

Chapter 11 · The foam

Crema is an emulsion with a gas problem.

What you will learn
  • Explain why only espresso makes crema: pressure to dissolve CO2, shear to emulsify oils.
  • Use the Laplace law on a crema bubble and say why small bubbles outlast large ones.
  • Read crema as a gauge of gas content and freshness, and state its limits as evidence.
  • Compare espresso and filter side by side: same physics, different decades of pressure, strength and time.

No filter brew can make crema, and the reason is pure physics. Crema is a foam of CO2 bubbles wrapped in coffee oils and surface-active compounds, an emulsion and a foam in one. It needs two ingredients only espresso provides: pressure, to force large amounts of CO2 into solution and then let it nucleate into microbubbles as the liquid exits to atmospheric pressure, and shear, the violent turbulence of the puck and the basket holes, to emulsify the bean's oils into droplets fine enough to stabilise the bubbles.

This is why crema tracks freshness so faithfully: it is made of the same roasting gas as the bloom. Fresh coffee, rich in CO2, pours a thick, persistent crema. Stale coffee cannot, the gas is gone, and no technique can foam what is not there. Robusta-heavy blends typically give more crema (the usual mechanism offered, more CO2 and more foam-stabilising compounds, is plausible but unverified). Treat crema as data, not decoration (a visible readout of gas content and extraction turbulence) while remembering it contributes bitterness of its own, which is why many tasters stir it in or skim it off before judging the shot beneath.

Diagram · Anatomy of a shot

A settled espresso separates into three visible strata, a cross-section of everything the previous chapters did.

Schematic. The layers are a density gradient, not three separate liquids: the darkest, densest fraction sinks, the gas-lifted emulsion floats. Stirring recombines them into the homogeneous shot the control chart assumes.

Espresso vs. filter, side by side
PropertyFilterEspresso
Driving forceGravity, a few cm (about 1–2 in) of water head, ≈ 785 Pa (0.11 psi) for pool plus bed liquid (the pool alone is ≈ 490 Pa (0.07 psi))A pump at ~9 bar (131 psi), roughly 1,150× the pressure drop
GrindMedium, ~600 µm (0.024 in) main populationFine, ~200 µm (0.0079 in), because contact time is far shorter
Bed geometryDeep, loose cone or flat bed, 2–4 cm (0.8–1.6 in)A shallow, tamped, compacted puck, ~12 mm (0.47 in)
Ratio & strength1:15–1:17, landing at 1.15–1.45% TDS1:2 in the cup, landing at 7–12% TDS
Extraction targetIdentical: 18–22%. The window doesn't move; only the clock and the pressure do.
Contact time~2½–3½ minutes~25–30 seconds
Signature failureStalling and gentle channeling from migrated finesViolent channeling through cracks and density streaks
Gas managementThe bloom, 30–45 s at atmospheric pressure (14.7 psi)Pre-infusion, seconds at a few bar (roughly 30–45 psi)
What only pressure buys—Emulsified oils and CO2 foam: crema

Crema by the numbers: the Laplace law in a bubble

Chapter 12 puts the Laplace law to work on milk foam. The same law runs crema, and one worked example shows why crema coarsens and dies.

ΔP = 2γ ∕ r The Laplace law: the pressure inside a bubble exceeds the pressure outside by 2γ/r, one curved surface, as in a foam bubble.

Legend: every symbol

  • ΔP: the pressure excess inside the bubble over the liquid around it.Units: pascals (Pa) · Typical: thousands of Pa in microfoam-scale bubbles
  • γ: surface tension of the liquid forming the bubble wall.Units: newtons per metre (N/m) · Typical: ≈ 0.048 for coffee liquids, the value Chapter 12 uses
  • r: the bubble's radius, half its diameter.Units: metres (m) · Typical: crema bubbles of roughly 10–50 µm diameter

Worked example: two crema bubbles

  1. A small bubble, diameter 10 µm (0.0004 in), so r = 5 µm = 0.000005 m: ΔP = 2 × 0.048 ∕ 0.000005 = 19,200 Pa ≈ 0.19 bar (2.8 psi).
  2. A larger bubble, diameter 50 µm, so r = 25 µm: ΔP = 0.096 ∕ 0.000025 = 3,840 Pa ≈ 0.038 bar (0.56 psi).
  3. The small bubble's gas sits about 15,000 Pa (19,200 − 3,840 = 15,360) above the large bubble's. Gas dissolves out of the small bubble, through the wall, and into the large one.

Reading it: a mixed foam carries the seeds of its own coarsening: small bubbles feed large ones until the texture turns coarse and drains, in crema as in milk foam. Fresh coffee delays the ending by supplying new CO2; it cannot repeal the pressure difference.

Key takeaways
  • Crema is a foam of CO2 bubbles stabilised by emulsified oils: it needs gas, pressure and shear together.
  • Crema tracks freshness because it is made of the same roasting gas as the bloom; stale coffee cannot foam.
  • Small bubbles hold higher internal pressure (ΔP = 2γ/r), which drives the gas migration that coarsens and collapses foam.
  • Crema is data, not decoration, and it carries bitterness of its own: stir or skim before judging the shot.

Chapter 12 · Milk & latte art

Latte art is foam physics, poured.

What you will learn
  • Describe milk as a colloid, and name the parts that stabilise foam.
  • Use the Laplace law to predict how bubble size sets foam stability and texture class.
  • Run the two steaming phases inside the 60–65 °C (140–149 °F) window.
  • Explain contrast: why white foam stays white against the crema.

A latte pattern looks like decoration. Physically, it is a controlled collision between two foams and two fluids. Below sits the espresso, a dense liquid wearing the CO2 foam of Chapter 11. Into it you pour microfoam: milk that a steam wand has filled with microscopic air bubbles and heated into a glossy, pourable colloid. The pattern is simply what buoyancy, momentum and surface tension draw when the second foam lands on the first, which means every wobbly heart and every clean rosetta is reporting on bubble size, temperature and flow, whether the barista reads it or not.

Three questions decide whether art is even possible. Did the steam build bubbles small enough to behave like a liquid rather than a froth? Did the heat stop inside the narrow window where milk proteins stabilise foam instead of collapsing it? And does the pour spend its momentum in the right order, first mixing, then drawing? This chapter takes them in turn.

~10–30 µm (0.0004–0.0012 in)microfoam bubble diameter, small enough to pour like paint and raft as one glossy sheet (a barista rule of thumb)
60–65 °C (140–149 °F)the steaming window: hot enough for peak perceived sweetness, below the ~70 °C (158 °F) where whey proteins denature and foam dies
+~30%typical volume expansion for latte milk, cappuccino foam runs +50–100%, and pours as a solid, not a liquid (barista rules of thumb)

Milk is a colloid with the tools built in

Milk is roughly 87% water carrying three dispersed systems at once: lactose (~4.8%) dissolved as a true solution; fat (~3.5–4% in whole milk) suspended as globules a few micrometres across; and protein (~3.3%), casein travelling in micelles, and the whey proteins, chiefly β-lactoglobulin, dissolved in the serum. Foam needs a surfactant: a molecule with a water-loving end and a water-fearing end that will rush to any new air–water surface and coat it. Milk's proteins are exactly that. The moment the steam wand tears air into the milk, protein molecules migrate to each bubble's surface, unfold, and link into an elastic skin, the same interfacial trick that stabilises crema, run by a different protein in a different drink.

  • Protein builds the foam. Casein adsorbs fast and gives body; whey proteins form the stronger, more elastic films once gently warmed. Skim milk, all protein and no fat, foams stiff and tall, and tastes thin.
  • Fat is a rival. Fat globules and free fat compete for the bubble surface and can puncture protein films, so whole milk foams a little less readily, but its fat carries flavour and gives the foam its creamy texture. The trade is stability for richness.
  • Lactose is the sweetness dial. Lactose is heat-stable enough for steaming, though some of it converts to lactulose; warm milk tastes sweeter largely because sweet perception rises with temperature, one reason the 60–65 °C (140–149 °F) window tastes sweetest, and why overshooting it reads as flat as well as cooked.
  • Plant milks are a different colloid. Oat, soy and almond drinks bring less or different protein and more added oils and stabilisers; barista formulations exist precisely to restore the protein-and-fat balance this section describes.

Why must the bubbles be small? Because a bubble is a pressurised vessel, and its internal pressure is set by its radius. Surface tension γ squeezes the bubble's skin; the smaller the bubble, the harder the squeeze. The relation is the Laplace pressure:

ΔP = 2γ ∕ r The pressure inside a bubble exceeds the pressure outside by 2γ/r, one curved surface, as in a foam bubble in liquid. Halve the radius and the pressure doubles.

Legend: every symbol

  • ΔP: excess pressure inside the bubble, above the surrounding milk.Units: pascals (Pa) · Typical: ≈ 5,300–6,000 Pa (0.77–0.87 psi) in a 30 µm (0.0012 in) microfoam bubble · ≈ 530–600 Pa (0.08–0.09 psi) in a 300 µm (0.012 in) froth bubble, at warm-milk surface tensions
  • γ (gamma), surface tension of milk at the air interface; proteins lower it from pure water's 0.072 N/m.Units: N/m · Milk runs ≈ 40–50 mN/m at 20 °C (68 °F) and falls with temperature, so warm milk at 60–65 °C (140–149 °F) sits at γ ≈ 0.040–0.045 N/m; the worked example uses 0.042 N/m. Do not import espresso's 0.048 N/m here: that value (Illy & Navarini, Food Biophysics, 2011) was measured on espresso, not milk
  • r: bubble radius (half the diameter).Units: metres (m), quoted here in micrometres (µm) / inches · Typical: 5–15 µm (0.0002–0.0006 in) radius in microfoam · 150 µm+ (0.006 in+) in coarse froth

Worked example: microfoam vs. froth

  1. Microfoam bubble, diameter 30 µm (0.0012 in), so r = 15 µm = 1.5 × 10−5 m. With warm milk's γ ≈ 0.042 N/m: ΔP = 2 × 0.042 ∕ 1.5 × 10−5 = ≈ 5,600 Pa (0.81 psi) (5,300–6,000 Pa across the γ range).
  2. Coarse froth bubble, diameter 300 µm (0.012 in), r = 1.5 × 10−4 m. ΔP = 2 × 0.042 ∕ 1.5 × 10−4 = ≈ 560 Pa (0.08 psi).
  3. Ten times the radius, one tenth the pressure, and the pressure difference between neighbouring bubbles is what drives gas through the liquid films from small bubbles into large ones.

What it means at the pitcher: a foam of mixed sizes is unstable by arithmetic. Gas migrates from the high-pressure small bubbles to the low-pressure large ones, Ostwald ripening, so froth coarsens, drains and separates within a minute or two. A foam of uniformly tiny bubbles has almost no pressure differences to exploit, so it holds together, pours glossy, and survives the trip to the cup. Uniformity, not just smallness, is the goal.

Laplace pressure vs. bubble size

Excess pressure inside a milk bubble against its diameter, from ΔP = 2γ/r with γ ≈ 0.042 N/m for warm milk. The curve is a hyperbola: pressure explodes as bubbles shrink. Diameter axis is logarithmic.

Model: ΔP = 2γ/r for a bubble in liquid (a free soap bubble in air, with two surfaces, would be 4γ/r), plotted against diameter with r = d/2 and γ ≈ 0.042 N/m for warm milk. A 30 µm (0.0012 in) microfoam bubble (15 µm radius) sits at ≈ 5,600 Pa (0.81 psi); a 300 µm (0.012 in) froth bubble at ≈ 560 Pa (0.08 psi). The physics that matters is the shape of the curve and the ten-to-one pressure gap between the two marked foams, which survives the corrected γ.

Steaming: two phases, one temperature window

The steam wand does two jobs at once, it injects both air and heat (the steam itself condenses into the milk, adding roughly a tenth more water), and good technique separates them in time:

  • Phase 1, aeration, while the milk is cold. Wand tip at the surface, so the jet tears air in with a hissing, paper-tearing sound. Air goes in early for two physical reasons: cold, fluid milk lets fresh bubbles be coated by protein before they can merge, and bubbles made cold will expand as they warm, aerate late and the same air becomes oversized froth. For latte milk, stop adding air around 35–40 °C (95–104 °F), once the volume has grown by roughly a third.
  • Phase 2, texturing, in the vortex. Sink the tip and angle the pitcher so the milk rolls in a whirlpool. The vortex is a shear machine: it drags the large bubbles from phase 1 down, stretches and breaks them into microfoam sizes, and folds the foam through the liquid until no separate layer remains. Done well, the pitcher holds one homogeneous fluid (“wet paint”) not milk with foam on top.
  • The ceiling, ~70 °C (158 °F). Whey proteins begin to denature at about 70 °C (158 °F); past that, foam stability falls away progressively and cooked, sulfurous notes appear, while perceived sweetness fades. This is a one-way door, denaturation doesn't reverse as the milk cools. Steam to 60–65 °C (140–149 °F) (the pitcher too hot to hold comfortably), and let carryover heat do the rest.
  • Polish, then pour promptly. Swirl the pitcher to re-fold any foam that has started to separate and knock out the odd large bubble with a tap on the counter. Then pour within seconds: drainage and Ostwald ripening started the moment the steam stopped, and the Laplace arithmetic above gives a separated foam no way back.

One tick explained: the 48 °C (118 °F) label is only a scale mark halfway along the bar, nothing in the milk changes at 48 °C. The meaningful temperatures are the ones in the text: aeration ends ~35–40 °C (95–104 °F), the target is 60–65 °C (140–149 °F), and the ceiling is ~70 °C (158 °F). The whole steaming window on one bar: air goes in cold, texture builds in the vortex, and the green band (60–65 °C (140–149 °F)) is where sweetness peaks and the proteins still hold. The red end is a one-way door.

The pour, in four moves

One continuous pour, two physical regimes. Height spends momentum on mixing; closeness spends it on drawing.

1 · High & thin

stream punches through the crema

momentum → mixing

↓

2 · Low & close

foam can no longer dive, it rafts

buoyancy → the canvas

↓

3 · Wiggle or push

oscillation lays the rosetta’s leaves

flow rate → pattern size

↓

4 · Lift & pull through

a thin stream cuts the stem & heart

momentum, spent last

Why the sequence works: a fast, high stream has the momentum to submerge and stir the espresso, keeping the base one even brown. Brought low, the same milk arrives too gently to dive — and being full of air, it is less dense than the espresso, so it spreads across the surface as a white raft. Every classic pattern is those two regimes plus one gesture: a side-to-side wiggle folds the raft into a rosetta’s leaves, repeated pushes stack a tulip, a still pour pools into a heart.

Contrast: why the white stays white

Definition in the cup is a density and surface story. Microfoam is milk plus air (measurably lighter than the espresso beneath) so once it stops being driven downward it floats, and the crema's own surface tension helps it spread as a sheet rather than bead up. The brown ring that frames a good pattern is crema that the milk stream pushed aside but never submerged: pour too timidly in phase 1 and the base stays patchy; pour the pattern from too high and the foam dives and greys. Contrast fails for fluid-mechanical reasons, not artistic ones.

  • Pattern sinks and vanishes, pitcher still too high in the pattern phase: the stream's momentum carries the foam under the surface. Drop the spout to a centimetre (about 0.4 in) above the cup and tilt the cup toward it.
  • Blob, no leaves, foam too coarse or too stiff: bubbles made late, milk overheated, or foam that sat and separated. The raft lands as a solid instead of flowing into folds.
  • Washed-out, grey-brown art, milk too thin (too little air: nothing to raft) or a thin, stale crema with no surface to draw on, Chapter 11's gas problem returning.
  • Asymmetric pattern, the cup wasn't level or the pour wasn't centred: the raft spreads downhill and off-axis, obeying gravity exactly as Part 1 would predict.

Latte art, then, is the whole guide in miniature: a colloid stabilised by surface chemistry, a size distribution set by shear, a stability clock set by one pressure equation, and a final pattern drawn by momentum and buoyancy. The barista's hand is just the last instrument. Get the bubbles small and uniform, stop the heat inside the window, and spend the pour's momentum in the right order, the drawing takes care of itself.

Key takeaways
  • Microfoam is a bubble-size achievement: uniform small bubbles have nothing to ripen into, so the foam stays glossy.
  • The Laplace pressure gap between small and large bubbles is the engine of coarsening.
  • Aerate cold, texture in the vortex, stop at 60–65 °C (140–149 °F): past about 70 °C (158 °F) the proteins and sugars turn against you.
  • Latte art is foam physics poured: the pattern is a map of bubble size and pour height.

Part 3 · Introduction

The Physics of Pour Over

Parts 1 and 2 treated the coffee bed as if it floated in space, a porous medium with a permeability, a depth, a temperature. In a real brew the bed takes the shape of whatever holds it, and that shape is not neutral. A dripper decides how deep the bed is at every point, where the water is allowed to leave, and whether the exit restricts the flow or your hand does. Chapters 13–16 put the vessel itself into the equations: geometry first, then four real brewers, then what controlled measurements actually found, then an experiment you can run on your own counter.

Geometry as the pipeline’s boundary condition is drawn in One pipeline, three drivers (Figure 5).

This drawer is Part 3's introduction, Chapters 13–16 follow below as their own dropdowns.

60°the V60's cone angle, walls steep enough that the bed piles deep in the centre and thins toward the rim
1 · 3 · openexits: a cone's one large opening, a Kalita Wave's three small holes, an Orea's open ring (five holes only when its separate base is fitted), who meters the flow, you or the brewer
0.24 pts TDSthe smallest TDS difference between any two coffees the triangle tests could tell apart (flat-bottom/fine vs semi-conical/medium, geometry plus grind, a 28% relative strength increase); the authors present it as a minimum estimate that could be lower, not a universal threshold

Chapter 13 · The boundary condition

Geometry sets the path.

What you will learn
