  • Compare cone and flat-bottom beds: depth profile, drainage and where resistance is spent.
  • Use the local Darcy rule q(x) ∝ (h + L(x))/L(x) to reason about flow at a point in the bed.
  • Identify bypass paths in each shape, and what ribs and flutes do about them.
  • State which geometry claims are measured and which are still hypotheses.

Pour over is percolation: water trickling down through a bed of grounds, dissolving as it goes. Anything that changes the journey, how far the water travels, how fast, and whether every ground gets the same treatment, changes the cup. The dripper's shape decides the shape of the bed, and the bed's shape decides the journey. In the language of Chapter 5, geometry is where the L in Darcy's law comes from, and the crucial point is that in most brewers L is not a number. It is a function of position. (The porous-bed modelling behind this local reading runs from Moroney et al. 2015 [5] to Moroney et al. 2019 [6].)

In a cone: deep centre, thin rim, one exit (Diagram)

The grounds pile up deep in the middle and thin at the edges. Water poured in the centre travels through a lot of coffee; water near the walls travels through very little. All of it funnels toward one opening at the tip. The outlet's diameter is not published by Hario (retailer figures of ~20–25 mm conflict), and the folded filter tip protruding through it adds resistance of its own, so “barely restricts” is a qualitative judgement, not a measurement; in practice the bed, the grind and your pour rate do most of the flow control.

On a flat bottom: a wide, even bed with metered exits (Diagram)

The grounds spread into a shallow layer that is even over the central flat base, with depth increasing modestly toward the walls: more uniform than a cone, not uniform. Wherever water enters, it passes through roughly the same amount of coffee, then leaves through several small holes spread across the base, holes that add their own resistance and smooth out differences in how you pour.

q(x) ∝ (h + L(x)) ∕ L(x) Darcy's law, read locally: at any point x in the bed, the flow per unit area follows the local driving head, pool depth h plus the liquid in the bed at that point, divided by the bed depth there. Chapter 5's law, with the depth allowed to vary.

Legend: every symbol

  • q(x): local flux: flow per unit area at position x in the bed.Units: mL/s per cm² (fl oz/s per in²) · Typical: set by the pool above the bed; the pool presses everywhere, but the head at each point includes the liquid in the bed there, so depth differences become flow differences, softened ones
  • L(x): bed depth at position x: the length of the path water must percolate through there.Units: cm (in) · Illustrative profile only, not measured: cone centre depth ≈ 3–4.5 cm (1.2–1.8 in) depending on tip, fold and settling, with depth → 0 at the wall; flat bed ≈ 1.6–2.4 cm (0.6–0.9 in) for a 20 g (0.71 oz) dose, depending on whether the footprint is the 40–45 mm (1.6–1.8 in) paper base or the wider brewer floor. The worked example uses the cone at 4.5 cm centre / 1.5 cm rim and the flat bed at ≈ 1.6 cm, with those footprint and tip assumptions; do not reuse the numbers as facts elsewhere
  • x — position across the bed, from centre to rim.The variable the brewer's shape controls: a flat floor makes L(x) constant; cone walls make L(x) a steep ramp

Worked example: one cone, two brews at once

  1. Take the worked example's cone (illustrative profile, not measured): bed 4.5 cm (1.77 in) deep at the centre and 1.5 cm (0.59 in) deep near the rim, under a pool h = 5 cm (2 in), for a 20 g (0.71 oz) dose in a size-02 cone.
  2. Local flux scales as (h + L) ∕ L: rim flux ∕ centre flux = [(5 + 1.5) ∕ 1.5] ∕ [(5 + 4.5) ∕ 4.5] = 4.33 ∕ 2.11 = ≈ 2.1×. The 3× figure you may expect from 1/L alone is only the h ≫ L limit; as the pool drains toward h = 0 the ratio falls toward 1, and flow convergence inside a real cone makes the true contrast smaller still than this one-dimensional estimate.
  3. Water near the rim therefore moves about twice as fast through about a third as much coffee, a fraction of the centre's contact, on a fraction of the grounds.
  4. Result: the centre trends toward over-extraction while the rim under-extracts, both errors in the same cup, the sour-and-bitter signature of Chapter 10, produced here by geometry alone.

Try yours: after your next cone brew, look at the spent bed. A deep crater or a ring of pale, washed-out grounds at the rim is L(x) made visible, the rim ran a shorter, faster brew than the centre did.

Two failure modes follow directly. Channeling (Chapter 10) is L(x) collapsing locally: a crack or dry pocket offers one streamline a near-zero path length, and flow concentrates there. Bypass is the limiting case, water that skips the bed entirely, running between the paper and the brewer wall or over the paper's edge, reaching the cup having extracted nothing. With 15% bypass and a through-bed stream at 1.35% TDS, the cup reads 0.85 × 1.35% ≈ 1.15% and the yield is ≈ 16%. 19% is the counterfactual yield if that bypassed water had passed through the bed at the same stream strength; the cup's 16% is not an under-report, it is what was actually extracted. The fault is still plumbing, but the arithmetic was never lying.

Depth itself is a dose question, and the honest state of the numbers is this: the 3–5 cm (1.2–2.0 in) bed-depth figure is a batch-brewer rule of thumb (Rao), written for commercial drip machines. No equivalent measured standard exists for one-cup pour-over; Gagné's working range is ~17–23 mm (0.7–0.9 in), which the flat bed's ~1.6 cm (0.63 in) roughly satisfies and the cone's 4.5 cm (1.77 in) centre exceeds. Do not present 2.5–5 cm as a pour-over target. That is still why brewer size matters: 15 g (0.53 oz) makes a thin, channel-prone layer in a large cone but a healthy bed in a small one. Match the dose to the brewer, or L(x) shrinks everywhere at once.

Bed depth across the brewer: cone vs. flat (Chart)

The same dose, two geometries, illustrative profiles only, not measured. The cone concentrates the bed into a deep centre with a thin rim; the flat bed is even over its central base and deepens modestly toward the walls, so Darcy's resistance is far more uniform in one brewer and varies roughly twofold (at a 5 cm pool) in the other.

Schematic profiles for a ~20 g dose, illustrative only, not measured: cone depth falling linearly from 4.5 cm (1.77 in) at the centre to 1.5 cm (0.59 in) at the rim, the worked example's cone (a real 60° cone's bed continues thinner toward the folded filter tip, depth → 0 at the wall; centre depth runs ≈ 3–4.5 cm depending on tip, fold and settling); flat bed at ≈ 1.6 cm (0.63 in) over the 40–45 mm paper base, up to ≈ 2.4 cm if the wider brewer floor is the footprint, deepening modestly toward the walls. Exact depths vary with brewer size, dose and how the grounds settle; the shapes of the two curves are the physics, the decimals are not.

Cross-sections: where the water actually goes (Diagram)

Key takeaways
  • Geometry decides where bed depth, and therefore flow resistance, is spent.
  • A cone concentrates depth at the centre over one exit; a flat bed spreads depth evenly over metered exits.
  • The same brewer is a different system with a different filter, dose or pour: shape never acts alone.
  • Wall contact, paper deformation and drainage resistance compete; more grooves do not automatically mean faster flow.

Chapter 14 · The hardware

Four brewers, three jobs.

What you will learn
  • Ask the three questions of any brewer: how it shapes the bed, vents air and supports the paper, and meters the exit.
  • Trace each reference brewer (V60, Origami, Kalita Wave, Orea) from design to flow to bed to taste.
  • Estimate a bypass share and compute what it does to the cup's TDS and extraction yield.
  • Separate manufacturer fact, measured result and expert judgement in a brewer claim.

Every design detail on a dripper is doing one of three jobs: (1) shaping the bed, cone walls, flat floors, a narrower body; (2) venting air and supporting the paper, ribs, flutes, crimps, teeth, so the wet filter never seals against the wall and chokes the flow; and (3) metering the exit, one big hole, three small holes, five holes in a clip-on base, or no floor at all. Ask those three questions of any brewer and you can predict most of its cup before you brew it. Here are the four reference designs, each followed from design → flow → bed → taste. Dose and time ranges in this chapter are this guide's starting points, not manufacturer specifications. And a standing caution for the whole chapter: no head-to-head evenness or extraction data are presented for these four brewers, so comparative rankings below (“most even extractor”, “often a touch faster”, “extraction climbs noticeably”) are expert judgement, predictions to test (Chapter 16), not results.

Hario V60: the reference cone
  • 60° cone, smooth and steep. The steep walls slide the grounds down into a deep, narrow pile. There is nowhere for coffee to hide, it all stacks toward the tip.
  • Spiral ribs inside the wall. The ribs hold the wet paper slightly off the wall. That gap lets air escape upward as water drains (so flow doesn't “glug” and stall) and gives water at the edges a path down instead of sealing the filter shut. Two honest qualifications: the air-escape account is one explanation, and in an open dripper air has other ways out, so treat it as an account, not a settled mechanism; and the same channels that prevent sealing also carry bypass flow down the walls (Gagné estimates 5–15% in a V60). More or bigger grooves do not monotonically mean faster flow or higher extraction; they trade wall drainage against bypass.
  • One large central hole. The opening restricts flow very little, qualitatively speaking: Hario does not publish its diameter (retailer figures of ~20–25 mm conflict), and the folded filter tip protruding through it contributes resistance of its own. The V60 has no real built-in speed limit, your grind and your pour rate are the flow control.
  • Thin cone filter. V60 papers are relatively thin and fast, adding little resistance and trapping fewer oils than a thick paper, part of the clean-cup reputation.

From design to taste: flow converges diagonally toward the single hole, fast and highly responsive — pour faster and the whole brew speeds up. The bed is deep in the centre, thin at the rim, so by the 1/L rule the centre resists more and extracts longer while the edges see a short, quick path. It is the most technique-sensitive brewer here: uneven pouring creates channels, pouring past the paper's edge creates bypass. Brewed well, the cup is high in clarity and separation of flavours, with lively acidity and lighter body, it tends to reveal a coffee, including its flaws.

Clarity
Acidity
Sweetness
Body

Tendency bars, longer = stronger tendency, schematic 0–100% scale, no units. Tendencies, not measurements, the direction experienced brewers and the Chapter 15 panel data point, for the same coffee across brewers. Practical notes: medium-fine grind (roughly 400–700 µm · 0.016–0.028 in); typical total time 2:15–3:15. Plastic costs least and, as a poor conductor with low thermal mass, takes little heat from the brew itself; ceramic needs preheating, because its mass drinks the first pour's heat until it is warm (Chapter 6's numbers: water's specific heat ≈ 4.18 kJ/(kg·K), thermal conductivity ≈ 0.67 W/(m·K)). Size 01 suits 12–18 g (0.42–0.63 oz) doses; the 02 wants 20 g+ (0.71 oz+) to keep the bed deep enough.

Origami Dripper: one body, two brewers
  • 20 vertical ribs (flutes). Straight flutes run top to bottom, inspired by folded paper. Like the V60's spirals they hold the filter off the porcelain so air can escape and water can move at the walls, with no spiral twist to the flow.
  • Wide, fully open base (≈ 25 mm · 0.98 in). There is no hole pattern at all, just an opening. Whatever filter you use spans it, so the paper and bed, not the brewer, set the drainage.
  • Dual filter compatibility, the whole point. A cone filter seats deep and makes a true cone bed. A Kalita Wave filter sits higher: its pleats engage the ribs (the pleat-and-rib interlock is a plausible mechanism, not a measured one), and its flat base gives the bed a small (~45 mm · 1.8 in) flat floor under a still-conical bed, an intermediate geometry, not a Kalita-equivalent flat bed.
  • Mino-yaki porcelain (or lightweight “Air” resin). Porcelain is heavier and more stable, and needs preheating, since its thermal mass takes heat from the first pour until warm; the Air version is plastic-light for travel.

From design to taste, it splits in two: with a cone filter, flow behaves like a V60, often a touch faster in experienced hands (the opening is wider and the ribs are generous; a judgement, not a measurement), deep bed, central drainage, the same channeling sensitivity, the same bright and clear cup. With a wave filter, the pleats fill the air channels and slow everything down; the bed flattens and shallows, drainage spreads across the paper's flat base, and extraction evens out into a rounder, sweeter cup. It is the only brewer here that lets you A/B the entire subject of this part for the price of a paper filter, Jia Ning Du won the 2019 World Brewers Cup using flat-bottom filters in an Origami.

Clarity (cone / wave)
Acidity (cone-led)
Sweetness (wave-led)
Body (wave-led)

Practical notes: size S ≈ V60 01 / Kalita 155; size M ≈ V60 02 / Kalita 185. It needs its holder or ring stand on many servers. If you can only buy one brewer from this chapter, this is the most flexible choice.

Kalita Wave: the flat benchmark
  • Flat bottom, gently sloped walls. The grounds settle into a shallow disc that is even over the central flat base, deepening modestly toward the walls: no deep centre, no thin-rim problem.
  • Three small holes. The three holes add a significant, head-dependent resistance in series with the bed and the paper. They damp pour-rate differences and stretch contact time, but they do not cap flow absolutely: pour hard enough and the pool still rises. Kalita does not publish the hole diameter.
  • The “Wave” corrugated filter. The filter's 20 waves make the paper touch the brewer only at the crests. The valleys form air channels and keep the wet paper from sealing against the wall and choking drainage, the flat-bed equivalent of the V60's ribs, done by the paper itself.
  • Two sizes. 155 for one cup (roughly 12–20 g · 0.42–0.71 oz), 185 for two to four (roughly 20–40 g · 0.71–1.41 oz). Like the V60, an undersized dose makes a too-thin bed.

From design to taste: flow is slow and steady, damped by the three holes' resistance in series with the bed, water pools gently above the bed and percolates down in parallel columns rather than converging, closer to a slow shower than a funnel. Even depth means even resistance: every part of the bed offers water roughly the same journey. It is, in this guide's judgement, the most even extractor of the four by default, and the least channel-prone (a prediction from its geometry, not a measured ranking); its failure mode is the opposite, stalling, when fine grinds plus heavy swirling migrate fines onto the filter over the three holes (Chapter 5's fines migration, with only three exits to clog). Grind a touch coarser than a V60 and pour gently. The cup: balanced and sweet, softer acidity, rounder body.

Sweetness
Balance
Body
Clarity

Practical notes: medium grind, one or two clicks coarser than your V60 setting; typical total time 3:00–3:45. Wave papers cost noticeably more per brew than V60 papers, the one real running-cost downside.

Orea: the fast modern flat bed
  • An open ring, not a floor. The V3 funnel itself is an open ring: in Orea's words, “you don't have a series of small holes that can easily clog.” Fitted with no base, there are no holes at all and the underside is largely open; brewed coffee exits freely instead of queuing for a hole.
  • Five holes, but in the separate V3 base. The base that clips under the ring carries five holes, one large centre hole plus four around it. With the base fitted, flow is no longer “largely open”, so do not hold both pictures of the V3 at once. Whether its total drainage area beats the Kalita's three holes is unverifiable: neither maker publishes hole diameters.
  • 32 teeth (V3 MK2). The MK2 adds 32 small teeth around the bed. They open tiny air pockets that relieve pressure all around the bed and give already-extracted water small escape paths at the edges, the anti-stall feature that lets it handle flat papers and finer grinds without clogging.
  • Narrower, taller bed than a Kalita. The Orea squeezes a 185-size filter into a narrower body, so the same dose makes a somewhat deeper bed than in a Wave, a middle path between flat-even and cone-deep.
  • Flat papers + the Negotiator = near-zero bypass. Press a flat paper (Orea Flat, or the Sibarist FAST Flat made for it) into shape with the Negotiator tool and the paper hugs the walls, forcing water through the bed. Sibarist claims 15–40% faster flow and zero bypass for the FAST Flat; that is a vendor claim, not independently measured, and any extraction gain at equal brew time is a hypothesis, not a measured result in this guide. The V4 system extends the idea with four swappable bases, Classic, Fast, Open and Apex, of which Apex is a conical insert, not a flat base at all.

From design to taste: the fastest flat bed here, often V60-like drawdown speeds despite the flat geometry, because neither the base nor (with Sibarist paper) the filter meters much. That speed is a tool: it lets you grind finer than the other brewers without stalling. Even extraction is pursued by removing bypass rather than by restricting flow, so with a negotiated flat paper, extraction is expected to climb at the same brew time (the guide's prediction, not a measured result). The cup is the unusual Orea signature: flat-bed sweetness with cone-like clarity and quality acidity — sweet, clear and intense rather than soft and round. The main risk flips back toward the cone's: pour too aggressively into the open base and you can rush under-extraction.

Practical notes: V3 suits roughly 12–28 g (0.42–0.99 oz) doses. Start a click or two finer than your Kalita grind and expect a faster finish. Budget note: the brewer, Negotiator and Sibarist papers are the priciest kit in this chapter.

Three more family members worth naming. The Chemex is a cone whose very thick filter dominates its geometry: Chemex claims its bonded filters are 20–30% heavier than other brands (a manufacturer claim), and paper resistance, not bed shape, runs that brew, which is why it tastes so clean; its spout doubles as an air channel, a groove that lets air escape as coffee drains so the flow does not glug. The Fellow Stagg X is better described as a steep-walled truncated-cone flat-bottom hybrid: a 10-hole pattern with bumps that lift the flat-bottom filter off the holes to prevent clogging (they do not meter flow), and, by Fellow's own specification, steep walls that increase the height of the coffee column, 300 mL (10 oz) single-cup capacity. Its deep bed raises contact, so it behaves less like a Kalita than its flat base suggests. And the April Brewer: a flat bottom with a single large central hole, three support ridges holding the flat filter, and air pockets in the base that regulate pressure under the paper. Nothing meters its exit, so its flow is fast and the grind and the pour set the pace, the flat-bed geometry with a cone's honesty about who is in charge. All of them still answer the same three questions: bed shape, venting, exit.

Worked example: what 10% bypass does to a cup

Chapter 13 defines bypass: water that reaches the cup without passing through the bed. Gagné's estimate for a V60 is 5–15% of the pour. Here is what the middle of that range does to the two numbers of Chapter 3.

  1. The reference brew: 20 g (0.71 oz) dose, 320 g (11.3 oz) of water, the bed keeps 40 g, the beverage is 280 g (9.9 oz).
  2. Suppose 10% of the pour, 32 g, bypasses down the walls and arrives in the cup as plain water. The other 288 g does the extracting, and the liquor that leaves the bed makes up 248 g of the 280 g beverage.
  3. Say that liquor leaves the bed at 1.49% TDS. Dissolved solids in the cup: 1.49% × 248 g = 3.70 g. The bypass adds water but no solids.
  4. Cup TDS = 3.70 g ∕ 280 g = 1.32%. Extraction yield = 1.32% × 280 ∕ 20 = 18.5%: the same solids, spread over more water.

Reading it: bypass dilutes strength without changing the dissolved mass, so TDS falls while the yield computed from the cup still counts the solids honestly. But the bed itself saw less water per gram than the recipe says, so the recipe overstates the water the coffee actually met. Keep the pour inside the paper's edge, and the arithmetic stays simple.

Key takeaways
  • Every design detail does one of three jobs: shaping the bed, venting and supporting the paper, metering the exit.
  • The V60 has no built-in speed limit; the Kalita Wave builds flow control into its exits; the Orea leaves metering to paper and bed.
  • Bypass is a silent diluter: 10% bypass can pull a 1.49% liquor down to about 1.32% in the cup.
  • No head-to-head evenness data are presented for these four brewers; the rankings here are predictions to test in Chapter 16.

Chapter 15 · The evidence

Shape, measured.

What you will learn
  • Summarise the Frost, Ristenpart & Guinard (2019) design: baskets, coffees, panels and measurements.
  • Distinguish main effects from interactions in the study's results.
  • Read a TDS difference properly: absolute points, relative change, and what the panel could detect.
  • List the three caveats that limit how far the results transfer to hand pour-over.

Geometry arguments are easy to make and hard to test, the cup always confounds shape with strength. The key controlled study comes from the UC Davis Coffee Center: Frost, Ristenpart & Guinard (2019), Journal of Food Science. They compared semi-conical and flat-bottom brew baskets in drip brewers (Breville Precision Brewer, Gold Cup setting, 66 g coffee to 1,200 g water, 4 mL/s, 95 °C · 203 °F), varying basket shape, roast level and grind size, combining blind discrimination tests (45 tasters), a trained descriptive panel, consumer testing (85 people) and TDS measurements. One design fact matters for everything below: the two “roast levels” were two different coffees, a dark-roast Latin American blend (Agtron 32.0) and a light-roast Colombian/Ethiopian blend (Agtron 48.8), so every “roast effect” in the study is confounded with coffee and origin [14]. Read the paper (DOI).

45 · 8545 tasters in the blind discrimination (triangle) tests · 85 people in the consumer test behind the liking clusters, nobody knew which basket brewed which cup
0.24 pts TDSthe smallest TDS difference between any two coffees the triangle tests could tell apart (flat-bottom/fine vs semi-conical/medium, geometry plus grind, a 28% relative strength increase); the authors present it as a minimum estimate that could be lower, not a universal threshold
3 of 26flavour attributes moved by geometry alone, but 6 more moved through roast × geometry interactions

What the panels found
  • People could taste the shape. In blind triangle tests, tasters reliably told the two baskets apart (statistically significant, P < 0.05), while the grind contrast was not reliably detectable. Read that narrowly: within the triangle tests' narrow grind contrast (800 vs 1,000 µm median), geometry was discriminable and grind was not. Larger grind changes were not tested in the triangle phase.
  • Semi-conical = stronger. Coffee from the semi-conical basket had significantly higher TDS. The study's 0.24 percentage points TDS figure needs care: it was the smallest difference between any two discriminable triangle-test coffees, and that pair (flat-bottom/fine vs semi-conical/medium) differed in geometry plus grind, a 28% relative strength increase. The authors present it as a minimum estimate that could be lower. It is not the geometry-alone effect, and it is not a universal sensory threshold or JND.
  • Flat = sweeter, and that is nearly the whole main-effect story. Sweetness is a genuine geometry main effect (flat 25.28 vs semi-conical 22.05, p < 0.05), one of only three attributes geometry moved on its own, alongside smoke aroma and tobacco flavour. Two attributions this guide previously made do not survive the paper's Table 3: dried-fruit and floral were not flat-basket geometry effects in light roast (floral geometry means: flat 35.32 vs semi-conical 35.11, essentially equal; dried fruit showed no significant geometry effect), and chocolate and cocoa were not flat-basket effects in dark roast (chocolate 24.36 vs 24.74; cocoa 21.49 vs 21.97, equal). Those belong to roast, or to noise, not to shape.
  • Semi-conical = brighter in light roast, harsher in dark. The semi-conical basket scored higher for citrus, berry and sour notes in light roasts, and for bitterness, burnt wood and earthy notes in dark roasts. All of these are roast × geometry interactions, not main effects: shape changed what the roast expressed.
  • It's the interactions that matter. Geometry on its own was significant for only 3 of 26 flavour attributes (smoke aroma, sweetness and tobacco flavour). Roast × geometry interactions were significant for 6 attributes (berry, bitterness, burnt wood/ash, citrus, earthy and sourness) and grind × geometry for 2, shape changes how other variables express themselves.
  • Sample sizes, test by test, with their limits. Blind discrimination (triangle) tests: n = 45. The trained descriptive panel had 12 panellists (six female, six male, ages 18–34), prepared with 5 training sessions over 2 weeks, rating 26 attributes on a 15 cm line scale, and note how they were chosen: selected from the triangle tasters for correctly discriminating at least 4 coffee pairs, a selected, better-than-average panel. Consumer testing: n = 85, of whom 80% were aged 18–24, 62.4% women, 43.5% Asian/Pacific Islander, and 57.6% drank 0–1 cup of coffee a day.
  • No universal winner, and a narrow base. Consumer liking (n = 85) split into four preference clusters (n = 16 / 25 / 25 / 19). For every cluster, some combination of geometry and roast was liked less. Given who the 85 were, the clusters show that drinkers differ; they do not generalise to “different drinkers” at large.

Read the study carefully: three caveats
  • It was drip machines, not hand pour-over. The baskets sat in automatic drip brewers with controlled flow. The geometry lesson transfers, but a hand-poured V60 adds your pouring technique on top.
  • “Semi-conical” isn't a V60. The study's semi-conical basket is elongated and non-axisymmetric, with a 2 cm (0.8 in) flat bottom: a truncated trough, not a 60° cone. The direction of an effect may transfer to a V60; the magnitude, and even the sign of some interactions, need not.
  • Strength and extraction were linked. Part of why the cups tasted different is that one was simply stronger (higher TDS). A fair home test should measure TDS, which is exactly what the experiment in Chapter 16 does.

The takeaway: geometry influences extraction distribution and hydraulic behaviour, but it does not independently determine extraction quality or flavour. It works through and with roast, grind and flow. Anyone who tells you one shape is simply “better” is skipping the interesting part.

Side by side: cone (V60) vs. flat (Kalita Wave)

Conical, V60

  • Bed depth, deeper, piled in the centre
  • Bed shape, narrow at the bottom, tapered
  • Drainage, one large central hole; your grind & pour set the speed
  • Flow sensitivity — high; technique shows in the cup
  • Extraction pattern, variable with bed depth; centre vs. edges differ
  • Typical grind, medium-fine (about 400–700 µm · 0.016–0.028 in)
  • Typical total time*, about 2:15–3:15
  • Flavour associations, clarity, acidity, citrus & berry (tendencies; citrus and berry are roast × geometry interactions in the study*)
  • Forgiveness, lower floor, higher ceiling

Flat-bottom, Kalita Wave

  • Bed depth, shallower, spread evenly
  • Bed shape, wide and flat
  • Drainage, three small holes; the brewer meters the speed
  • Flow sensitivity, lower; small mistakes are smoothed out
  • Extraction pattern, more uniform across the bed
  • Typical grind, medium, a touch coarser than V60
  • Typical total time*, about 3:00–3:45
  • Flavour associations, sweetness, balance (tendencies; sweetness is the study's one clear flat-basket flavour effect, dried fruit and chocolate were not geometry effects*)
  • Forgiveness, higher floor, slightly lower ceiling

*Times are common starting targets for a ~300–400 g (10.6–14.1 oz · 10.1–13.5 fl oz) brew from home-brewing guides, not rules, dose, grind and coffee change them. Let taste, not the timer, have the last word. On the study references: Frost et al. tested Breville drip baskets, not a V60 or a Kalita Wave; the tendencies above are transfers, not measurements of these two brewers.

The variables that can outweigh shape

Shape sets the stage; these set the performance, roughly in order of impact. Buying a different dripper before fixing your grind or your pour is like buying a different pan before learning heat control.

  • Grind size & consistency, biggest lever. Grind controls both surface area (Chapter 2's diffusion distance) and bed openness (Chapter 5's permeability). Uneven grind can't be fixed by any bed shape: the fines race far ahead of the boulders in the same brew, though measured espresso work (Smrke et al. 2024, Chapter 4) shows the fines' largest effect is slowing the water down rather than pushing extraction up, since yield followed shot time on the same curve with or without added fines.
  • Pouring technique & agitation — biggest lever. Where you pour, how fast, and how much you swirl decides saturation and channeling, decisive in a cone, gentler in a flat bed. Agitation also stirs fines toward the filter and can stall drawdown.
  • Water temperature, strong. Hotter water extracts faster (Chapter 6's Arrhenius law). The SCA brewing window is about 90–96 °C (194–205 °F) at contact; a few degrees can shift a brew as much as a shape change.
  • Ratio & dose, strong. Coffee-to-water ratio sets strength, and the dose sets bed depth in a given brewer. Start near 1:15–1:17 (e.g. 20 g · 0.71 oz coffee to 320 g · 11.3 oz / 10.8 fl oz water) and adjust to taste.
  • Filter paper, often overlooked. Paper thickness and speed change flow as much as holes do, a thick Chemex filter dominates its cone shape, and fast flat papers transform an Orea. Paper also traps oils, shaping clarity and body.
  • Bypass & outlet design, often overlooked. Water that slips around the bed dilutes without extracting. Hole number, size and filter fit (not just bed shape) decide how much bypass and restriction a brewer has.

Worked example: reading Frost's TDS numbers

Three numbers from this chapter, read slowly. This is the skill the whole chapter is teaching.

  1. The 0.24 points. The smallest TDS difference the triangle tasters could tell apart was 0.24 percentage points, between coffees at about 0.86% and 1.10% TDS (the levels implied by the paper's own pair of numbers). Relative change: 0.24 ∕ 0.86 ≈ 0.28, a 28% jump in strength. A “small” absolute gap was a large relative one, because the base was low.
  2. The sweetness effect. Flat 25.28 vs semi-conical 22.05 on the panel's 15 cm scale: a difference of 3.23 points, which is 3.23 ∕ 22.05 ≈ 15% relative to the semi-conical mean, and about a fifth of the whole scale (3.23 ∕ 15 ≈ 0.22).
  3. The non-effect. Floral: flat 35.32 vs semi-conical 35.11, a difference of 0.21, about 0.6% relative. Same arithmetic, opposite conclusion: that is what “essentially equal” looks like in numbers.

Reading it: never quote a difference without its base. Points, percent and share of scale are three different claims, and a result can be large in one and trivial in another. The authors' own caution applies throughout: 0.24 points is a minimum estimate from one design, not a universal threshold.

Key takeaways
  • Geometry alone moved only 3 of 26 flavour attributes; the bigger story is interactions: shape changes what roast and grind express.
  • Sweetness is the study's one clear flat-basket flavour effect (25.28 vs 22.05 on the panel scale).
  • The 0.24-point TDS figure is a minimum estimate from a pair differing in geometry plus grind, not a universal taste threshold.
  • It was drip machines and a truncated semi-conical basket, not a V60: direction may transfer, magnitude need not.

Chapter 16 · The experiment

Change one thing: the brewer.

What you will learn
  • Design a one-variable home experiment on the UC Davis pattern: lock everything except the brewer.
  • Run the protocol: bloom, pulses, drawdown, beverage mass, TDS and blind tasting.
  • Analyse repeats with mean, range and standard deviation, and report the spread, not the best cup.
  • State a prediction before brewing, and let your logged results overrule it.

A hypothesis-testing home experiment modelled on the UC Davis design, change only the brewer. It tests predictions; it does not control everything a laboratory would, and its results are yours, for your coffee and your hands. You'll need a Hario V60, a Kalita Wave, the same bag of coffee, a scale, a timer, a gooseneck kettle if you have one, and ideally a coffee refractometer (a borrowed or café one works, tasting notes alone are still worthwhile without it).

Lock everything else down: same coffee and roast date · 20 g (0.71 oz) dose in both brews · 320 g (11.3 oz · 10.8 fl oz) water (1:16) · same water at 94 °C (201 °F) · same grind setting* · same pour pattern and timing. *Purists run it twice: once at the identical grind (tests pure geometry) and once with each brewer dialled to the same total time (tests each at its best). Both are informative, just label which is which.

0:00–0:40Bloom · 40–50 g (1.4–1.8 oz), wet all the grounds, swirl gently, let the CO2 escape (Chapter 8)
0:40–1:30Pour in pulses to 320 g (11.3 oz), slow spirals from the centre out, same pattern, height and speed in both brewers
→ finishDrawdown, watch the stream slow to drips and write the time down. This is where the shapes separate
  • 1 · Rinse both filters with hot water, this removes paper taste and preheats the brewers.
  • 2 · Bloom: add grounds, pour 40–50 g (1.4–1.8 oz · 1.4–1.7 fl oz) of water, 2–2.5× the dose, the range this guide standardises on: enough to wet every ground with margin, not so much that extraction starts in earnest, swirl gently, wait 40 seconds. Start the timer at first pour.
  • 3 · Pour in pulses to 320 g (11.3 oz) total by about 1:30, using the same spiral pattern and pour height for both brewers.
  • 4 · Record drawdown time, when the stream slows to occasional drips. Note the bed's look afterward: flat and even, cratered, or muddy on top (a sign of fines).
  • 5 · Weigh the finished beverage. It will be less than 320 g (11.3 oz), grounds hold on to roughly 2 g (0.07 oz) of water per gram (0.035 oz) of coffee.
  • 6 · Measure TDS if you have a refractometer: cool a spoonful, place it on the prism, read the %. Then run it through the calculator in Chapter 3 to get extraction yield for each brewer. No refractometer? Skip to taste, and repeat the brew on another day to check repeatability instead.
  • 7 · Taste blind. Have someone pour both into identical cups and label the bottoms, and randomise the order you brew and taste in, so fatigue and expectation do not line up with one brewer. Note sweetness, acidity, bitterness, clarity and body before you peek.
  • 8 · Repeat each brewer at least 3 times across a few days, logging all of the runs, drawdown time, beverage mass, TDS, extraction yield and taste notes, and report the spread (range, or standard deviation if you compute it), not just the best cup. The spread of your results is the repeatability measurement. The prediction to test, stated before you start and with no prior evidence cited in this guide: the flat bed's times and tastes cluster tighter than the cone's.

The predictions, labelled as predictions: the V60 finishes faster, tastes brighter, and varies more between attempts; the Wave finishes slower, tastes rounder and sweeter, and repeats more easily, with its results clustering tighter. If your logged results differ, trust yours: your coffee, water and hands are the experiment that matters.

So which should you pick?
  • Pick the cone if… you chase clarity and bright, distinct flavours, mostly brew light roasts, and enjoy dialling in a recipe. Start with a V60; try an Origami if you want both shapes in one brewer.
  • Pick the flat bed if… you want a sweet, balanced cup that comes out right on a busy morning, brew for more than one person, or are just starting out. Start with a Kalita Wave 185; try an Orea if you like fast brews and experimenting with papers.
  • Own both if… you brew a wide range of coffees. Many home brewers do exactly this: flat bed for daily consistency and darker roasts, cone for special light-roast bags on weekends. The research says preference is personal, your three brews above settle it.

The bottom line: geometry influences extraction distribution and hydraulic behaviour, but it does not independently determine extraction quality or flavour. A cone concentrates the action, deeper bed, single exit, more in your hands. A flat bed spreads the action, even bed, distributed drainage, more built-in forgiveness. Choose the shape that matches your coffee and your mornings, then let grind, temperature and pour do the fine-tuning.

Worked example: analysing five repeats

Step 8 above asks for the spread, not just the best cup. Here is the analysis on example numbers (an illustration of the method, not measured results): five V60 brews and five Kalita Wave brews, same coffee, TDS read on the same refractometer.

  1. V60 readings: 1.30, 1.34, 1.27, 1.33, 1.31. Mean = (1.30 + 1.34 + 1.27 + 1.33 + 1.31) ∕ 5 = 6.55 ∕ 5 = 1.31%.
  2. Range = 1.34 − 1.27 = 0.07 points. Standard deviation: the readings sit −0.01, +0.03, −0.04, +0.02 and 0.00 from the mean; squared and summed, that is 0.0030; divide by 4 (one fewer than the count, the usual sample rule) to get 0.00075; the square root is ≈ 0.03 points.
  3. Wave readings: 1.31, 1.32, 1.30, 1.32, 1.31. Mean = 1.31%, range = 0.02 points, standard deviation ≈ 0.01 points.
  4. Same means, different spreads: on these example numbers the two brewers agree on strength and differ on repeatability, which is exactly the prediction this chapter asks you to test.

Reading it: report both numbers every time: “1.31%, spread 0.03” for the cone against “1.31%, spread 0.01” for the flat bed. A mean without a spread hides the property that decides busy mornings. With your own logs, run the identical arithmetic; five repeats per brewer is the minimum that makes a spread worth quoting.

Key takeaways
  • Change one thing: if two variables move, the experiment answers nothing.
  • Repeatability is a measurement: the spread of your repeats is the result, not a nuisance.
  • Five brews per brewer across a few days beat one perfect brew: report mean and spread for both.
  • Blind tasting defends the instrument: expectation bends scores before the coffee reaches the tongue.

Part 4 · Introduction

The Science Behind It

Parts 1–3 built the physics of the cup. Part 4 maps the knowledge itself: the scientific disciplines it draws on, the researchers and educators who produced it, the peer-reviewed library underneath it, and the engineering models and experimental method that tie it together, so you can tell, for anything in this guide, what kind of evidence it stands on.

Where the five processes meet, and how the guide itself is organised, is mapped in How everything fits together (Figures 2–5).

This drawer is Part 4's introduction, Chapters 17–21 follow below as their own dropdowns.

Chapter 17 · The map of the field

Seven disciplines, one cup.

What you will learn
  • Name the seven disciplines that meet in a cup, and the chapters each one powers.
  • Place any coffee claim on the evidence ladder: peer-reviewed, technical education, industry research or hypothesis.
  • Match a brewing question to the discipline that can actually answer it.

No single science owns coffee. A brew is a fluid-mechanics problem, a mass-transfer problem, a heat-transfer problem and a chemistry problem running simultaneously inside a fractured particle, and it ends as a neuroscience problem, in a taster. Each chapter of this guide belongs to a discipline, and each discipline brings its own instruments and its own standard of proof. This chapter is the map: what each field covers, where it applies in the brew, and who works in it.

It starts with a rule the whole of Part 4 follows. Claims come in grades, and the grade is part of the claim:

How a claim earns its place here

Four grades of evidence, strongest first. A claim is only ever as good as the grade it can honestly carry.

Peer-reviewed

authors · journal · methods

↓

Technical education

educators’ own experiments

↓

Industry research

labs · manufacturers · institutes

↓

Hypothesis

proposed · not yet validated

The standing rule: measured results, theoretical models, expert interpretations and personal observations are four different things. Where this guide uses one, it says which.

Fluid mechanics

The science of Chapters 5 and 9: how water moves through the bed, the filter and the puck. Applies to: pour-over water movement, bed saturation, filter drainage, brewer rib geometry, espresso pressure, flow distribution.

Key researchers: William Ristenpart · Jonathan Gagné · Kevin Moroney · Marco Ellero

Laminar flowTurbulent flowCapillary actionPressure differentialsDarcy’s lawPorous mediaPermeabilityChannelingFlow resistance

Mass transfer & extraction kinetics

The science of Chapters 2 and 3: how dissolved compounds move from inside a particle into the water, and how fast. Applies to: extraction yield, bed saturation, brew time, particle size, extraction uniformity.

Key researchers: Christopher Hendon · William Ristenpart · Kevin Moroney · Jonathan Gagné

Fick’s laws of diffusionMolecular diffusionSolubilityConcentration gradientsMass transfer coefficientsExtraction kineticsSelective extractionSurface area : volume

Thermodynamics & heat transfer

The science of Chapters 1 and 6: where the heat goes, and how it rewrites every rate in the system. Applies to: brewer materials, water temperature, slurry temperature, roasting, extraction kinetics.

Thermal conductivitySpecific heat capacityConvectionConductionEvaporative coolingTemperature gradientsThermal equilibrium

Particle mechanics & tribology

The science of Chapter 4: how beans fracture, what sizes result, and how particles rub, charge and migrate. Applies to: burr geometry, grinding consistency, fines production, grinder alignment, static reduction, particle migration.

Key researchers: Erol Uman · Christopher Hendon · Matt Perger · Lance Hedrick

Fracture mechanicsParticle size distributionParticle morphologyBimodal distributionsElectrostatic chargingMechanical energySurface areaFriction & wear

Brewer geometry & material science

The science of Part 3: the vessel as an engineered object whose shape and surface set the boundary conditions. Applies to: cone versus flat-bottom brewers, V60 rib configuration, Kalita Wave geometry, April brewer geometry, Origami geometry, filter paper construction.

Geometric optimizationHydraulic resistanceSurface roughnessBoundary layersPorosityFilter permeabilityDrainage dynamics

Analytical & physical chemistry

The science of Chapter 7: what is actually in the water and the cup, measured molecule by molecule. Applies to: coffee water composition, flavour development, roasting chemistry, beverage composition, aroma formation.

Key researchers: Christopher Hendon · Malin Nording · Jean-Xavier Guinard

pHTitratable acidityOrganic acidsWater mineralizationIon interactionsChemical kineticsMaillard reactionsLipid chemistryVolatile compounds

Sensory science & neuroscience

The discipline that measures the output everything else is for: perception itself. It is what turns “the panel preferred it” from an anecdote into a measurement, the Frost study in Chapter 15 is this discipline at work. Applies to: cupping, flavour identification, perceived sweetness, perceived acidity, mouthfeel, blind sensory evaluation.

Olfactory perceptionRetronasal olfactionTaste receptorsPsychophysicsSensory adaptationMultisensory integrationStatistical sensory analysis

Key takeaways
  • One cup, seven disciplines: fluid mechanics, mass transfer, thermodynamics, particle mechanics, geometry and materials, analytical chemistry, sensory science.
  • The evidence ladder grades every claim in the guide; a claim is worth what its rung is worth.
  • Most brewing arguments are two disciplines talking past each other: name the discipline and the argument usually dissolves.

Chapter 18 · The people

Who produced the physics.

What you will learn
  • Name the researchers behind the guide's core models, and the institutions they work in.
  • Distinguish the scientists and engineers from the technical educators, and what each group contributes.
  • Follow one result from its paper to the chapter that uses it.

Coffee science has two kinds of contributor, and the distinction matters for how much weight a claim can carry. Scientists and engineers publish peer-reviewed work, measured, modelled, and checked by other experts before it appears. Technical educators run careful experiments of their own and translate the literature into practice; their results are real, but they have not passed peer review. Neither is “better”, they answer different questions. What follows is the field’s working roster, with the evidence grade attached.

The scientists & engineers: nine profiles
  • Christopher Hendon, computational and physical chemist working on coffee extraction, water chemistry and molecular interactions. His 2014 paper showed how dissolved magnesium, calcium and sodium interact with coffee compounds and shape extraction (doi:10.1021/jf501687c); in 2020 he co-authored the mathematical model of espresso that anchors Chapter 9 (doi:10.1016/j.matt.2019.12.019).
  • William Ristenpart, chemical engineer at the UC Davis Coffee Center: fluid mechanics, transport phenomena, colloid science and coffee process engineering. Author of The Design of Coffee: An Engineering Approach, and a lead figure in the Coffee Science Foundation’s brewing-fundamentals research, the engineering framing behind Chapters 5 and 15.
  • Jonathan Gagné, physicist whose experimental brewing research covers grind distribution, percolation, water flow, extraction kinetics, brewer geometry and temperature dynamics, published in the books The Physics of Filter Coffee and The Physics of Espresso and at Coffee Ad Astra [47]. The percolation and temperature work runs through Parts 1 and 3 of this guide.
  • Jean-Xavier Guinard, sensory scientist at the UC Davis Coffee Center: coffee sensory evaluation, flavour perception, consumer preferences and flavour classification. The sensory half of the basket-geometry study in Chapter 15 is his discipline in action.
  • Kevin Moroney — applied mathematician modelling porous coffee beds with computational fluid dynamics. His 2019 PLOS ONE paper modelled water distribution and extraction uniformity through a bed, the mathematics behind “evenness” in Chapters 5 and 13 (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0219906). Affiliations: Moroney, Lee and O'Brien work at MACSI (the Mathematics Applications Consortium for Science and Industry), Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Limerick; the 2015 multiscale model [5] was written with F. Suijver and J. Marra of Philips Research, Eindhoven (Chemical Engineering Science 137 (2015) 216–234).
  • Erol Uman, grinding researcher measuring particle size distributions. His 2016 Scientific Reports study showed how bean origin and bean temperature change the distribution a grinder produces, Chapter 4’s evidence that the grind is a population, not a number (doi:10.1038/srep24483).
  • Malin Nording, analytical chemist working in metabolomics, mass spectrometry and NMR. Her 2024 Heliyon study measured, by GC-MS and NMR, how magnesium and calcium change which organic acids extract, Chapter 7’s water chemistry, verified molecule by molecule (doi:10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e26625).
  • Marco Ellero, computational fluid dynamicist simulating espresso extraction: particle migration, coffee-bed permeability and hydrodynamic erosion. Co-author of the 2019 mesoscopic espresso simulation in the library below.
  • Luciano Navarini, food scientist in industrial coffee research: espresso extraction, coffee-bed structure, extraction kinetics and coffee processing. The industrial-laboratory perspective, industry research, in the evidence ladder’s terms.

The technical educators: six profiles
  • James Hoffmann, coffee educator, author and experimentalist: brewing methodology, grinder comparisons, espresso extraction, equipment testing, sensory evaluation, roasting and processing. His contribution is translation, turning coffee research and practical experimentation into accessible brewing knowledge. Evidence: technical education and practical experimentation.
  • Lance Hedrick, coffee educator and technical experimentalist: grinder engineering, burr geometry, espresso extraction, pour-over technique, pressure profiling, particle distribution. Known for technical equipment comparisons and experiments that explain extraction mechanics. Evidence: technical education and independent experimentation.
  • Scott Rao [46], coffee consultant and technical author: extraction theory, espresso preparation, roasting science, brew ratios, processing and extraction consistency. Provides practical frameworks and technical interpretations of extraction.
  • Matt Perger, coffee competitor, researcher and equipment innovator: grinder engineering, particle size distribution, extraction optimization, equipment and brewing consistency. An experimental approach to grinder performance.
  • Lukas Zahradnik, coffee competitor and technical practitioner: espresso extraction, brewing variables, equipment optimization and sensory evaluation, a practical exploration of espresso preparation and repeatability.
  • Patrik Rolf, coffee entrepreneur and technical brewing educator at April Coffee: pour-over brewing, brewer design, extraction recipes, roasting and brewing experimentation. His brewer-design work is Part 3’s geometry questions asked from the maker’s side.

The institutions
  • UC Davis Coffee Center, the university research centre where Ristenpart and Guinard work: coffee engineering, brewing science, sensory research and coffee education under one roof.
  • Coffee Science Foundation, funds and publishes peer-reviewed coffee research, including the brewing-fundamentals programme, industry money, journal standards.
  • Specialty Coffee Association, the trade body behind the standards this guide uses: the brewing control chart’s preferred window, water quality targets, brewing measurement and sensory protocols.
  • Coffee Excellence Center — research institute focused on coffee quality, analytical chemistry, coffee processing, and research and education.

Key takeaways
  • The porous-bed mathematics comes largely from Limerick: Moroney, Lee and O'Brien at MACSI, with Suijver and Marra at Philips Research on the 2015 model.
  • Educators translate and test in public; their claims carry the technical-education grade, below peer review and above anecdote.
  • Institutions matter: the UC Davis Coffee Center and ZHAW run the panels and instruments behind the sensory and fines results.

Twelve papers under the guide.

What you will learn
  • List the twelve papers the guide stands on, and the claim each one carries.
  • Read a coffee paper's methods before its conclusions: sample, controls, confounds.
  • Check a citation: authors, year, journal, DOI, and whether the paper supports the claim made for it.

In plain terms: this is the reading list the guide stands on. The twelve papers below are the core shelf; further claims across the guide rest on additional cited papers, References [15]–[25]. The twelfth entry, Frost et al. 2019, was added in this edition: it is the evidence base for Chapters 15 and 21 and was previously cited only in References (it belongs on this shelf) published research with named authors, a journal, and a method other scientists can check. Each entry gives the paper’s area and its DOI, the permanent address that takes you straight to it.

  • The Role of Dissolved Cations in Coffee Extraction, Hendon, Colonna-Dashwood & Colonna-Dashwood, 2014, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry. Water chemistry and molecular interactions, the paper behind Chapter 7. doi:10.1021/jf501687c
  • The Effect of Bean Origin and Temperature on Grinding Roasted Coffee, Uman et al., 2016, Scientific Reports 6, 24483. Particle mechanics and grinding, the paper behind Chapter 4. doi:10.1038/srep24483
  • Modelling of Coffee Extraction During Brewing Using Multiscale Methods: An Experimentally Validated Model, Moroney, Lee, O'Brien, Suijver & Marra, 2015, Chemical Engineering Science. Extraction kinetics and mathematical modeling. doi:10.1016/j.ces.2015.06.003
  • Analysing Extraction Uniformity from Porous Coffee Beds Using Mathematical Modelling and Computational Fluid Dynamics Approaches, Moroney, O’Connell, Meikle-Janney, O’Brien, Walker & Lee, 2019, PLOS ONE. Computational fluid dynamics and porous media. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0219906
  • Mathematical Model for Coffee Extraction Based on the Volume Averaging Theory, Sano, Kubota, Kawarazaki, Kawamura, Kashiwai & Kuwahara, 2019, Journal of Food Engineering. Mathematical modeling of drip and espresso extraction. doi:10.1016/j.jfoodeng.2019.05.025
  • Mesoscopic Modelling and Simulation of Espresso Coffee Extraction, Ellero & Navarini, 2019, Journal of Food Engineering. Particle migration and espresso extraction. doi:10.1016/j.jfoodeng.2019.05.038
  • Systematically Improving Espresso: Insights from Mathematical Modeling and Experiment, Cameron, Morisco, Hofstetter, Uman, Wilkinson, Kennedy, Fontenot, Lee, Hendon & Foster, 2020, Matter. Espresso engineering and optimization, the model behind Chapter 9. doi:10.1016/j.matt.2019.12.019
  • Modeling the Effect of Flow-Induced Mechanical Erosion During Coffee Filtration, Mo, Johnston, Navarini & Ellero, 2021, Physics of Fluids. Hydrodynamic forces and coffee bed deformation, flow slowly reshaping the bed it passes through. doi:10.1063/5.0059707
  • Strategies to Mitigate Electrostatic Charging During Coffee Grinding, Méndez Harper, Bumbaugh & Hendon, 2024, iScience. Electrostatics and particle distribution, why grounds cling, scatter, and skew the distribution. doi:10.1016/j.isci.2024.110639
  • Influence of Divalent Cations on the Extraction of Organic Acids in Coffee Determined by GC-MS and NMR, Bratthäll, Figueira & Nording, 2024, Heliyon 10(5), e26625. Water chemistry and analytical chemistry. doi:10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e26625
  • Direct Electrochemical Appraisal of Black Coffee Quality Using Cyclic Voltammetry, Bumbaugh, Pennington, Wehn, Rheingold, Williams, Aleman & Hendon, 2026, Nature Communications. Electrochemistry and beverage quality measurement, the newest entry: quality read from the coffee’s electrical signature rather than a refractometer. doi:10.1038/s41467-026-71526-5
  • Effect of Basket Geometry on the Sensory Quality and Consumer Acceptance of Drip Brewed Coffee, Frost, Ristenpart & Guinard, 2019, Journal of Food Science 84(8), 2297–2312. Sensory science and brewer geometry — the study behind Chapters 15 and 21: the smallest discriminable TDS gap between any two coffees was 0.24 percentage points (a geometry-plus-grind pair, presented by the authors as a minimum estimate), with discrimination tested on 45 tasters and consumer liking on 85 people. doi:10.1111/1750-3841.14696

How to read a coffee paper
  • Start with the method, not the headline. What was actually varied, what was held fixed, and what was measured? A paper’s conclusions can never be stronger than that design.
  • Check the replication. How many brews, how many tasters, how many beans? One-off results are weather; replicated results are climate.
  • Separate measurement from interpretation. The results section is what happened; the discussion is what the authors think it means. Both are valuable, they are not the same grade of evidence.
  • A model is validated only where it was tested. An espresso model checked at 9 bar (131 psi) says nothing, by itself, about a gravity dripper, the equations may transfer, the validation does not.
  • Sensory claims need blind panels. If the tasters knew which cup was which, treat the preference as a hypothesis, however expert the tasters are.

Key takeaways
  • Twelve papers carry most of the guide's measured claims; everything else is labelled by its evidence grade.
  • A DOI is a permanent link to the paper itself; prefer it over any summary of the paper.
  • The library is a floor, not a ceiling: the bibliography adds standards, books and the further-reading lists.

Chapter 20 · Models & method

Four more equations, and how to test them.

What you will learn
  • Use the rest of the transport toolkit: Fick's flux, flow rate, Reynolds number and SA/V.
  • Decide, with the Reynolds number, whether Darcy's law is the right model for a bed.
  • Run an experiment you can believe: controls, repeats, blinding and honest reporting.
  • Choose from the nine experiments and the measurement toolkit the test that answers your question.

In plain terms: four short equations complete the toolkit, how diffusion flows, how fast you are pouring, whether the flow is gentle or turbulent, and why small particles extract so much faster. After them, the chapter closes with the working method of the whole field: how to run an experiment whose result you can actually believe, and the order to learn all of this in.

How the variables flow into the cup

Four knobs you control, two processes they act through, one set of numbers you measure. Every recipe change in this guide travels this exact path.

Four knobs you control

Grind size

Temperature

Water chemistry

Time · ratio · pour

↓

Extraction

flow through the bed (Darcy)

+ diffusion out of the particle (Fick)

↓

The cup

strength (TDS) · extraction yield

and the flavour you taste

Work backwards when a cup misses: taste points at the cup, the numbers point at extraction, and only then do you know which knob to turn, one at a time.

J = −D · (dC ∕ dx) Fick’s first law, J: diffusion flux · D: diffusion coefficient · dC/dx: the concentration gradient. Its partner, Fick’s second law, ∂C/∂t = D∇²C, says how concentration at a point changes over time; Chapter 2's d² law is that equation's timescale read off a sphere.

Legend: every symbol

  • J: diffusion flux: how much dissolved material crosses a unit area per second, driven purely by the gradient.Units: mol/(m²·s) (or g/(m²·s)) · Direction: always from high concentration toward low, that is what the minus sign says
  • D: diffusion coefficient of the compound in the wet particle.Units: m²/s · Typical: ~2.5 × 10−9 m²/s in this guide’s model, the same lumped, fitted effective D as Chapter 2, not a measured intraparticle value
  • dC/dx: the concentration gradient: how steeply concentration falls with distance from the particle’s core to its surface.Units: (g/m³)/m · Typical: steepest at the start of the brew, when the particle is loaded and the surrounding water is fresh; flattens as the water saturates, which is why agitation (Chapter 2) restarts extraction

Worked example: the flux out of a fresh particle

  1. At the start of a brew, take the concentration inside a particle as ≈ 300 g/L (about 300 g per 33.8 fl oz, i.e. per litre) of soluble material (the bean is ~30% soluble, packed dense) and the fresh water outside as ≈ 0 g/L.
  2. The drop happens across roughly the particle’s radius: for a 600 µm (0.024 in) particle, Δx ≈ 300 µm (0.012 in) = 3 × 10−4 m. So dC/dx ≈ (300,000 g/m³ − 0) ∕ 3 × 10−4 m = 1 × 109 g/m⁴.
  3. Multiply by D = 2.5 × 10−9 m²/s: J = 2.5 × 10−9 × 1 × 109 = 2.5 g/(m²·s) on paper. Read that as an order-of-magnitude initial flux only: it is inconsistent with Chapter 2's τ model by roughly 9×, because a linear gradient across the radius is not the spherical-diffusion solution. Do not quote 2.5 g/(m²·s) as a flux; the number's job is to show the gradient's scale at the first instant.
  4. As the brew proceeds the inside empties and the outside fills, the gradient flattens, and J falls with it, the mathematical shape of “extraction slows down”.

Try yours: halve the particle size and the gradient’s distance halves too, the same concentration drop across half the distance doubles the gradient, and diffusion time (Chapter 2) falls fourfold. Fick’s law and the d² law are the same physics read twice.

Q = Volume ∕ Time The simplest equation in the guide, and the one your scale and timer already measure

Legend: every symbol

  • Q: average flow rate over the interval you measured.Units: mL/s, g/s or fl oz/s (for water, 1 mL ≈ 1 g ≈ 0.034 fl oz) · Typical: a 320 g (11.3 oz · 10.8 fl oz) pour-over delivered in ~150 s of pouring averages ≈ 2.1 g/s (0.07 fl oz/s)
  • Volume: the water delivered (or drained) in the interval.Units: mL, g, fl oz or oz · Read straight off the scale under the brewer (1 fl oz of water ≈ 29.6 g)
  • Time — the length of the interval.Units: seconds (s) · Measure delivery and drawdown separately, they answer different questions

Worked example: is the bed or your hand in charge?

  1. You pour 320 g (11.3 oz) in pulses over 150 s: delivery Q = 320 ∕ 150 ≈ 2.1 g/s (0.07 fl oz/s).
  2. After the last pour, the pool takes 45 s to drain the final 60 g (2.1 oz): drainage Q = 60 ∕ 45 ≈ 1.3 g/s (0.04 fl oz/s).
  3. Drainage is slower than delivery, so the bed (Darcy’s law, Chapter 5) is metering the end of this brew, not your kettle.

Try yours: time your drawdown after the last pour and divide the pooled water by the seconds. If that Q collapses brew over brew at the same recipe, permeability is falling, think fines (Chapter 4) before you think grind setting.

Re = ρvD ∕ μ Reynolds number, the ratio of inertial to viscous forces: which kind of flow you have

Legend: every symbol

  • Re: Reynolds number, dimensionless. Below ~1, flow in a porous bed is smooth, laminar “creeping” flow, Darcy’s law’s home ground. Thousands and up means turbulence.Typical: ≈ 0.05–0.5 inside a coffee bed (pore-scale Re, built from the interstitial velocity and the pore-throat diameter, as in the worked example) · ~2,000 in a kettle spout’s stream
  • ρ (rho), density of the water.Units: kg/m³ (lb/ft³) · Typical: ≈ 963 kg/m³ (60.1 lb/ft³) at 93 °C (199 °F) (≈ 1,000 kg/m³ · 62.4 lb/ft³ at room temperature)
  • v: flow velocity through the pores.Units: m/s (in/s) · Typical: ~3 × 10−4 m/s (0.012 in/s) percolating through a filter bed, which is 18 mm/min (0.72 in/min)
  • D: the characteristic length: here, the pore size.Units: m (in) · Typical: ~50 µm (0.0020 in) = 5 × 10−5 m between filter particles. (Not the diffusion coefficient, the same letter, a different job; context decides.)
  • μ (mu), dynamic viscosity of the water.Units: Pa·s · Typical: ≈ 0.30 × 10−3 Pa·s at 93 °C (199 °F), about a third of its room-temperature value (Chapter 6)

Worked example: checking Darcy’s law applies

  1. Insert the bed values: ρ = 963, v = 3 × 10−4, D = 5 × 10−5, μ = 0.30 × 10−3.
  2. Numerator: 963 × 3 × 10−4 × 5 × 10−5 = 1.44 × 10−5.
  3. Divide by μ: 1.44 × 10−5 ∕ 0.30 × 10−3 ≈ 0.05. Across realistic beds the pore-scale Re spans ≈ 0.05–0.5, always far below 1.
  4. Re ≈ 0.05 is far below 1: deep in the laminar regime, so Darcy’s linear law is the right model inside the bed, exactly the assumption Chapters 5 and 9 rely on.

Try yours: run the same arithmetic on the kettle stream (v ≈ 0.5 m/s · 1.6 ft/s, D ≈ 6 mm · 0.24 in spout) and Re lands in the thousands, turbulent. One brew, two flow regimes: turbulence in the air, creeping flow in the bed.

SA ∕ V = 6 ∕ d Surface-area-to-volume ratio of a spherical particle, the geometry hiding inside “finer extracts faster”

Legend: every symbol

  • SA: surface area of the particle: the only place water can enter and solubles can leave.Units: m² · For a sphere, SA = πd²
  • V: volume of the particle: proportional to how much soluble material it holds.Units: m³ · For a sphere, V = πd³ ∕ 6, dividing the two gives 6/d
  • d: particle diameter.Units: m (or µm / in, consistently) · Typical: 600 µm (0.024 in) filter particle · 60 µm (0.0024 in) fine

Worked example: why fines punch above their mass

  1. Filter particle, d = 600 µm (0.024 in): SA/V = 6 ∕ 600 = 0.01 per µm (254 per in).
  2. Fine, d = 60 µm (0.0024 in): SA/V = 6 ∕ 60 = 0.1 per µm (2,540 per in).
  3. Ratio: 0.1 ∕ 0.01 = 10× more surface per unit of coffee — the same “~10×” stat as Chapter 4, now derived rather than asserted.

Try yours: compute 6/d for your espresso grind (~200 µm · 0.0079 in → 0.03 per µm · 762 per in): three times the filter particle’s surface per volume, one of the two reasons espresso can extract in 30 s (pressure-driven flow is the other). For the same law kept as a budget, surface per gram, particles per gram, and why a tenth of a dose's mass in fines carries about half its working surface, see Chapter 4's surface-area panel. Caveat, stated here and not only in Assumptions: 6/d is exact for a smooth sphere and a floor for real coffee, jagged shards carry more surface per volume than spheres of the same size, so every SA/V number in this guide understates the true interface.

The rest of the transport toolkit: pores, films and capillaries

Four pieces of physics the earlier chapters used without naming. Each is stated with its coffee-scale numbers, so the claims built on them can be checked.

  • Hagen–Poiseuille: why channels run away. Flow through a single round tube scales with the fourth power of its radius, Q ∝ r4; through a crack or slit it scales with the cube of the gap, Q ∝ h3. A channel only twice as wide as its neighbours carries about sixteen times the flow per tube. That exponent, not bad luck, is why channeling (Chapters 5 and 10) is a runaway process.
  • Kozeny–Carman: a scaling law for permeability, not a predictor of it. For a packed bed, k = d²φ³ ∕ [180(1 − φ)²], with d the particle size and φ the porosity (a settled filter bed sits around φ ≈ 0.35–0.45). Use it only as a scaling law: at fixed φ, k grows with d². As an absolute prediction it overpredicts coffee beds by roughly 100×: d = 600 µm (0.024 in) at φ = 0.40 gives k ≈ 3.6 × 10−10 m², against the ≈ 5 × 10−12 m² of Chapter 5's filter bed. The main reason is fines: the bed's effective diameter is set by its finest load-bearing fraction, and k ≈ 5 × 10−12 m² corresponds to an effective diameter of only about 71 µm. Tortuosity (next item) accounts for only about 2–4× of the gap, not the roughly 70× here (recomputation; Wadsworth et al. 2026 [36]). Fines attack twice: they shrink the effective d and fill voids, cutting φ; and near the percolation threshold, where the pore network is close to disconnecting, k falls much faster than the equation suggests.
  • Tortuosity: the path is longer than the bed. Pores wind, so the water's actual path through a bed is longer than the bed is deep, by a tortuosity factor of roughly 1.4–2 in packed beds. Darcy's L is the straight-line depth; the winding lowers measured permeabilities by only about 2–4× against the clean Kozeny–Carman estimate, a small part of that equation's roughly 100× overprediction. The larger reason is the fines-reduced effective diameter in the item above.
  • The film outside the particle. Chapter 2 models the inside of the particle; the outside has its own resistance, a thin boundary layer (film) the solute must cross into the moving water. In dimensionless terms, the Sherwood number compares film transfer to diffusion, and the Biot number compares external to internal resistance. In a percolating bed the film is thin and the flow keeps it refreshed, so this guide treats external resistance as small next to the intraparticle resistance, an assumption, stated here rather than hidden: in a still immersion brew the film is thicker and the assumption is weaker, which is one reason stirring a French press changes the cup.
  • Capillarity: small in the drain, huge in the wetting. A wetting liquid is pulled into a pore by the Young–Laplace pressure, set by surface tension and the contact angle; Washburn imbibition describes how fast the front advances. In a 50 µm (0.002 in) pore the capillary pressure is ≈ 4.8 kPa, about ten times the 490 Pa pool-only head of a 5 cm (2 in) pool. Once the bed is saturated, capillarity drops out of the Darcy balance; during the bloom and the first wetting, it is the largest pressure in the system, which is why dry pockets resist wetting so stubbornly.

The method: how to run an experiment you can believe
  1. Define a research question. One question, stated before you brew, “does a flat bed draw down more evenly than a cone at the same recipe?”
  2. Review the existing peer-reviewed literature. Chapter 19 is the starting shelf; check whether your question is already answered.
  3. Identify independent, dependent and controlled variables. The one you change, the ones you measure, and everything you hold fixed.
  4. Establish a repeatable brewing protocol. Written down, to the gram and the second, Chapter 16’s experiment is the template.
  5. Perform replicated experiments. Several brews per condition; a single brew proves nothing.
  6. Measure TDS, extraction yield, flow rate, temperature and drawdown time. Numbers first, impressions second.
  7. Conduct blind sensory evaluations. The taster must not know which cup is which.
  8. Analyse results statistically. Means, spread, and whether the difference clears the noise, and known reference points, like Chapter 15’s 0.24-point TDS comparison.
  9. Compare findings against published research. Agreement strengthens both; disagreement is a result, not a failure.
  10. Document limitations and alternative explanations. Every honest experiment ends with what it did not rule out.

Nine experiments worth running
  • V60 rib geometry versus flat-bottom geometry, Part 3’s question, run by the method above (Chapter 16 is the worked template).
  • Burr geometry and particle size distribution, same coffee, two burr sets, sieve or image the distributions.
  • Grind temperature and particle morphology, chilled versus room-temperature beans, after Uman et al. 2016 [4].
  • Water chemistry and extraction selectivity, two waters, one coffee, TDS plus blind tasting.
  • Pouring agitation and extraction uniformity, stirred versus still, everything else fixed.
  • Filter porosity and hydraulic resistance, two papers, one recipe, drawdown as the readout.
  • Brewing temperature and extraction kinetics, 88 °C (190 °F) versus 96 °C (205 °F), TDS sampled across time.
  • Fines migration and coffee bed permeability, sifted versus unsifted grounds, drawdown curves compared.
  • Coffee slurry temperature gradients, probes at the top and bottom of the bed through one brew.

The measurement toolkit

The instruments behind the library’s numbers, from the refractometer on your counter to the laboratory methods in the papers:
