A learning path, in order

If you are studying the field rather than browsing it, this is the order the knowledge base recommends, and it is the order this guide is built in:

  1. Fluid mechanics, how the water moves (Chapter 5).
  2. Mass transfer, how the coffee gets into it (Chapter 2).
  3. Particle mechanics — what the grind really is (Chapter 4).
  4. Thermodynamics, what sets every rate (Chapter 6).
  5. Brewer geometry, the boundary conditions (Part 3).
  6. Water chemistry, the solvent is an ingredient (Chapter 7).
  7. Analytical chemistry, measuring what is actually there (Chapter 19).
  8. Sensory science, measuring the point of it all (Chapter 15).
  9. Statistical experimental design, knowing whether any of it is true (this chapter).

Your next step: pick one experiment from the list above, run it by the ten-step method, and plot the result on the brewing control chart. That is the whole guide, used the way it was meant to be used.

Key takeaways
  • Fick's law, Darcy's law and the Reynolds number are one toolkit: flux, flow and flow regime.
  • Coffee-bed flow is deeply laminar (Re ≈ 0.05 in the worked example), which is why the linear Darcy law holds.
  • A believable experiment is designed before it is run: prediction, controls, repeats, spread.
  • Models are maps with stated assumptions; Chapter 20 is where this guide keeps its own.

Chapter 21 · The senses

Flavour is the final measurement.

What you will learn
  • Use the flavour wheel's families to name a note, starting wide and narrowing down.
  • Explain why the senses sit downstream of the measured meeting point in Figure 4: numbers first, verdict second.
  • Explain orthonasal and retronasal aroma, and why most of 'taste' is smell.
  • Judge whether a TDS gap is worth arguing about, using relative change and the Frost comparison.
  • Run the standard cupping protocol and say what it removes, and why.

Every instrument in this guide (refractometer, scale, timer, thermometer) is a proxy. The quantity they all stand in for is a perception: what a human nervous system reports when the cup arrives. Sensory science is the discipline that measures that endpoint with the same rigour the other chapters apply to water and particles, and it explains several things the physics alone cannot, starting with this: most of what you call taste is smell.

Your tongue reports five basic tastes (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami) plus texture, temperature and a mild chemical burn or tingle. The hundreds of distinct notes in coffee (blueberry, jasmine, cocoa, tobacco) are not tastes at all. They are aromas, detected by the olfactory receptors in the nose, either orthonasally, by sniffing, or retronasally, when volatile compounds rise from the back of the mouth into the nasal cavity as you swallow. That is why coffee tastes like almost nothing with a blocked nose, and why the aroma of the bloom is a genuine preview of the cup.

Two routes to flavour

The same volatile molecules, two doors into the nose, and the brain merges both with the tongue's five tastes into one sensation it calls flavour.

Sniff, orthonasal

aroma in through the nose

the bloom, the dry grounds

↓

Sip, taste + texture

five tastes · body · temperature

the tongue’s report

↓

Swallow, retronasal

volatiles rise behind the palate

where the notes live

↓

Flavour

one merged perception

what the chart can’t measure

Practical consequence: slurping is instrumentation, not rudeness, it sprays the coffee across the mouth and drives volatiles up the retronasal route. And temperature matters twice: a cooling cup releases different volatiles and shifts taste balance, which is why cupping protocol tastes the same bowl at several temperatures.

Visual · The flavour wheel, simplified

The Specialty Coffee Association's flavour wheel organises coffee's aroma vocabulary from the centre out, broad families first, specific notes at the rim. This is a nine-family simplification of the wheel's inner ring; the full wheel carries 99 flavour attributes, drawn from the World Coffee Research Sensory Lexicon's 110 attributes.

How professionals use it: start at the centre (which family?), move outward (which note within it?). The wheel is a shared vocabulary, not a scoring system, its job is to make “I taste something bright and red” into “berry, maybe raspberry,” a claim another taster can check. Geometry moved these families measurably in Chapter 15's study, but precisely: as a main effect it moved only 3 of 26 attributes (sweetness toward the flat basket, with smoke aroma and tobacco flavour); berry, citrus and sourness moved via roast × geometry interactions, toward the semi-conical basket in light roast.

What extraction tastes like

The four headline sensations map onto the physics of the earlier chapters in a consistent order, because the compounds arrive in shifts (Chapter 2) and perception weights them differently:

Acidity
Sweetness
Bitterness
Body

How to read these bars, and every tendency bar in this guide (Chapters 6, 14 and 21): longer = stronger tendency or intensity, on a 0–100% schematic scale. They summarise direction, not measurements, and carry no units.

A balanced cup's profile, schematically. Slide extraction down and acidity dominates while sweetness collapses (sour, thin); slide it up and bitterness and dryness take over while sweetness hollows out.

  • Acidity is mostly the small organic acids (citric, malic, phosphoric, lactic, acetic) arriving in the fast shift. Chlorogenic acids and their lactones and phenylindanes drive bitterness and astringency instead. Perceived as brightness when balanced, sourness when the sugars never arrive to cover it. It is a taste (sour receptors), sharpened or muted by the water's alkalinity before it ever reaches you.
  • Sweetness in black coffee is largely a perception trick played honestly: the actual sugar concentration is low, but ripe-fruit aromatics arriving retronasally are read by the brain as sweetness, and adequate extraction of the middle shift lets them show. Under-extract and sweetness is the first casualty.
  • Bitterness is two stories at once. The slow bitter compounds (chlorogenic lactones, phenylindanes) arrive in the slow shift, which is why bitterness climbs with extraction and roast level. But bitterness as a sensation is highest in the earliest, strongest fractions and falls as TDS falls (Batali et al. 2020 [37]), and caffeine is bitter and early. “Bitter last” describes the compounds, not the sensation.
  • Body is not a taste but a texture: dissolved melanoidins, emulsified oils and fine suspended material raise the liquid's viscosity and coat the mouth. Paper filters strip much of it (clarity's price); espresso's emulsion carries the most.

Thresholds: how small a difference can you taste?
  • Strength: the 0.24-point comparison. Frost et al. (2019), the UC Davis work in Chapter 15, found the smallest TDS difference between any two coffees their triangle tasters could tell apart was 0.24 percentage points, and that pair differed in geometry plus grind (a 28% relative strength increase). The authors present it as a minimum estimate that could be lower; it is not a universal threshold, and smaller gaps are not automatically “the same strength.” If two brews differ by 0.1% TDS, though, arguing about which is stronger is still arguing about weather.
  • Differences are proportional, not absolute. Across taste and smell, the just-noticeable difference is roughly a fixed fraction of the amount already there (Weber's law), but the fraction depends on the sense: about 2% for lifted weight, about 8% for brightness, about 0.3% for pitch. No single fraction holds across senses, and no coffee-specific Weber fraction has been measured, so any one number here would be an illustration, not a measurement. A change that is obvious in a delicate filter brew can vanish inside a strong espresso.
  • Adaptation is real. Receptors fatigue within a tasting session: the fifth cup is judged by a different instrument than the first. Professionals spit, rinse, and re-taste the reference, protocol exists to defend the instrument.
  • Expectation bends the reading. In unblinded tasting, price, origin stories and crema colour all shift scores. This is not dishonesty; it is how perception works, and it is why Chapter 19 insists sensory claims need blind panels before they count as measurements.

Cupping: the standard tasting protocol

Cupping is sensory science's answer to the brewing problem: remove every brewing variable so the coffee is the only thing being measured. It is immersion, not percolation (no flow, no bed geometry, nothing from Part 3 applies) which is exactly the point. The protocol below follows SCA Coffee Value Assessment Standard 102-2024, which superseded the 2004 cupping protocol and form on 4 November 2024.

  1. Grind 8.25 g (0.29 oz) per bowl (medium-coarse) into identical bowls; evaluate the dry aroma first (orthonasal).
  2. Add 150 mL of water at 93 °C ± 3 °C (199 °F ± 5 °F) (8.25 g per 150 mL, a 1:18.18 ratio) and start a timer. A crust of grounds forms on the surface.
  3. At 4 minutes, break the crust with a spoon, pushing the grounds down and smelling the burst of aroma released, the most information-dense moment of the protocol.
  4. Skim the floating foam and grounds from the surface.
  5. Taste as it cools, once the bowl has cooled to about 70 °C (158 °F), roughly 8–10 minutes in, slurping from a spoon to drive the retronasal route, and re-taste at several temperatures, rating fragrance, aroma, flavour, aftertaste, acidity, sweetness and mouthfeel for intensity (descriptive, 15-point scales), and rating impression of quality on the affective form, the only part that produces a score. (Body and balance are not CVA sections.)

Roast, origin and processing (Chapter 1's variables) are what cupping is built to reveal: washed coffees read cleaner and brighter, naturals fruitier and heavier, dark roasts progressively dominated by the roasted family of the wheel, whatever the origin.

Worked example: how big is a 0.10-point TDS gap?

Two cups on the counter: one at 1.30% TDS, one at 1.40%. Is the stronger one obviously stronger? Run the three readings of Chapter 15's worked example on it.

  1. Absolute: 1.40 − 1.30 = 0.10 percentage points.
  2. Relative: 0.10 ∕ 1.30 ≈ 0.077, about an 8% relative change in strength.
  3. Against the evidence: the smallest TDS difference a blind triangle panel has been shown to detect (Chapter 15) is 0.24 points, and its authors call that a minimum estimate that could be lower. This gap is less than half of it.

Reading it: an 8% relative step sits in the neighbourhood of the just-noticeable fractions measured for other senses (about 8% for brightness, from the thresholds panel above), and well under the one coffee measurement we have. The honest verdict is “borderline: some tasters, some days”, which is why this chapter trusts blind, repeated tasting over single confident sips.

Key takeaways
  • Flavour is the final measurement, made by an instrument that fatigues, adapts and expects: protocol defends it.
  • Differences are proportional, not absolute: a 0.10-point TDS gap at 1.30% is about an 8% relative change.
  • The flavour wheel's nine families simplify a vocabulary of over a hundred defined descriptors.
  • Cupping removes the brewing variables so the coffee is the only thing measured; that is its strength and its limit.

Synthesis

Protocols, derived — not memorised.

A recipe is just a set of initial conditions. Here are starting points for each method, with the physical reason attached to every step, so when a cup misses, you know which equation to argue with.

These protocols are the pipeline of Figures 3–5 written as instructions: same stages, same drivers, one method per row.

Filter: the reference brew
  • 20 g (0.71 oz) coffee, 320 g (11.3 oz · 10.8 fl oz) water (1:16), ratio sets the strength axis of the chart.
  • Water at 93–96 °C (199–205 °F), vessel preheated, so the slurry, not the kettle, sits in the fast-Arrhenius zone.
  • Medium grind, ~600 µm (0.024 in) population, diffusion time matched to a ~3 minute brew.
  • Bloom: 40–50 g (1.4–1.8 oz · 1.4–1.7 fl oz) water, swirl, 30–45 s, degassing and full wetting before flow begins.
  • Pour in pulses to 320 g (11.3 oz), gentle spirals, refreshes boundary layers without blasting fines into the paper.
  • Drawdown done by ~3:00–3:30, Darcy's report card. Much slower: fines or too fine a grind. Much faster: too coarse, or a channel.
  • Taste, then move one variable, sour and thin: extract more (finer, hotter, longer). Bitter and dry: extract less. Weak but balanced: strengthen the ratio.

Espresso: the reference shot
  • 18 g (0.63 oz) in, 36 g (1.27 oz) out (1:2), the ratio that lands espresso strength at 7–12% TDS.
  • Distribute evenly (WDT), tamp level — permeability engineering: kill density streaks before pressure finds them.
  • Pre-infuse a few seconds if your machine allows, swell, seal and degas the puck gently.
  • Full pressure: 25–30 s to target mass, 36 g (1.27 oz) in 25–30 s is an average beverage flow of ≈ 1.2–1.4 mL/s (0.04–0.05 fl oz/s); the through-puck water flow behind it is ≈ 2.0 mL/s (0.07 fl oz/s), the difference staying in the puck (Chapter 9). The clock reads out the puck's permeability. Gushing: grind finer. Choking: coarser.
  • Watch the streams, an early blond jet off-centre is a channel announcing itself; fix the prep, not the pressure.
  • Taste, then move one variable, sour: extend time or grind finer. Bitter and thin together: suspect channeling, not the ratio.

Pour over: cone and flat starting points
  • Cone (V60), 20 g (0.71 oz), 320 g (11.3 oz · 10.8 fl oz) water (1:16). Medium-fine grind, ~400–700 µm (0.016–0.028 in). The single large hole restricts nothing, so your pour rate is the flow control: steady spirals, total time ~2:15–3:15. Match the dose to the size, an 02 wants 20 g+ (0.71 oz+) to keep the bed deep enough (Chapter 13).
  • Flat (Kalita Wave), 20 g (0.71 oz), 320 g (11.3 oz · 10.8 fl oz) water (1:16). Medium grind, a touch coarser than your V60 setting. The three small holes meter the flow for you: pour gently, agitate little late in the brew so fines don't migrate onto the exits, total time ~3:00–3:45.
  • Same physics, different L(x). Both brews run the identical bloom, ratio and temperature logic as the filter protocol above, Part 3 only changes the bed's shape and who controls the exit. If a flat bed stalls, think fines (Chapter 5); if a cone tastes sour and bitter, think uneven path lengths (Chapter 13) before touching the grind.

Milk: the latte art protocol
  • Cold milk, cold pitcher, you need the aeration phase finished before the milk warms; starting cold buys time for protein to coat every bubble (Chapter 12).
  • Aerate early, to ~35–40 °C (95–104 °F), tip at the surface until the volume grows by roughly a third for a latte. Air added later becomes coarse froth that shear can no longer shrink.
  • Texture in the vortex to 60–65 °C (140–149 °F), tip submerged, pitcher angled, milk rolling: shear breaks bubbles down to microfoam and folds them through. Stop before ~70 °C (158 °F), denatured whey can't hold a foam.
  • Swirl, tap, pour at once, re-integrate any separation, then pour within seconds; drainage and Ostwald ripening are already running.
  • High & thin to mix, low & close to draw, momentum first for an even brown base, then let buoyancy raft the foam: wiggle for a rosetta, push for a tulip, lift and pull through to finish.

Troubleshooting: symptom → physics → fix
  • Sour, thin, salty, the fast compounds arrived, the sugars didn't: under-extraction. Grind finer, brew hotter, or give it more time, one at a time.
  • Bitter, dry, hollow, the slow shift over-extracted. Grind coarser, cool the water slightly, or shorten contact.
  • Sour and bitter together, not a dial-in error: uneven flow. Some coffee over-extracted while the rest sat dry. Fix evenness (distribution, level bed, gentler pours) before touching any number.
  • Balanced but weak — extraction is right, strength is wrong. Tighten the ratio; leave grind and temperature alone.
  • Balanced but harsh and heavy, the mirror image: open the ratio up.
  • Drawdown stalls (filter), permeability collapsed at the paper: fines migration. Pour more gently, agitate less late in the brew, consider a faster paper or a slightly coarser grind.
  • Shot gushes pale (espresso), k too high or a channel: grind finer first; if the jet is off-centre, fix distribution before grind.
  • Shot chokes to drips, k too low: coarser grind, or check the dose isn't overfilling the basket and fracturing against the shower screen.
  • Milk foam separates or pours in blobs, the foam aged past its Laplace clock, or was overheated into denaturation. Swirl to re-integrate and pour immediately; if it was steamed past ~70 °C (158 °F), start over, that change doesn't reverse.
  • Cup drifted after a grinder clean or burr change, the distribution changed, not the setting: retained grounds were cleared, burrs reseated at a slightly different alignment, or a new tooth pattern is cutting a different fines share (Chapter 4). Purge a few grams, then re-dial by drawdown and taste, not by the number on the dial.
  • Flat despite good numbers, suspect the inputs, not the process: stale, degassed beans (Chapter 8) or muted water alkalinity (Chapter 7) can hold a technically perfect brew down.

Measure two numbers. Change one variable.
Repeat until the cup agrees with the chart.

Synthesis · Next steps

From reading to practice.

The guide ends where Chapter 20 says all knowledge starts: with your own replicated experiments. Here is a four-week on-ramp (one variable a week, everything else held at the reference protocols) and the log to record it in. Print this page from your browser and keep the log by the kettle; a filled row is a data point, and a page of them is the climate to the single brew's weather.

Check yourself: self-test with answers

Two or three questions per part, drawn from the chapters. Answer before you open the key, each answer is folded shut, like everything else in this guide. If you miss one, the chapter named in the answer is the one to re-read.

Scoring: one point per question answered correctly before opening its key. 10–12: dialled in. 7–9: solid; re-read the chapters your misses name. 6 or fewer: work the four-week plan below, then retake the test.

1 · (Ch. 2) You halve the particle size. What happens to the diffusion time, and why?
Show answer

It falls to a quarter. Diffusion time scales with d² (τ ≈ d²/D): half the distance, squared, is a quarter of the time, the single most important scaling in the guide. Re-read the chapter.

2 · (Ch. 3) A brew reads 1.30% TDS with an extraction yield of 19%. Your next cup tastes weak but balanced. Which variable do you change?
Show answer

The ratio only, tighten it (less water per gram). Extraction is already in the 18–22% window, so grind, time and temperature stay untouched; strength is the ratio's job. Re-read the chapter.

3 · (Ch. 4) Why do fines, at ~10% of a dose's mass, matter far beyond 10%?
Show answer

Surface scales as 1/d: at 60 µm vs 600 µm a gram of fines presents ~10× the surface, so ~10% of the mass carries ≈ 53% of the working surface, and the fines also migrate and throttle the bed's permeability (Ch. 5). Measured espresso work adds the nuance: their biggest effect is slowing flow, and extraction follows the extra time. Re-read the chapter.

4 · (Ch. 5) In Darcy's law, what does doubling the pool depth above a filter bed do to flow?
Show answer

Less than you would think: it does not double Q. The driving head is ρg(h + L), the pool plus the liquid inside the bed, so doubling the pool from 5 cm to 10 cm (2 in to 4 in) over a 3 cm (1.2 in) bed raises Q by (0.10 + 0.03) ∕ (0.05 + 0.03) ≈ ×1.63, and even with no pool at all the bed still drains at ≈ 1.5 mL/s on its own weight. It is still why a topped-up dripper drains faster than a nearly empty one, just by less than the pool-only arithmetic promises. Re-read the chapter.

5 · (Ch. 6) Your kettle says 94 °C (201 °F). Why might two brewers still run different extractions?
Show answer

The slurry, not the kettle, sets the rate, and the slurry's temperature depends on preheating, vessel mass and cooling (Newton's law). A cold ceramic brewer can run its slurry ~6–7 °C (~11–13 °F) below a preheated one, worth roughly 7% of extraction rate per 5 °C by the Arrhenius rule. Re-read the chapter.

6 · (Ch. 7) Two waters both read 150 mg/L TDS. Can they brew differently?
Show answer

Yes. TDS sums all ions and cannot tell hardness from alkalinity, or Ca²⁺ from Mg²⁺. The GH/KH split (and which cations make the hardness) is what acts on extraction and acidity (Hendon 2014; Bratthäll et al. 2024). Re-read the chapter.

7 · (Ch. 9) A shot pulls 36 g (1.27 oz) in 27 s. What is the average beverage flow, and how does it relate to the ~2.0 mL/s through the puck?
Show answer

36 ∕ 27 ≈ 1.33 mL/s (0.045 fl oz/s) into the cup. The puck was pushed ≈ 54 g (1.9 oz) of water at ≈ 2.0 mL/s and kept ≈ 18 g (0.63 oz), two different flows, and confusing them breaks the Darcy arithmetic. Re-read the chapter.

8 · (Ch. 10) A shot tastes sour and bitter at once. Grind finer or coarser?
Show answer

Neither first. Sour-and-bitter together is the signature of uneven flow, one region over-extracted, the rest under. Fix distribution and evenness (WDT, level tamp, sound puck prep) before touching the grind. Re-read the chapter.

9 · (Ch. 12) Why does uniform microfoam outlast mixed-size froth?
Show answer

Laplace pressure, ΔP = 2γ/r: small bubbles are squeezed harder than large ones, so in a mixed foam gas migrates from small bubbles to large ones (Ostwald ripening) and the foam coarsens. Uniform bubbles share one pressure, there is no gradient to drive the migration. Re-read the chapter.

10 · (Ch. 13) In a cone, why can one cup be over- and under-extracted at the same time?
Show answer

L(x) varies: with the worked example's illustrative bed, 4.5 cm (1.77 in) at the centre, 1.5 cm (0.59 in) at the rim, local flux scales as (h + L)/L, so at a 5 cm (2 in) pool rim water moves ~2.1× faster through ~⅓ the coffee. Centre trends over, rim trends under, in the same brew. Re-read the chapter.

11 · (Ch. 15) What does the Frost study's 0.24 figure actually describe, and what were its two headline sample sizes?
Show answer

0.24 percentage points TDS was the smallest difference between any two discriminable triangle-test coffees, and that pair (flat-bottom/fine vs semi-conical/medium) differed in geometry plus grind, a 28% relative strength increase. The authors present it as a minimum estimate that could be lower; it is not the geometry-alone effect and not a universal threshold. Blind discrimination tests: 45 tasters; consumer testing (the liking clusters): 85 people. Re-read the chapter.

12 · (Ch. 20–21) Two brews plot on the same control-chart point but taste different. Is your palate wrong?
Show answer

No. TDS and EY are two coordinates, not the whole description, they cannot separate roast colour or acid balance (the gap cyclic voltammetry, Bumbaugh et al. 2026, aims at). The chart navigates; the senses judge. Re-read the chapter.

A four-week practice plan
  1. Week 1, Baseline. Brew the reference filter protocol (Protocols) five times, unchanged. Log every brew. Your only job is to discover your own repeatability, the spread in time and taste when you change nothing.
  2. Week 2, Grind. Same recipe, three grind settings: your baseline, one step finer, one step coarser, two brews each. Taste blind if you can. You are feeling the d² law (Chapter 2) and permeability (Chapter 5) with your tongue.
  3. Week 3, Temperature. Baseline grind, water at 88 °C (190 °F) versus 96 °C (205 °F). Compare against the Arrhenius chart's prediction (~±7% rate per 5 °C) and note whether the balance, not just the strength, moved (Chapter 6).
  4. Week 4, One experiment of yours. Pick from Chapter 20's nine: two waters (Chapter 7's recipe makes this easy), two papers, stirred versus still. Run it by the ten-step method, three brews per side, and write down what it did not rule out.

Every chapter, one try-this: Ch. 1, brew the same coffee at two roast levels and compare drawdown at one grind. Ch. 2, time a brew with sifted fines removed. Ch. 3, put your last five brews on the control chart. Ch. 4, weigh what your grinder retains, and if you can borrow a grinder with the other burr geometry (flat vs. conical), brew one coffee through both at the same setting and compare drawdown and fines. Ch. 5, deliberately stall a brew, then rescue the next with gentler pours. Ch. 6, brew preheated versus cold ceramic. Ch. 7, the two-water blind test. Ch. 8, skip the bloom once, and taste what it cost. Ch. 9–10, pull one shot with no WDT and watch the basket. Ch. 11, taste a shot with crema stirred in versus skimmed. Ch. 12, steam two pitchers, one to 60 °C (140 °F), one to 75 °C (167 °F), and compare the foam after one minute. Ch. 13–16 — the Chapter 16 experiment itself. Ch. 21, cup one coffee at three temperatures and score it each time.

Brew log: print and keep by the kettle
DateCoffeeDoseRatioTempTimeTDSEYNotes, one variable changed

Dose in g (oz), temperature in °C (°F), time as total brew time, TDS from a cooled, filtered sample. EY comes from the Chapter 3 calculator. The Notes column has one rule: it names the single thing you changed, or “baseline” when you changed nothing.

The download is a blank log with the same columns, ready to fill in on a phone or computer. To keep a paper copy by the kettle instead, print this page from your browser: the log table is set to print cleanly.

Reference · Cheat sheet

The whole guide, on one screen.

Every window, constant and first move in the guide, gathered for the counter. Read your two numbers, find them below, make the one move it names. If a number here surprises you, the chapter behind it is one search away, and the Chapter 3 calculator and trend plotter turn your own readings into these diagnoses automatically.

Directions are the physics of Chapters 2–7; sizes vary by coffee. The fines row is the measured version (Smrke et al. 2024, Chapter 4): fines buy time, and time does the extracting.

Taste thresholds: what you can actually detect
  • Strength: the 0.24-point comparison. In Frost et al. (2019), 0.24 percentage points TDS was the smallest gap between any two coffees triangle tasters could tell apart, and that pair differed in geometry plus grind; the authors call it a minimum estimate, not a universal threshold (Chapters 15 and 21). Brew-to-brew variability is of a similar order, so argue about something else.
  • Differences are proportional. The just-noticeable difference runs at a roughly fixed fraction of what is already there (Weber's law; the fraction varies by sense, from about 0.3% for pitch to about 8% for brightness), so a change that shouts in a delicate filter brew can vanish inside an espresso.
  • Temperature moves taste twice. A cooling cup releases different volatiles and shifts the sweet–sour balance, which is why cupping scores the same bowl at several temperatures (Chapter 21).
  • Your threshold is yours. These are panel averages. The brew log in Next Steps is how you find your own.

Constants worth memorising
  • The bookkeeping: beverage mass = brew water − retention × dose. Extraction yield = TDS × beverage mass ÷ dose.
  • The diffusion clock: τ grows with d², halve the particle size, quarter the extraction time.
  • The temperature lever: +5 °C (+9 °F) ≈ +7% extraction rate near 93 °C (199 °F), with Ea ≈ 16 kJ/mol (Wang & Lim 2021 [34]).
  • Water, 2009 SCAA standard: TDS 150 mg/L (≈150 ppm; range 75–250), calcium hardness 68 mg/L as CaCO3 (range 17–85), alkalinity at or near 40 mg/L, pH 7.0 (6.5–7.5).
  • Water, SCA Standard 310-2021: calcium hardness 50–175 ppm as CaCO3, alkalinity 40–70 ppm, pH 6–8, no TDS target.
  • Water, SCAE Water Chart (2016, a different document): total hardness 50–175 ppm as CaCO3, alkalinity 40–75 ppm, pH 6.5–8.
  • The bloom: ~2× the dose in water (40–50 g · 1.4–1.8 oz for a 20 g · 0.71 oz dose), 30–45 s.
  • The reference shot: 18 g (0.63 oz) in, 36 g (1.27 oz) out, 25–30 s at 9 bar (131 psi).
  • The milk window: texture by 60–65 °C (140–149 °F); past ~70 °C (158 °F) the foam is finished and doesn't recover.
  • The method: measure two numbers, change one variable, log every brew. The printable log is in Next Steps.

Reference

The equations, at a glance.

These are the equations that run the whole guide. Each one is stated in its chapter with a full legend (every symbol defined, with units and typical values) and a worked example to follow step by step. This page is the index: the formula, what it governs, and where its full treatment lives. Watch the reused symbols: τ is the diffusion time in Chapter 2, but the cooling constant τc in Chapter 6; D is the diffusion coefficient in the d² law and Fick's law, but the pore diameter in the Reynolds number; Q is the instantaneous flow in Darcy's law, but the average flow (volume ÷ time) in Chapter 20. Each equation's own chapter owns its symbols.

  • PV = nRT
    Ideal gas law, why a sealed fermentation tank pressurises as microbes add CO2 to its headspace, and why it needs an airlock. Full legend and worked example in Chapter 1 (processing: the sealed tank).
  • CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−
    Carbonic acid equilibrium, dissolved CO2 forms a weak acid in the tank's juices, a small extra push on pH alongside the fermentation acids. Chapter 1 (processing: the sealed tank).
  • N(t) = N0 · 2t∕g
    Microbial growth, a population doubling every g hours grows exponentially early on, the reason a fermentation tank's first day decides so much. A general rule of thumb, not a coffee-specific rate. Chapter 1 (processing: the sealed tank).
  • τ ≈ d² ∕ D
    Diffusion time, how long a particle of diameter d needs to extract. The square is why grind distribution rules everything. Chapter 2.
  • Pe = vL ∕ D
    Péclet number, advection versus diffusion: Pe ≈ 6 in the pores between particles, ≈ 0 inside a particle, where diffusion is the only way out. Worked example in Chapter 2.
  • Extraction yield = TDS × beverage mass ∕ dose
    Extraction yield, the bookkeeping that turns a refractometer reading into the vertical axis of the brewing control chart. Target: 18–22%. Chapter 3.
  • Q = kA ΔP ∕ (μL)  ·  ΔP = ρg(h + L) ≈ 785 Pa (0.11 psi)
    Darcy's law, filter — gravity-driven flow through the bed; the head counts the pool plus the liquid in the bed. Pool depth, permeability, viscosity and bed depth set the drawdown. Chapter 5.
  • q(x) ∝ (h + L(x)) ∕ L(x)
    Geometry inside Darcy's law, read locally, flow per unit area follows the local head (pool plus bed liquid) over the bed depth at that point. In a cone L varies from centre to rim, so the extraction does too; in a flat bed L is nearly constant and the flow is nearly uniform. Not a seventh law, Darcy's law with the brewer's shape substituted in. Chapter 13.
  • rate(T) ∝ exp(−Ea ∕ RT)
    Arrhenius law, extraction rate grows exponentially with absolute temperature. Every +5 °C (+9 °F) ≈ +7% rate, with Ea ≈ 16 kJ/mol (Wang & Lim 2021). Chapter 6.
  • T(t) = Troom + (T0 − Troom) · e−t∕τc
    Newton's law of cooling, the slurry cools exponentially toward room temperature, so the brew's throttle eases off as it runs. Chapter 6.
  • Q = kA ΔP ∕ (μL)  ·  ΔP ≈ 9 bar (131 psi)
    Darcy's law, espresso, the same law with a pump: 9 bar (131 psi) ≈ a 92 m (302 ft) water column, held back by a puck whose permeability you manufacture. Chapter 9.
  • ΔP = 2γ ∕ r
    Laplace pressure, the excess pressure inside a bubble, inversely proportional to its radius. Uniform microfoam bubbles share one pressure and stay stable; mixed froth ripens and separates. Chapter 12 works it with γ ≈ 0.042 N/m for warm milk, and Home Lab Test 4 computes it live: a bubble 10 µm (0.0004 in) across (r = 5 µm) holds ΔP = 2 × 0.042 ∕ 5 × 10−6 = 16,800 Pa (2.44 psi), while one 100 µm (0.0039 in) across (r = 50 µm) holds only 1,680 Pa (0.24 psi). That tenfold gap is the pressure difference that drives ripening.
  • J = −D · (dC ∕ dx)
    Fick’s first law, diffusion flux is the diffusion coefficient times the steepness of the concentration gradient. The engine inside every particle, and the reason fresh water at the surface restarts extraction. Chapter 20.
  • Q = Volume ∕ Time
    Flow rate, delivery and drainage measured with a scale and a timer. Comparing the two tells you whether your hand or the bed is metering the brew. Chapter 20.
  • Re = ρvD ∕ μ
    Reynolds number, the check that Darcy’s law applies: inside a coffee bed Re ≈ 0.05, deep in laminar flow; in the kettle stream it is in the thousands. Chapter 20.
  • SA ∕ V = 6 ∕ d
    Surface-area-to-volume ratio, why a gram of fines has ~10× the working surface of a gram of filter particles, derived rather than asserted. Chapter 20, and converted there into surface per gram for real, bimodal grinds in Chapter 4.

Reference · Terms and definitions

Terms & definitions.

The technical terms this guide leans on, defined in one place: plain language first, precisely second, and listed in alphabetical order. Where a chapter leans on a term hardest, the definition says so, and dotted-underlined terms in the chapters (for example, “melanoidin” in Chapter 1) link here. Jump to a letter: A · B · C · D · E · F · G · H · I · L · M · O · P · Q · R · S · T · U · W. Use the guide search at the top to find a term by name.

  • Activation energy (Ea): the energy barrier a compound must clear to dissolve and react; the Ea in the Arrhenius law. This guide's model uses ≈ 16 kJ/mol, the coffee-specific value reported by Wang & Lim (2021). Different compounds have different barriers, the deep reason temperature changes a cup's balance, not just its strength (Chapter 6).
  • Advection: transport by bulk flow: water physically carrying dissolved compounds along. Dominates between particles; absent inside them.
  • Aerobic: “with oxygen”. In coffee processing it means fermentation in an open tank, with air free to circulate; it is the baseline fermentation inside the classic washed process, and the contrast case for anaerobic (sealed-tank) fermentation. Temperature sets its clock, and its main acids are acetic, citric and malic (Chapter 1).
  • Agitation: any deliberate disturbance of the brew: swirling, stirring, excavating the bloom, pulsed pouring. Physically, it replaces the saturated boundary layer at each particle with fresher water and restarts diffusion's gradient (Chapter 2).
  • Airlock: a small water-filled valve in the lid of a fermentation tank. Gas made inside bubbles out through the water; air cannot come back in the same way. It is the pressure relief that lets a sealed tank survive its own fermentation (Chapter 1).
  • Alkalinity: the water's acid-neutralising (buffering) capacity, mostly bicarbonate. Sets how much of coffee's acidity survives into the cup.
  • Anaerobic: “without oxygen”. In coffee processing it means fermentation in a sealed vessel that keeps outside air away, so the tank runs low in oxygen (not perfectly free of it) for 24 to 192 hours in the trials this guide cites. The microbes inside shift to yeasts and lactic acid bacteria, and lactic acid becomes the main acid formed (Chapter 1).
  • Arrhenius law: reaction rates grow exponentially with temperature: k ∝ exp(−Ea/RT). The reason small temperature changes have outsized effects.
  • Basket: the perforated steel cup that sits inside a portafilter and holds the puck. Its diameter and hole pattern set the puck's cross-section A and its drainage, bed geometry for espresso (Chapters 9 and 14's logic, under pressure).
  • Bimodal: having two peaks. Ground coffee's particle size distribution is bimodal: a main population near the grind setting plus a fines population an order of magnitude smaller (Chapter 4).
  • Bloom: the first pour on filter coffee, and the pause after it, while roasting CO2 escapes and the bed fully wets.
  • Boundary layer: the thin shell of liquid clinging to a particle's surface. In a still brew it saturates with dissolved coffee and extraction stalls against it; agitation thins and replaces it (Chapter 2).
  • Breaker & finishing teeth: the two stages of a burr set: coarse breaker teeth near the entry crack beans into chunks; finer finishing teeth toward the exit shear chunks toward the gap size. A particle leaves only when it fits through the gap (Chapter 4).
  • Brew / beverage: a brew is both the act of brewing and the drink it makes. The beverage is the finished liquid in the cup, weighed after the bed has kept its share of the water; extraction yield is computed on beverage mass, not on the water poured (Chapter 3).
  • Brew ratio: the mass of water per mass of dry coffee, written 1:16 and so on. Sets the strength axis of the control chart; espresso's 1:2 is quoted in the cup, filter's in brew water (Chapters 3 and 9).
  • °Brix: a measure of how much sugar a liquid holds, read with a refractometer: roughly, grams of sugar per 100 g (3.5 oz) of liquid. In Chapter 1 it measures the fuel available to a fermentation: whole-cherry juice started one trial at 23.65 °Brix against 7.33 °Brix for pulped coffee.
  • Burr (one of the two toothed steel cutting elements of a burr grinder) a ring in a flat set, a cone or its ring in a conical set. The pair's tooth pattern, diameter and gap decide the particle size distribution before any recipe variable gets a say (Chapter 4).
  • Burr set: the pair of toothed steel rings (flat) or cone-and-ring (conical) that cuts coffee in a grinder. Its geometry (tooth pattern, diameter, the gap between the faces) sets the particle size distribution before any recipe variable gets a say (Chapter 4).
  • Bypass (water that reaches the cup without passing through the coffee bed) down the gap between paper and wall, or over the paper's edge. It dilutes the brew and extracts nothing, so it masquerades as under-extraction in the numbers.
  • Caffeic acid: one of the phenolic acids formed when chlorogenic acids break down in roasting; contributes to acidity and, further transformed, to bitterness (Chapter 1).
  • Caffeine: coffee's best-known alkaloid: a mild stimulant and a modest contributor to bitterness. It is highly soluble and extracts relatively early; roast level changes it little, robusta carries roughly twice arabica's caffeine (Chapters 1 and 21).
  • Caramelisation: the browning of sugars by heat alone (no amino acids involved), unlike the Maillard reaction, which needs both sugars and amino acids. Produces sweet, caramel and eventually burnt notes during roasting (Chapter 1).
  • Carbonic maceration: an anaerobic set-up borrowed from winemaking: the air is drawn out of a sealed bag or tank of coffee, then pure CO2 is pumped in, so fermentation runs in a carbon dioxide atmosphere. Studies often use this name for the vacuum-then-CO2 method (Chapter 1).
  • Cation: a positively charged ion. In brewing water the cations that matter are the divalent Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ (hardness) and the monovalent Na⁺ and K⁺; charge density decides how strongly each interacts with coffee's flavour compounds (Chapter 7).
  • Channeling: flow concentrating into a low-resistance path, over-extracting one region while bypassing the rest. Sour and bitter at once is its signature.
  • Choking: a shot (or brew) whose flow has collapsed to drips because the bed's permeability is too low: too fine a grind, too much dose, or a fines layer sealing the exit. The opposite failure from gushing (Chapters 5 and 9).
  • Chlorogenic acids: a family of phenolic acids abundant in green coffee. They break down during roasting into quinic and caffeic acids, shaping both acidity and bitterness; robusta carries more than arabica (Chapter 1).
  • Concentration gradient: how steeply the concentration of a dissolved compound changes with distance. Diffusion flows down it (Fick's law); when it flattens, extraction slows to a stop (Chapters 2 and 20).
  • Conical burr: a burr set in which a cone sits inside a ring; gravity feeds beans down the cone's flank on a short, steep path, usually at lower speed. Typically a wider distribution with a fatter fines shoulder than a flat set (Chapter 4).
  • Crema: espresso's foam: CO2 microbubbles stabilised by emulsified coffee oils, possible only under pressure.
  • Cupping: the standardised immersion tasting protocol of Chapter 21: fixed ratio, no flow, crust broken at four minutes, tasted as it cools. Built to measure the coffee, not the brewing.
  • Darcy's law: flow through a porous medium: Q = kA·ΔP/(μL). Governs drippers and pucks alike.
  • Demucilager: a machine that removes the mucilage layer from depulped coffee by friction, instead of fermenting it loose and washing it off. A DESLIM mechanical demucilager cuts washed processing’s water use from about 40 litres per kilogram of dry parchment to under 1 litre per kilogram (Chapter 1).
  • Denaturation: the irreversible unfolding of a protein under heat. In milk, whey proteins denaturing above ~70 °C (158 °F) lose their ability to stabilise foam, the physical reason overheated milk won't pour art.
  • Depulping: squeezing the seeds out of the coffee cherry with a machine (a depulper), removing skin and pulp. It is the first step of the washed, honey and aerobic methods; washed coffee is depulped within 24 hours of harvest (Chapter 1).
  • Dial-in: the iterative process of adjusting grind, dose, ratio and time until a shot or brew lands in its target window. In this guide's terms: manufacturing a permeability, then verifying it with two numbers (Chapters 3 and 9).
  • Diffusion: molecular random walk down a concentration gradient; the only way out of a coffee particle. Time scales with the square of particle size.
  • Dose: the mass of dry coffee a brew starts with, in grams (ounces). One of the calculator's four inputs, and the denominator of extraction yield (Chapter 3).
  • Drawdown: the draining phase after the last pour in a percolation brew. Its duration is Darcy's law reporting on the bed: slow means permeability has fallen (fines, compaction); fast means a coarse bed or a channel.
  • Dripper: the brewer that holds the filter and grounds above the cup in pour-over brewing (V60, Kalita Wave, Origami, Orea in Part 3). Its shape sets the bed geometry of Chapter 13.
  • Emulsion: a stable mixture of two liquids that do not dissolve in each other, held as tiny droplets: coffee oils in water, in crema (Chapter 11); fat globules in milk (Chapter 12). Stability comes from surfactants coating the droplets.
  • Espresso: the brewing method of Part 2: water forced through a compacted puck at ~9 bar (131 psi), producing a small, strong beverage (7–12% TDS) in 25–30 s, and, uniquely, crema. Also the beverage itself.
  • Extraction: the whole transfer this guide is about: soluble compounds leaving the ground coffee and entering the water, by surface washing and by diffusion out of each particle. Extraction yield (below) is its bookkeeping; strength (TDS) is its concentration in the cup.
  • Extraction yield (EY): the percentage of the dry coffee's mass that ended up dissolved in the beverage. Target window: 18–22%.
  • Facultative anaerobe: a microbe that can live with oxygen or without it, switching its metabolism to match what is available. Many of the yeasts and bacteria in a sealed coffee tank are facultative anaerobes, which is why they survive the handover from the tank's first, oxygenated hours to its anaerobic rest (Chapter 1).
  • Fick’s law: diffusion flux is proportional to the concentration gradient: J = −D·(dC/dx). Chapter 2’s d² law is this, integrated over a particle.
  • Fines: the small-size population of ground coffee (tens of µm · a few thousandths of an inch). Extract almost instantly; migrate to the filter and throttle flow.
  • First crack: the audible fracture of the bean at ≈ 196 °C (385 °F) during roasting, when internal steam and CO2 pressure splits the structure open, the moment the bean becomes porous enough to brew (Chapter 1).
  • Flat burr: a burr set of two rings facing each other; centrifugal force walks particles outward across the full radius, meeting more cutting edges per particle. Typically a narrower main distribution than a conical set (Chapter 4).
  • Gold cup: the SCA's name for the preferred window on the brewing control chart. Classic Golden Cup Standard (2018): 18–22% extraction yield at 1.15–1.35% TDS; the Version 3 chart (revised March 2019) widens the strength side to 1.15–1.45% TDS (Reference [1]). A population preference from taste panels, not a physical law (Chapter 3).
  • Hypothesis: a proposed mechanism that has not yet survived a controlled test. The lowest grade on Part 4’s evidence ladder, a starting point, not a conclusion.
  • Immersion: brewing by steeping: grounds sit in the water for the whole brew (French press, cupping), so there is no flow through a bed and Darcy's law does not apply, diffusion and temperature still do. The opposite of percolation.
  • Lactic acid: the main acid formed in sealed-tank coffee fermentation in several trials, made by lactic acid bacteria from sugars. After 180 hours of self-induced anaerobic fermentation, dried natural coffee held 13.20 g/kg (about 0.21 oz per lb) of it, from none at the start (Chapter 1).
  • Lactic acid bacteria: a family of bacteria that turn sugars mainly into lactic acid and can work without oxygen. In a sealed coffee tank they take over once the oxygen is used up; in the Colombian trial the dominant one was Weissella, followed by Leuconostoc and Lactiplantibacillus (Chapter 1).
  • Laplace pressure: the excess pressure inside a bubble: ΔP = 2γ/r. Smaller bubbles are squeezed harder, which is why mixed-size foams coarsen and uniform microfoam endures.
  • Limescale: calcium carbonate (CaCO3) precipitated when calcium-bearing, bicarbonate-bearing water is heated: Ca²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻ → CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O. The same chemistry as temporary hardness, deposited on kettle elements and espresso boilers (Chapter 7).
  • Log-normal distribution: a distribution whose logarithm is bell-shaped: lopsided, with a peak (mode) below its median and a long tail toward large values. Ground coffee's size populations follow it, which is why the PSD chart's main peak sits near 520 µm (0.020 in) while its median is ≈ 600 µm (0.024 in) (Chapter 4).
  • Maillard reactions: the network of reactions between sugars and amino acids under heat that builds coffee's brown pigments and hundreds of aromatics during roasting (Chapter 1).
  • Melanoidins: the large brown polymer molecules produced by the Maillard reactions. Water-soluble, they give brewed coffee much of its colour and a share of its body and mouthfeel (Chapters 1 and 21).
  • Micelle: a cluster that surfactant molecules form in water, water-loving ends out. Coffee's surface-active compounds and milk proteins organise at interfaces in related ways, the molecular housekeeping behind stable emulsions and foams (Chapters 11 and 12).
  • Microfoam: steamed milk whose air is dispersed as uniform bubbles of ~10–30 µm (0.0004–0.0012 in), coated in milk protein. It pours like wet paint and rafts on espresso as the white of latte art.
  • Mineralization: the dissolved mineral content of water, and the act of setting it: hardness ions (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺) plus the bicarbonate buffer, each with its own target. Not a single number, TDS reads their sum and cannot tell them apart (Chapter 7).
  • Mucilage: the sticky, sugary gel layer between a coffee cherry’s pulp and the parchment around the seed. Washed processing ferments it loose and rinses it away; honey processing leaves some or all of it on the parchment to dry (Chapter 1).
  • Mode: the most common value in a distribution: the peak of the PSD curve. Not the same as the median or the mean when the distribution is lopsided (Chapter 4).
  • Ostwald ripening: the coarsening of a foam as gas diffuses from small, high-pressure bubbles into large, low-pressure ones. The clock that starts the moment steaming stops.
  • Parchment: the papery shell that encloses a coffee seed after depulping, named for its texture when dry. Coffee is dried, rested and traded “in parchment” with this shell on; hulling removes it just before export (Chapter 1).
  • Peer-reviewed: research checked by independent experts before publication, with named authors, a journal and a stated method. The highest grade on the evidence ladder.
  • Percolation: brewing by passing water through a bed of grounds (pour over, drip), as opposed to immersion, where the grounds steep in the water (French press). The subject of Part 3.
  • Permeability (k): how easily a porous bed lets fluid through; set by pore size, and the true variable behind grind and tamp.
  • Portafilter: the handled holder that locks into an espresso machine's group head, carrying the basket and the puck. A bottomless (naked) portafilter exposes the basket's underside so channels can be seen as they form (Chapter 10).
  • Pre-infusion: gentle wetting of the espresso puck at low pressure before full 9 bar (131 psi), to swell, seal and degas it.
  • Puck: the compressed bed of ground coffee inside the espresso basket: a manufactured porous medium whose permeability the barista sets with grind, dose, distribution and tamp (Chapter 9).
  • Pulped natural: the original name, from Brazil in the 1990s, for what is now usually called the honey process: the cherry is pulped, and the mucilage-coated parchment dries without a fermentation tank or a wash (Chapter 1).
  • Péclet number: the ratio of advective to diffusive transport. High in the bed's channels, ~zero inside a particle.
  • Quinic acid: a bitter-leaning acid formed as chlorogenic acids break down in roasting and further during brewing and holding; part of why dark roasts and stale brews turn harsh (Chapters 1 and 21).
  • Refractometer: the instrument that reads TDS: it measures how much a liquid bends light (its refractive index), which rises with dissolved solids. Samples must be cooled and filtered to read honestly (Chapter 3).
  • Remineralization: adding measured minerals back into distilled or reverse-osmosis water: salts by weight, a dosed concentrate, a mineral packet, or a cartridge. Filtration's mirror image, building the water instead of stripping it (Chapter 7).
  • Retention: used two ways in this guide. Bed retention: the brew water a spent bed keeps, ≈ 2 g (0.07 oz) per gram of coffee in filter, ≈ 1 g per gram in a puck, the calculator's fourth input. Grinder retention: the ground coffee left inside a grinder after dosing, which exchanges with the next dose and blurs grind changes.
  • Retronasal olfaction: smell perceived from inside: volatile compounds rising from the back of the mouth into the nasal cavity during eating and drinking. Most of coffee's flavour notes arrive by this route (Chapter 21).
  • Reynolds number (Re): the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a flow. Re ≪ 1 in a coffee bed (laminar, Darcy applies); Re in the thousands in a kettle stream (turbulent).
  • Self-induced anaerobic fermentation (SIAF): coffee sealed in a tank or bucket whose own microbes make it anaerobic: they use up the oxygen inside, CO2 builds up, and an airlock vents the gas without letting air in. First applied to coffee in 2020 (Chapter 1).
  • Slurry: the brewing mixture itself: grounds suspended in hot water inside the dripper. Its temperature (not the kettle's) is the one the Arrhenius law acts on (Chapter 6).
  • Specific surface area: a grind's external surface per unit mass: 6/(ρ·d) for spherical particles, in cm²/g (in²/g). It is the per-gram form of SA/V, ≈ 71 cm²/g (11 in²/g) at 600 µm (0.024 in), ≈ 714 cm²/g (111 in²/g) at 60 µm (0.0024 in), and the reason fines dominate extraction's interface (Chapters 4 and 20).
  • Strength: how concentrated the beverage is: its TDS percentage. One of the control chart's two axes, set mainly by the brew ratio. Not the same as extraction: a brew can be strong and under-extracted, or weak and fully extracted (Chapter 3).
  • Surface-area-to-volume ratio: for a spherical particle, 6/d. Extraction happens at surfaces while solubles hide in volumes, so smaller particles extract disproportionately fast.
  • Surfactant: a molecule with a water-loving end and a water-fearing end that coats interfaces and stabilises foams and emulsions. Milk proteins are the surfactants of microfoam; coffee's own surface-active compounds stabilise crema (Chapters 11 and 12).
  • Stall: a percolation brew whose drawdown slows to a stop mid-brew, usually because migrated fines have sealed the filter paper and collapsed the bed's permeability (Chapter 5).
  • Tamping: compressing the espresso puck with a tamper to a uniform density and a level surface. A permeability-manufacturing step, not a strength contest: beyond full compaction, extra force changes little (Chapter 10).
  • TDS: total dissolved solids: the strength of the beverage, as a percentage. Filter ≈ 1.15–1.45%; espresso ≈ 7–12%.
  • Threshold (sensory): the smallest difference a taster can reliably detect. Frost et al.'s 0.24 percentage points TDS (Chapter 15) is the smallest gap between any two discriminable coffees in one study, a minimum estimate, not a universal threshold; in general, differences are proportional (Weber's law), with the fraction varying by sense (Chapter 21).
  • Tribology: the science of friction, wear and surfaces in contact. In coffee it governs burr–bean contact, fracture and the static charging of grounds, one of Chapter 17's seven disciplines, and the physics behind Chapter 4's burr geometry.
  • Unimodal: having one peak. Brew-oriented burr geometries push the particle size distribution toward unimodal (a single main population with the fines shoulder minimised) the opposite design goal from espresso burrs, which keep a deliberate fines share (Chapter 4).
  • WDT: Weiss Distribution Technique: stirring the dry grounds in the basket with fine needles before tamping, to break clumps and erase the density streaks that become channels (Chapter 10).

Reference · Assumptions made

Assumptions, stated.

Every number in this guide stands on assumptions. This section collects them all in one place: what each equation and chart assumes, where the model breaks down, and which numbers are measured or standard, which are model values, and which are illustrative, chosen to be plausible and clearly labelled, not measured. If you remember one rule, make it this: the shapes of the curves and the directions of the effects are the physics; the exact constants are a model's, and your coffee's will differ.

The standing assumptions: read these first
  • Models are idealisations. Particles are treated as spheres, beds as uniform, temperatures as single numbers. Real particles are jagged shards, real beds vary point to point, and a real slurry has a temperature field, not a temperature. The models predict tendencies and orders of magnitude, not your next cup to a decimal place.
  • “In this guide's model” means illustrative. Constants flagged that way, the diffusion coefficient D ≈ 2.5 × 10−9 m²/s, the activation energy Ea ≈ 16 kJ/mol (Wang & Lim 2021's coffee-specific value, applied here as one number for hundreds of compounds), the cooling time constants, the degassing pools, the bed permeabilities, are representative values chosen so the arithmetic lands in the range of real brews. They are not measurements of your coffee.
  • Measured and standard values are labelled as such. The control-chart window (18–22% EY, 1.15–1.45% TDS), the SCA water targets, the Frost study's findings and the papers in the library stand on published work, cited in References. Everything else should be read as framework.
  • Water is treated as ≈ 1 g = 1 mL. True near room temperature; at 93 °C (199 °F) water's density is ≈ 0.96 g/mL, a ~4% effect the guide ignores in ratio arithmetic, as does standard coffee practice.
  • Conversions are rounded. Imperial figures are given to two or three significant figures (1 oz = 28.35 g, 1 fl oz of water ≈ 29.6 g, °F = °C × 9/5 + 32). Rounding never changes a conclusion in the guide; where it might, the metric value governs.
  • Taste language is population language. “Trends sour”, “reads as bitter” describe what panels and most tasters report on average. Individual palates differ, Chapter 15's four preference clusters are the standing reminder.
  • Anaerobic oxygen levels are inferred, not measured (Ch. 1). Chapter 1's processing section describes sealed tanks as low in oxygen based on how the vessels are set up: sealed, with the microbes consuming what oxygen starts inside. None of the five SIAF trials consulted for that subsection, among those that describe their vessels, reports a measured oxygen concentration inside the tank. “Anaerobic” there therefore names the set-up and its expected conditions, not a quantity anyone in those trials read off an instrument.

Equation by equation
  • τ ≈ d²/D (Ch. 2): Assumes: a spherical particle, one effective D for all compounds, first-order approach to equilibrium, no instant surface wash-off. Breaks down: real particles are irregular and wash off faster than the model early on; large molecules diffuse slower than small ones, which the single D hides, the compounds chart (separate τ per class) is the partial correction. The d² scaling between sizes survives all of this.
  • Péclet number (Ch. 2): Assumes the quoted velocities and length scales. Pe ≈ 6 in the pores and ≈ 0 inside particles are order-of-magnitude statements, not measurements.
  • Extraction yield bookkeeping (Ch. 3): Assumes beverage mass is known: measured directly, or estimated with bed retention ≈ 2 g per g (filter; real range ≈ 1.4–2.6) and ≈ 1 g per g (espresso puck). Assumes the refractometer was zeroed on brew water and the sample cooled and filtered; a hot, unfiltered sample inflates TDS and every EY computed from it.
  • Darcy's law (Ch. 5, 9, 13): Assumes laminar flow (checked with the Reynolds number, Ch. 20), a rigid bed, constant permeability k during the brew, and a Newtonian fluid. Breaks down exactly where coffee gets interesting: fines migrate, pucks erode and swell, beds compact, k is really k(t, x). Treat every Darcy number here as a snapshot, and the ratio reasoning (double ΔP → double Q) as the durable part. One measured limit now qualifies even that, for espresso: the puck is poroelastic (it compacts as pressure rises) so flow plateaus above ~5 bar (73 psi) and then falls (Waszkiewicz et al. 2026, References [20]). The Darcy treatment in Chapters 5 and 9 is the rigid-bed approximation; Chapter 9's closing panel gives the correction.
  • Arrhenius law (Ch. 6): Assumes one activation energy, Ea ≈ 16 kJ/mol (Wang & Lim 2021's coffee-specific value), for what is really hundreds of compounds each with its own Ea. Your coffee's exact rate ratios will differ by compound, which is the chapter's own point about balance.
  • Newton's law of cooling (Ch. 6): Assumes a single lumped slurry temperature cooling toward a constant room temperature with one time constant τc, and no heat added mid-brew. Real pour-overs receive fresh hot pulses that partially reheat the slurry, so the chart is best read as the trajectory between pours and as a preheated-versus-cold comparison, not a second-by-second trace.
  • Laplace pressure (Ch. 12) (Assumes a single curved surface (a bubble in liquid, 2γ/r) a free soap film would be 4γ/r) and γ ≈ 0.042 N/m for warm milk (milk is 40–50 mN/m at 20 °C and falls with temperature; the 0.048 N/m figure sometimes quoted is espresso's, Illy & Navarini 2011, and is not applied to milk here). Real γ varies with temperature, fat content and protein state; the 10:1 pressure ratio between microfoam and froth sizes is robust to those changes.
  • Fick's law, flow rate, Reynolds, SA/V (Ch. 20): Fick's worked example uses an estimated internal concentration (≈ 300 g/L); the flux it produces is an initial, order-of-magnitude value. Reynolds uses representative pore velocity and size. SA/V assumes spheres, real shards have more surface per volume, so 6/d is a floor, not an exact value. The per-gram form in Chapter 4 (specific surface area) additionally assumes a single particle density, ρ ≈ 1,400 kg/m³ (87 lb/ft³) (an illustrative mid-range value for roasted coffee particles) and counts external geometric surface only; the internal pore surface is larger by orders of magnitude and is deliberately not estimated.

Chart by chart: what is drawn, and what it really is
  • Extraction kinetics chart (Ch. 2), Model curves, 30% × (1 − e−t/τ) with particle time constants τ ≈ 25 / 144 / 484 s for 250 / 600 / 1,100 µm. The 30% asymptote is the single-particle soluble share; bed-level tools use a 24% practical ceiling instead.
  • Compounds chart (Ch. 2), Model curves with class time constants τ ≈ 20 / 90 / 220 s (salts & acids / sugars / heavy bitter compounds). The ordering (acids first, heavies last) is established; the constants are illustrative.
  • Brewing control chart (Ch. 3), A real, standard framework (SCA). Its ratio lines assume the 2 g per g retention above; the preferred rectangle is a population preference from taste panels, not a physical law, plenty of excellent coffee lives outside it.
  • Particle size distribution (Ch. 4), A model: two log-normal populations (fines ≈ 60 µm · 0.002 in at ~10% of mass; main median ≈ 600 µm · 0.024 in), plotted peak-normalised. Your grinder's actual distribution differs in shares and positions; bimodality does not.
  • Drawdown, Arrhenius, cooling, degassing curves (Ch. 5–8), Models with the constants stated beside each chart. The degassing two-pool split (72% / 28%) and time constants (6 d / 40 d) are illustrative fits to the familiar pattern, not published measurements.
  • Darcy lines & pressure profile (Ch. 9), Straight Darcy lines with permeabilities chosen to pass ≈ 2 mL/s (0.07 fl oz/s) at 9 bar (131 psi); real machines add pump curves, and real pucks erode. The pressure profiles are illustrative shapes, not recorded traces.
  • Espresso-vs-filter race (Ch. 10), Effective bed-level time constants (12 s / 75 s) and a 24% practical ceiling, reconciled with Chapter 2's single-particle numbers in that chart's note. Read it as a comparison of clocks, not as two measured extractions.
  • Laplace chart (Ch. 12), Exact arithmetic from ΔP = 2γ/r at the stated γ; the microfoam/froth annotations are typical size ranges, not measurements of a specific pitcher.
  • Bed-depth profiles (Ch. 13), Schematic and illustrative, not measured: cone depth drawn falling linearly from 4.5 cm (1.77 in) at the centre to 1.5 cm (0.59 in) at the rim, the Chapter 13 worked example's numbers (real centre depth ≈ 3–4.5 cm, depth → 0 at the wall); flat bed ≈ 1.6–2.4 cm depending on footprint, deepening modestly toward the walls. Real beds settle unevenly; the centre-to-rim contrast (≈ 2.1× in flux at a 5 cm pool) is the claim, not the decimals.
  • Brewer taste bars (Ch. 14) & sensory bars (Ch. 21), Tendency visualisations summarising panel findings and experienced consensus. They are not measurements and carry no units; the Frost findings behind several of them are the measured part (Ch. 15).
  • Water targets diagram (Ch. 7), The SCA standard's ranges and targets as published; the alkalinity bar shows a narrow band around “at or near 40 mg/L (≈40 ppm)” because the standard specifies a point, not a range. The Route C recipe's resulting hardness and alkalinity are computed from the salts' molar masses assuming complete dissolution in distilled water, verify with a test kit, as the chapter instructs.
  • Four-waters diagram (Ch. 7), The built-water row is the SCA standard's targets. The soft-tap (45 / 38 mg/L · ≈45 / 38 ppm) and hard-tap (260 / 190 mg/L · ≈260 / 190 ppm) rows are plausible worked examples chosen to show the two failure shapes, not measurements of any city's supply — the chapter's instruction to test your own water is the operative content.
  • Burr geometry diagram (Ch. 4), Schematic cross-sections, not engineering drawings: tooth counts, angles and proportions are simplified to show the two particle paths. The diameter ranges quoted (flat 50–98 mm · 1.97–3.86 in; conical ≈ 38–83 mm · 1.50–3.27 in) cover common home and café burr sets, from 50 mm flat burrs (Eureka Mignon line) to 83 mm conical burrs (Weber HG-2 / KEY); the claims about distribution width are stated as tendencies because tooth design and alignment can outweigh the flat/conical family difference.
  • Surface-area-per-gram chart (Ch. 4), The 1/d curve at ρ ≈ 1,400 kg/m³ (87 lb/ft³), spheres assumed: a floor for external surface, as above. The bimodal surface split (≈ 53% of surface on ≈ 10% of mass) follows exactly from the Chapter 4 PSD model's two populations and shares; change the fines share and the split moves with it, the sensitivity is the lesson.
  • Ion-by-ion claims (Ch. 7), The cation binding ordering (Mg²⁺ strongest, then Ca²⁺, Na⁺ weakest) follows Hendon et al. 2014's computational and experimental work, and the acid-selectivity point follows Bratthäll et al. 2024, both in the library. Binding energies are compound-specific, so “strongest” is a summary across the compounds studied, not a law for every molecule in coffee.
  • Roast spectrum diagram (Ch. 1), Directional summary (solubility and porosity rise, density and chlorogenic acids fall with roast). Roast level labels are loose industry terms, not standardised quantities.
  • Sealed-tank diagram (Ch. 1, Figure 11), Schematic: the oxygen, CO₂ and pH curves are smooth shapes anchored to trial endpoints (pH 5.8 to 4.4 within 72 hours; runs lasting up to 192 hours; oxygen consumed early), not traces measured in a single tank. The ideal-gas worked example uses an illustrative amount of CO₂ (0.5 mol) to size the pressure effect, and the growth example uses an illustrative doubling time of 1 hour; microbial growth speeding up with warmth is stated as a general rule of thumb, not a rate measured in coffee.

Where the whole framework stops
  • Immersion brewing is out of scope for the flow models. French press and cupping have no percolation; Darcy's law and drawdown say nothing there, though diffusion and temperature still apply.
  • The Frost geometry results come from drip-machine baskets. Direction transfers to hand pour-over; magnitudes may not (Chapter 15's caveats).
  • Nothing here models an individual coffee. Variety, processing, roast and age move every constant. The guide's claim is narrower and stronger: the structure of the problem (which variable pushes which way, and roughly how hard) is the same for every coffee.
  • Sensory thresholds are population estimates. Your threshold is yours; the brew log in Next Steps is how you measure it.

Reference · Bibliography

References & further reading.

Numbered sources for the guide's measured and standard claims. The twelve papers of Chapter 19's library appear here as [3]–[14], Frost et al. [14], the evidence base of Chapters 15 and 21, was added to the library in this edition; each DOI is a permanent link to the paper. Frameworks and standards follow, then a short further-reading list keyed to the chapters. Additions in this edition ([15]–[20]) are the 2024–2026 papers woven into Chapters 4, 5 and 9. A further addition, [21]–[25], covers anaerobic processing in Chapter 1, and [26]–[33] cover the washed, natural, honey and aerobic methods in the same processing section. This edition adds [44]–[47]: Lockhart's 1957 primary paper behind the control chart, the 2023 Guinard et al. revision of that chart, Scott Rao's extraction books, and the Coffee Ad Astra experiment archive. The audit edition adds [34]–[43]: Wang & Lim (the activation energy of Chapter 6), Corrochano (espresso permeability, Chapter 9), Wadsworth (percolation and permeability, Chapters 5 and 20), Batali (bitterness in brew fractions, Chapters 2 and 21), and the correctly attributed fermentation papers (Martins, da Silva Vale, Silva, Jimenez, Soares, Fu). Where a claim in the guide rests on a video, on industry data or on a community experiment rather than a journal, the chapter labels it at the point of use (peer-reviewed, technical education, industry data, or hypothesis) and the further-reading list below carries the links.

  31. Cafe Imports. Processing 101. Importer's guide to the washed, natural and honey methods, Chapter 1's processing section: the step order of each method and what stays on the seed while it dries.
  32. Particular Coffee. Fermentation science. Guide to coffee fermentation, Chapter 1's processing section: the microbial sequence in a washed ferment (yeasts first, then lactic acid bacteria, then acetic acid bacteria) and pH falling from about 6.0 to 6.5 to about 4.0.
  33. Expert Cafe. Fermentation guide. Guide to aerobic coffee fermentation, Chapter 1's processing section: open-tank runs of 12 to 36 hours, temperature setting the clock (24 to 36 hours at 20 °C, about 12 hours at 30 °C, 48 to 72 hours at 10 to 15 °C), a clean-ferment pH target of 3.8 to 4.5, and vinegary over-fermentation below pH 3.5.
  34. Wang, X. & Lim, J. (2021). Modeling study of coffee extraction at different temperature and grind size conditions to better understand the cold and hot brewing process. Journal of Food Process Engineering 44, e13748. Reports an overall activation energy of ≈ 16 kJ/mol, the coffee-specific value this guide's Arrhenius model uses. doi:10.1111/jfpe.13748, Chapters 2 and 6.
  35. Corrochano, B. R. et al. (2015). A new methodology to estimate the steady-state permeability of roast and ground coffee in packed beds. Journal of Food Engineering 150, 106–116. Steady-state permeability values of 2.6 × 10−14 to 3.4 × 10−13 m². doi:10.1016/j.jfoodeng.2014.11.006, Chapter 9.
  36. Wadsworth et al. (2026). A model for the permeability of coffee pucks validated using X-ray computed micro-tomography. Royal Society Open Science 13, 252031. Near the percolation threshold, k falls much faster than the fixed-porosity square law. doi:10.1098/rsos.252031, Chapters 5 and 20.
  37. Batali, M. E. et al. (2020). Sensory and monosaccharide analysis of drip brew coffee fractions versus brewing time. Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture. In-cup bitterness is highest in the earliest, strongest fractions and falls as TDS falls. doi:10.1002/jsfa.10323, Chapters 2 and 21.
  38. Martins, P. M. M. et al. (2020). Coffee Growing Altitude Influences the Microbiota, Chemical Compounds and the Quality of Fermented Coffees. Food Research International 129, 108872. With da Mota et al. (2020) [22], among the first applications of self-induced anaerobic fermentation (SIAF) to coffee. Chapter 1's anaerobic section.
  39. da Silva Vale, A. S. et al. (2023). SIAF trial in which all coffees scored 84 points or more and pH fell from 5.8 to 4.4 in 72 hours. Foods 12, 37. doi:10.3390/foods12010037, Chapter 1's anaerobic section.
  40. Silva et al. (2024). SIAF trial reporting the best score of 87.50 (whole cherries, no water, 96 hours) against 83.30 natural and 83.60 pulped controls. Foods 13, 653. doi:10.3390/foods13050653, Chapter 1's anaerobic section.
  41. Jimenez et al. (2023). SIAF study reporting 13.20 g/kg lactic acid in dried natural coffee after 180 hours, and seed viability falling from 85–87.5% to 52.5–70% by 180 hours. Food Bioscience. doi:10.1016/j.fbio.2022.102218, Chapter 1's anaerobic section.
  42. Soares et al. (2025). Review of coffee fermentation science. Trends in Food Science & Technology. doi:10.1016/j.tifs.2025.105151, Chapter 1's processing section.
  43. Fu, X. et al. (2026). Metabolome analysis of processing methods regulating flavor precursors in Arabica coffee beans and correlation with sensory attributes. Beverage Plant Research 6, e029. (Yu and Hu are the paper's senior and corresponding authors; Fu is first author.) doi:10.48130/bpr-0026-0010, Chapter 1's processing section.
  44. Lockhart, E. E. (1957). The soluble solids in beverage coffee as an index to cup quality. Coffee Brewing Institute, New York. The primary source behind reference [1] and Chapter 3: the taste-panel work that tied cup quality to measured soluble solids and fixed the control chart's centre near 55 g/L (about 1:18). (A Coffee Brewing Institute publication; it carries no DOI.)
  45. Guinard, J.-X., Frost, S., Batali, M., Cotter, A., Lim, L. X. & Ristenpart, W. D. (2023). A new Coffee Brewing Control Chart relating sensory properties and consumer liking to brew strength, extraction yield, and brew ratio. Journal of Food Science 88(5), 2168–2177. doi:10.1111/1750-3841.16531. The 2023 sensory and consumer revision of the chart. This guide keeps the 2019 Version-3 chart [1] as its working framework, the version most refractometer software prints. Chapter 3.
  46. Rao, S. (2010). Everything but Espresso. Scott Rao Coffee Books; and Rao, S. (2020). Coffee Roasting: Best Practices. Scott Rao Coffee Books. The practitioner extraction frameworks (strength, yield and evenness, measured with a refractometer) behind the applied side of Chapters 3, 9 and 10; Rao's imprint also publishes Gagné's books in the further-reading list below. (Books; they carry no DOI.)
  47. Gagné, J. Coffee Ad Astra, the experiment archive behind many of this guide's percolation, bypass and temperature claims: coffeeadastra.com. Experiments are published there with their methods and data, which is what makes them citable; the chapters that use them label them technical education or hypothesis. Chapters 4, 5, 13 and 14.

  • Chapters 2, 5, 6 (the physics core), Ristenpart, W. D. & Kuhl, T. L., The Design of Coffee: An Engineering Approach (Ristenpart/Kuhl Publishing via CreateSpace Independent Publishing Platform, ISBN 9781537305578; 1st ed. 11 September 2015, 2nd ed. 14 September 2016, with a revised 2nd-edition printing dated 2017; self-published by the UC Davis authors, not published by UC Davis), the engineering textbook behind Part 4's framing; Gagné, J., The Physics of Filter Coffee (Scott Rao Coffee Books, 2021) and The Physics of Espresso (2025), and the Coffee Ad Astra experiments, percolation, temperature and geometry worked in depth.

  • Chapters 4, 9, 10 (grind & espresso practice), Cameron et al. [9] above, then the technical educators of Chapter 18: Hoffmann on method and equipment testing, Hedrick on burrs and distribution, Rao on extraction frameworks, Perger on particle size.
  • Chapters 9–10, on video (technical education), James Hoffmann's Understanding Espresso six-part series (2020), dose, ratio, time, grind, temperature, pressure, one variable per episode, the video companion to Part 2, and How to Dial in Espresso. Lance Hedrick: The 9 Bar Fallacy (Chapter 9's closing panel), Understanding Espresso Extraction, the WDT technique video (Chapter 10), and 58mm is a Mistake — basket diameter as bed geometry, the espresso echo of Part 3.
  • Chapters 5 and 13–14, on video (technical education), Hoffmann's The Ultimate V60 Technique and A Better 1 Cup V60 Technique: pour height, agitation and drawdown as practised craft, compare the jet-and-avalanche measurements of Park et al. [17].
  • Chapter 12, on video (technical education), Hoffmann, The Beginner's Guide to Latte Art (2025): milk texture and the pour, demonstrated against Chapter 12's bubble physics.
  • Books, the sequels and the water reference, Gagné, J., The Physics of Espresso (Scott Rao Coffee Books, published 2025, announced 14 August 2025, ISBN 9798350747737), the 196-page sequel to The Physics of Filter Coffee (Scott Rao Coffee Books, January 2021, ISBN 9780578246086, 249 pages, 11 chapters; some retailers list 250 or 251 pages counting front matter), applying the same programme to the puck (announcement and contents, Coffee ad Astra). Maxwell Colonna-Dashwood & Christopher H. Hendon, Water for Coffee (2015, self-published), Chapter 7's subject at book length, following the authors' 2014 paper (Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry 62, 4947–4950) [3]: in their binding calculations Mg²⁺ holds flavour compounds more strongly than Ca²⁺ or Na⁺, read alongside the measured caution of Bratthäll, Figueira & Nording [12].
  • Chapter 21 (the senses), the shared vocabulary, the World Coffee Research Sensory Lexicon (110 defined attributes; 1st edition 2016, version 2.0 October 2017, created at the Kansas State University Sensory Analysis Center, Edgar Chambers IV's lab), the SCA Coffee Taster's Flavor Wheel (first published 1995 by the SCAA, redesigned in 2016 with World Coffee Research), and the SCA Coffee Value Assessment: published June 2024 and adopted 4 November 2024 as Standards 102-2024 (preparation and mechanics), 103-2024 (descriptive), 104-2024 (affective) and 105-2025 (extrinsic), with a descriptive form using 15-point scales across 7 sections and a 9-point affective form that is the only source of the score: the standards behind Chapter 21's flavour families, summarised at Coffearium, flavour language and how we taste coffee (the ortho- vs. retronasal routes of Chapter 21).
  • Creator experiments & community findings (hypothesis-grade, labelled where used), Robert McKeon Aloe (@espressofun), blind vs. regular burrs on a Zerno Z1 (Instagram, November 2025), and Sprometheus's Z1 blind-burr tests via Perfect Daily Grind (December 2025), Chapter 4. Decent Espresso, “The Nine-Bar Question” (Instagram, August 2026), logged shots with flow peaking near 4.5–5 bar, Chapter 9. Science Sphere, “Pouring higher makes stronger coffee” (Instagram, September 2026), the popular summary of [17], sceptical comments included, Chapter 5. The Home-Barista “soup” thread, low-pressure technique for ultra-light roasts, Chapter 10.
  • Part 3 (geometry), Frost et al. [14] first; Patrik Rolf's April brewer writings for the maker's side of the same questions.

Legal & disclaimer.

It is not professional, technical, engineering, medical, dietary or commercial advice, and it is not a substitute for the instructions of your equipment's manufacturer or for qualified professional guidance. What you brew, build or modify on the basis of this guide is your own decision and responsibility.
