The research this guide rests on is cited where it is used and listed in full in References & further reading and the Chapter 19 library, with authors, journals, years and DOI or publisher links, so any claim can be traced to its source. Frameworks and standards are named with their owners — principally the Specialty Coffee Association (the brewing control chart framework and the water quality standard) and World Coffee Research (the Sensory Lexicon). Photographs are credited by source in the footer of this page. Videos and social-media posts by educators and creators (including James Hoffmann and Lance Hedrick) are linked, not copied, and remain the property of their creators; creator experiments are labelled as such where the guide relies on them, and are presented as hypotheses, not findings.
  • Fair use & cited material. This guide quotes, paraphrases and summarises published research, standards and educational material briefly, with attribution, for the non-commercial purposes of teaching, commentary and review, the kind of use copyright law generally treats as fair use / fair dealing. No paper, book, video or post is reproduced in substantial part, and no paywall is circumvented: readers are sent to the original sources, which are the authoritative versions. If you are a rights holder and believe any material here exceeds fair use or is misattributed, contact the author through the site where you found this guide; the material will be reviewed and, where appropriate, corrected or removed promptly.

Every diagram, chart, flow diagram, gauge and illustration in this guide, including the flavour wheel in Chapter 21, which is an original schematic organised around the published SCA / World Coffee Research flavour vocabulary, was drawn for this guide from the underlying published science and standard frameworks. None reproduces a figure, table or image from any paper, book or website. Where a visual is a model rather than a measurement, the note beside it and the Assumptions Made section say so.

Espresso machines involve near-boiling water, steam and pressures around 9 bar (131 psi); grinders have fast-moving burrs; kettles and boilers are electrical appliances used around water. Reference · Figures & Tables

Every visual, one shelf.

Every figure and table in the guide, gathered in one place and shown again in full, each with its number, its chapter, a plain-language description of what it shows and what to take from it, and a link back to where it lives in the text. The same numbered captions appear under the originals, so a figure means the same thing in both places. Charts that respond to the guide's calculators and sliders are shown as they first load; open the original to play with it.

About this guide. The Physics of Coffee is an independent, educational guide to the technical principles of brewing, Part 1 on filter, Part 2 on espresso and latte art, Part 3 on pour-over brewer geometry, Part 4 on the science behind it, its disciplines, researchers, published library, models and experimental method. Charts are either the coffee field's standard measurement frameworks or physical models with their assumptions stated beside them; treat the models as maps, not territory, and verify with a refractometer and your own palate.

Image sources (the retailer and product pages the images came from; these are image sources, not photographer credits): hero, Focco Coffee brewing guide; grounds, Pexels; roasted beans, ArtofIt image gallery; espresso extraction, Brew Espresso Coffee; Hario V60, Fussey & Baer; Origami Dripper, Café La Maison J; Kalita Wave, Temple Coffee; Orea V3, The Basic Barista. Frameworks referenced: the brewing control chart and water quality targets of the Specialty Coffee Association; basket-geometry findings from Frost, Ristenpart & Guinard (2019), Journal of Food Science. Part 4’s profiles, paper library and evidence policy follow the “Scientific and Engineering Principles of Specialty Coffee” knowledge base supplied with this guide; paper DOIs are reproduced exactly as given there.
